body_mass_index_bmi.title: Body Mass Index (BMI)
body_mass_index_bmi.summary: Weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. A screening index of relative weight — not a measure of body composition, adiposity, or individual health.

bands.label: Severe thinness
bands.action: Assess for undernutrition; see SAM/MAM artifacts

warnings: Not valid in pregnancy, ascites, gross oedema, amputation, or high muscle mass.
Paediatric interpretation requires age- and sex-specific z-scores, NOT these adult bands.
limitations: WHO adult cut-points; Asian populations often use lower action points (23 / 27.5).
Does not distinguish fat from lean mass or describe fat distribution.

flashcards.a: Weight (kg) ÷ height (m)²
Obesity — class I 30–34.9, II 35–39.9, III ≥40

flashcards.q: Name four states that invalidate BMI.
flashcards.a: Pregnancy, ascites, gross oedema, amputation (also high muscle mass)

sources: WHO. Obesity: preventing and managing the global epidemic. WHO Technical Report Series 894.

body_surface_area_bsa.title: Body Surface Area (BSA)
body_surface_area_bsa.summary: Square root of (height in cm × weight in kg ÷ 3600). The most widely used BSA estimate for drug dosing and physiological indexing.
warnings: BSA-based cytotoxic dosing must be independently double-checked and countersigned.
Different BSA formulae (Mosteller, Du Bois, Haycock, Boyd) give different answers — the prescribing protocol dictates which is valid.
limitations: Extremes of body habitus reduce accuracy.
Capping/adjusted BSA policies vary by centre.

flashcards.a: √(height cm × weight kg / 3600)

sources: Mosteller RD. Simplified calculation of body-surface area. N Engl J Med 1987;317:1098.

ideal_and_adjusted_body_weight.title: Ideal and Adjusted Body Weight
ideal_and_adjusted_body_weight.summary: Devine ideal body weight with adjusted body weight for obesity. Used where lean mass governs dosing (e.g. aminoglycosides, tidal volume).
warnings: Never assume one weight fits all drugs — check the drug monograph for which weight applies (actual, ideal, adjusted, or lean).
Lung-protective ventilation uses PREDICTED body weight by height and sex, not actual weight.
limitations: Not validated below 152 cm height; extrapolation is convention, not evidence.

flashcards.q: Which weight is used for lung-protective tidal volume?
flashcards.a: Predicted body weight (from height and sex) — 6 mL/kg PBW

muac_arm_circumference_for_malnutrition.title: MUAC — Arm Circumference for Malnutrition
muac_arm_circumference_for_malnutrition.summary: Circumference at the midpoint of the left upper arm. A standalone admission criterion for acute malnutrition in children 6–59 months, independent of weight-for-height.

bands.label: Severe acute malnutrition (SAM)
bands.action: Admit to therapeutic feeding; assess for complications and appetite

bands.label: Moderate acute malnutrition (MAM)
bands.action: Supplementary feeding programme

warnings: MUAC cut-offs above apply to children 6–59 months only.
Bilateral pitting oedema means SAM regardless of MUAC — always inspect both feet.
Adult and pregnancy MUAC thresholds differ and must come from the national protocol.
limitations: Tape must be non-stretch; arm relaxed; measured at the midpoint between acromion and olecranon.
Inter-observer variation is a known source of misclassification.

flashcards.q: MUAC cut-off for SAM in 6–59 months?

flashcards.a: No — bilateral pitting oedema is SAM whatever the MUAC

checkboxes: Midpoint marked between acromion and olecranon
Both feet checked for bilateral pitting oedema

sources: WHO guideline on the prevention and management of wasting and nutritional oedema in infants and children under 5 years, 2023.
governance.nigeria_overlay: Confirm against the current National Guideline for CMAM (Community Management of Acute Malnutrition), Federal Ministry of Health.

creatinine_clearance_cockcroft_gault.title: Creatinine Clearance (Cockcroft-Gault)
creatinine_clearance_cockcroft_gault.summary: Estimates creatinine clearance from age, weight, sex and serum creatinine. Still the reference equation for many drug-dosing licences even where eGFR is reported.

logic.note: CrCl (mL/min) = [(140 − age) × weight × F] / (0.814 × SCr µmol/L); F = 1.0 male, 0.85 female. If SCr in mg/dL: [(140−age)×wt×F]/(72×SCr).

warnings: Unreliable in acute kidney injury — creatinine lags behind true GFR.
Unreliable at extremes of muscle mass, amputation, and in advanced liver disease.
Which weight to use (actual, ideal, adjusted) is drug-specific — check the monograph.
limitations: Not indexed to body surface area; eGFR (CKD-EPI) is indexed and the two are NOT interchangeable for dosing.

flashcards.q: Why is Cockcroft-Gault unreliable in AKI?
flashcards.a: Serum creatinine has not equilibrated — it lags the true fall in GFR

anion_gap_albumin_corrected.title: Anion Gap (albumin-corrected)
anion_gap_albumin_corrected.summary: Sodium minus chloride minus bicarbonate, corrected for albumin. Separates high-anion-gap from normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

bands.label: Raised — high anion gap metabolic acidosis
bands.action: Work through GOLDMARK / MUDPILES

warnings: Correct for albumin. Every 10 g/L fall in albumin lowers the measured gap by about 2.5 mmol/L, masking a real acidosis.
The 2024 ADA consensus REMOVED anion gap from the DKA diagnostic and resolution criteria — use beta-hydroxybutyrate where available.
limitations: Whether potassium is included changes the reference range — state the convention used.
Laboratory method for chloride affects the gap.

flashcards.a: Add 2.5 mmol/L for every 10 g/L that albumin is below 40 g/L
Glycols, Oxoproline, L-lactate, D-lactate, Methanol, Aspirin, Renal failure, Ketoacidosis

flashcards.q: Is anion gap still a DKA criterion?
flashcards.a: No — removed in the 2024 ADA consensus; beta-hydroxybutyrate is preferred

sources: Umpierrez GE et al. Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report. Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275.

osmolality_and_osmolar_gap.title: Osmolality and Osmolar Gap
osmolality_and_osmolar_gap.summary: Calculated osmolality (2Na + glucose + urea) versus measured. Effective osmolality omits urea and is the value used in HHS criteria.

logic.note: Calculated total = 2×Na + glucose + urea (all mmol/L). Effective (tonicity) = 2×Na + glucose. Gap = measured − calculated total.

bands.label: Raised osmolar gap
bands.action: Consider toxic alcohols, mannitol, glycine, severe ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis

warnings: If glucose or urea are reported in mg/dL they must be converted first (glucose ÷ 18; urea/BUN ÷ 2.8) — silently mixing units is a known serious error.
A normal osmolar gap does NOT exclude toxic alcohol ingestion late in the course, when the parent alcohol has been metabolised.
limitations: Several published variants of the formula exist; gap thresholds are method-dependent.

flashcards.a: 2 × Na + glucose (mmol/L) — urea is excluded because it crosses membranes freely
Effective osmolality >300 mOsm/kg OR total >320 mOsm/kg

sources: Umpierrez GE et al. Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275 (HHS osmolality criteria).

corrected_sodium_in_high_sugar.title: Corrected Sodium (in high sugar)
corrected_sodium_in_high_sugar.summary: Hyperglycaemia draws water into the extracellular space and dilutes measured sodium. Correction reveals the true sodium and therefore the true water deficit.

logic.note: Katz: Na_corr = Na + 1.6 × [(glucose mmol/L − 5.5) / 5.5]. Hillier: factor 2.4 instead of 1.6.

warnings: A rising corrected sodium during DKA/HHS treatment is expected and does NOT by itself mean under-resuscitation.
Do not let sodium fall by more than about 10 mmol/L in 24 hours in HHS — rapid correction risks cerebral oedema.
limitations: Katz and Hillier disagree; state which was used. Neither is validated across all glucose ranges.

flashcards.a: 1.6 mmol/L Na per 5.5 mmol/L glucose above normal

corrected_calcium.title: Corrected Calcium
corrected_calcium.summary: Adjusts total calcium for albumin binding. Ionised calcium remains the definitive measurement where available.

bands.label: Hypocalcaemia
bands.action: Check magnesium, phosphate, vitamin D, PTH, renal function

bands.label: Severe hypercalcaemia
bands.action: Treat as an emergency — see hypercalcaemia pathway

warnings: Correction formulae perform poorly in critical illness, renal failure and acid-base disturbance — measure ionised calcium if the result will change management.
limitations: The 0.02 coefficient (mmol/L per g/L) is a population average; local laboratories may publish a different factor.

flashcards.a: Measured Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin g/L)

fena_prerenal_or_atn.title: FENa — Prerenal or ATN?
fena_prerenal_or_atn.summary: Compares sodium and creatinine handling in urine and plasma. Helps separate pre-renal from intrinsic (tubular) causes of acute kidney injury.
warnings: Invalid if diuretics have been given — use fractional excretion of urea (FEUrea; <35% suggests pre-renal) instead.
limitations: Misleading in CKD, obstruction, sepsis, and non-oliguric AKI.

flashcards.a: Pre-renal azotaemia
Recent diuretic use — use FEUrea instead

iv_fluid_drip_rate_ml_h_drops_min.title: IV Fluid Drip Rate (mL/h ↔ drops/min)
iv_fluid_drip_rate_ml_h_drops_min.summary: Pure arithmetic conversion between an ordered rate in mL per hour and a gravity-set drop rate. This artifact converts; it does not decide what fluid or what rate a patient should receive.

body.how_to_use_the_answer: Count the drops in the drip chamber for a full 60 seconds and adjust the roller clamp until you get this number. Recheck at every observation round.

inputs.label: Volume to infuse
inputs.note: How much fluid to give, in mL. Example: one 500 mL bag = 500.

inputs.label: Time
inputs.note: Over how many hours. Example: '500 mL over 4 hours' = 4. For 8-hourly bags, put 8.

inputs.label: Administration-set drop factor
inputs.note: Look at the giving set packet. It says something like '20 drops/mL'. Put that number here. Common ones: 20 for a normal adult set, 60 for a paediatric microdrip or burette, 15 on many blood sets. Do not guess — packets differ by brand.

warnings: READ THE DROP FACTOR OFF THE PACKET OF THE SET YOU ARE ACTUALLY USING. There is no standard number. A wrong drop factor is a wrong dose.
Blood sets are not the same as ordinary fluid sets. A blood set has a filter inside and its own drop factor printed on it. Do not use the number from a normal giving set.
A gravity drip drifts. If the bag is lowered, the patient turns, or the cannula kinks, the rate changes on its own. Recount the drops every time you do observations.

For some drugs the drip rate IS the dose — go too fast and you overdose the patient. This applies to insulin, potassium, adrenaline and other blood-pressure drugs, and oxytocin. For these, use an infusion pump or syringe driver (a machine that controls the rate itself). If no pump is available, say so in the notes, use a burette or paediatric microdrip set, and have someone watch the drip.
Potassium is the one people get wrong most often. Never give it as a fast push or a free-running drip. Follow the ward protocol for how much per hour and how much to dilute it.
limitations: Arithmetic only. It carries no opinion on the appropriateness of the volume, the fluid, or the duration.

flashcards.a: (Volume mL ÷ time hours) × drop factor ÷ 60

flashcards.q: Standard adult solution set drop factor?
flashcards.a: Commonly 20 drops/mL — but always verify on the packet
60 drops/mL, so mL/h equals drops/min

checkboxes: Fluid checked against the prescription (name, strength, volume)
Drop factor read from THIS set's packaging
Rate counted over a full 60 seconds

child_maintenance_fluid_4_2_1_rule.title: Child Maintenance Fluid (4-2-1 Rule)
child_maintenance_fluid_4_2_1_rule.summary: Weight-based maintenance water requirement. Maintenance is not resuscitation and not deficit replacement — the three are calculated and prescribed separately.

logic.note: First 10 kg: 100 mL/kg/day (4 mL/kg/h). Next 10 kg: 50 mL/kg/day (2 mL/kg/h). Each kg above 20: 20 mL/kg/day (1 mL/kg/h).

warnings: Isotonic fluid with glucose is now standard for maintenance in children. Hypotonic maintenance fluid has caused fatal hyponatraemic encephalopathy.
Reduce or withhold maintenance in SIADH, cardiac failure, oliguric renal failure, and raised intracranial pressure.
Severe acute malnutrition uses entirely different fluid rules (ReSoMal) — do NOT apply 4-2-1 to a child with SAM.
limitations: Derived from healthy-child energy expenditure; sick children rarely match the assumption.
Ongoing losses (vomiting, diarrhoea, stoma, drain, burns, fever) must be added separately.

flashcards.a: 4 mL/kg/h for first 10 kg, 2 mL/kg/h for next 10 kg, 1 mL/kg/h thereafter

flashcards.q: Maintenance fluid for a 26 kg child per hour?

flashcards.a: Risk of hospital-acquired hyponatraemia and cerebral oedema

sources: Holliday MA, Segar WE. The maintenance need for water in parenteral fluid therapy. Pediatrics 1957;19:823-32.

blood_transfusion_units_volumes_and_drip.title: Blood Transfusion — Units, Volumes and Drip Rate
blood_transfusion_units_volumes_and_drip.summary: Whole blood and packed red cells are DIFFERENT products with different volumes, haematocrits and indications. Conflating them is a documented cause of transfusion error.

terms: blood component reference — whole blood vs packed red cells
blood transfusion — units, volumes and drip rate

components.typical_volume_ml: ≈450–500 mL donation + ≈63 mL anticoagulant-preservative → ≈510–560 mL unit
components.main_use: Where component therapy is unavailable; some massive-haemorrhage protocols

components.expected_effect_adult: Hb rise ≈1 g/dL per unit in a 70 kg adult
components.main_use: Correction of symptomatic anaemia / oxygen-carrying capacity
Multiple factor deficiency with bleeding; massive transfusion
Thrombocytopenic bleeding; prevention at protocol thresholds

components.expected_effect_adult: Source of fibrinogen, FVIII, vWF, FXIII, fibronectin

paediatric_dosing.note: Small-volume paediatric transfusion must be pump- or syringe-controlled, never a free-running counting drops by eye.

warnings: THE FIGURES ABOVE ARE INDICATIVE RANGES. The volume printed on the actual unit label is the operative figure — always read the label.
Whole blood ≠ packed cells. They differ in volume, haematocrit, and expected haemoglobin increment.
Positive patient identification at the bedside, against the unit and the compatibility label, is the single highest-yield step in preventing fatal ABO-incompatible transfusion.
Observe closely for the first 15 minutes — most fatal acute reactions declare themselves early.
Never add drugs to a blood unit. Never co-infuse anything other than 0.9% sodium chloride through the same line unless local policy explicitly permits it.
limitations: Volumes and haematocrits differ between national blood services and between additive solutions.
Expected haemoglobin increment assumes no ongoing bleeding, haemolysis or splenic sequestration.

flashcards.q: Expected Hb rise from one PRBC unit in an adult?
flashcards.a: About 1 g/dL
10–20 mL/kg

flashcards.q: When do most fatal acute transfusion reactions declare themselves?
flashcards.a: In the first 15 minutes

flashcards.q: Which fluid may share a line with blood?
flashcards.a: 0.9% sodium chloride only, unless local policy states otherwise

checkboxes: Group and screen / crossmatch sample correctly labelled at the bedside
Unit label checked against patient identity band by two staff
Expiry date and pack integrity checked
Patient observed continuously for first 15 minutes
Observations at 15 min, then per protocol
Completion time recorded; unit bag retained per policy

governance.nigeria_overlay: Verify component specifications and volumes against the National Blood Service Commission (NBSC) standards and the transfusing facility's blood bank SOP.

also_known_as: blood component reference — whole blood vs packed red cells

transfusion_reaction_what_to_do_now.title: Transfusion Reaction — What To Do Now
transfusion_reaction_what_to_do_now.summary: Structured immediate response to a suspected acute transfusion reaction. The first action is always to stop the transfusion and keep the line open with saline.

terms: acute transfusion reaction — recognition and immediate response
transfusion reaction — what to do now

immediate_actions: Maintain venous access with 0.9% sodium chloride through a NEW giving set.
ABCDE assessment; call for senior help.
Recheck patient identity against the unit and compatibility label.
Record full observations including temperature, pulse, BP, respiratory rate, SpO₂, urine output and colour.

differentiation.features: Fever, rigors, loin/back pain, dark urine, hypotension, bleeding from puncture sites, sense of impending doom
differentiation.action: Stop. Resuscitate. Notify blood bank urgently. Return unit and set. Send repeat group/crossmatch, FBC, LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin, coagulation, DAT, urine for haemoglobin. Support renal perfusion.

differentiation.features: Temperature rise ≥1 °C, chills, no failing circulation — low BP, fast pulse, cold peripheries
differentiation.action: Stop and reassess to exclude serious causes. fever medicine like paracetamol. May cautiously restart only per policy.

differentiation.features: Urticaria alone (mild) → angio-oedema, stridor, wheeze, hypotension (severe)
differentiation.action: Mild: stop, antihistamine, may restart slowly. Severe: STOP permanently, adrenaline IM, full anaphylaxis pathway.

differentiation.features: Dyspnoea, orthopnoea, raised JVP, hypertension, positive fluid balance, bibasal crackles
differentiation.action: Stop or slow. Sit up. Oxygen. Diuretic. Careful fluid balance.

differentiation.features: Acute hypoxaemia, bilateral infiltrates, usually NOT volume overloaded, often hypotensive
differentiation.action: Stop. Respiratory support, may need ventilation. Notify blood service — donor implicated.
Stop. Cultures from patient and unit. Broad-spectrum antibiotics. Sepsis pathway.

always: Report every reaction to the blood bank and through the haemovigilance system.
Retain the unit, giving set and any remaining components for investigation.
Document the reaction, timing, actions and outcome in the record.

warnings: Fever plus hypotension during transfusion is acute haemolysis or sepsis until proven otherwise — do not assume a simple febrile reaction.
TACO and TRALI are frequently confused. TACO is volume-overloaded and usually hypertensive; TRALI is usually not volume-overloaded and often hypotensive.

flashcards.q: First action in a suspected transfusion reaction?
flashcards.a: Stop the transfusion; keep the line open with saline via a new set

flashcards.q: TACO vs TRALI on blood pressure?
flashcards.a: TACO usually hypertensive and fluid-overloaded; TRALI usually hypotensive and not overloaded

also_known_as: acute transfusion reaction — recognition and immediate response

mean_arterial_pressure_map.title: Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP)
mean_arterial_pressure_map.summary: Diastolic pressure plus one third of the pulse pressure. The perfusion pressure most often used as a resuscitation target.

bands.label: Below the usual adult resuscitation target
bands.action: Reassess perfusion, volume status and vasoactive support

bands.label: At or above the usual adult resuscitation target

warnings: The 65 mmHg target is a general adult sepsis default. Individualise — higher targets may be needed in chronic hypertension, and paediatric targets are age-dependent.
limitations: The one-third approximation degrades at extremes of heart rate and in aortic regurgitation.

flashcards.a: DBP + (SBP − DBP)/3
≥65 mmHg

cerebral_perfusion_pressure_cpp.title: Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP)
cerebral_perfusion_pressure_cpp.summary: Mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure. The driving pressure for cerebral blood flow.

bands.label: Below common target range
bands.action: Optimise MAP and lower ICP; escalate

bands.label: Common target range for severe TBI
Above common target — beware ARDS risk from aggressive pressure augmentation

warnings: Both MAP and ICP must be zeroed and referenced at the same anatomical level (usually the foramen of Monro / tragus) or the CPP is meaningless.
Targets are population defaults; autoregulation status varies between patients and over time.

flashcards.a: MAP − ICP

flashcards.q: Usual CPP target in severe TBI?
flashcards.a: 60–70 mmHg

glasgow_coma_scale_gcs.title: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
glasgow_coma_scale_gcs.summary: Eye, verbal and motor responses scored 3–15. Report the three components separately — the total alone hides clinically important patterns.

bands.label: Severe impairment of consciousness
bands.action: Airway is at risk — assess need for definitive airway; urgent imaging and senior review

warnings: GCS ≤8 conventionally signals an unprotected airway. Airway decisions rest on clinical assessment, not on the number alone.
Always record the components (E, V, M), the best response, and the side/limb tested.
Sedation, paralysis, intoxication, hypoglycaemia, hypoxia and dysphasia all confound the score — exclude and correct reversible causes first.
Children require the Paediatric GCS with an age-appropriate verbal scale.
limitations: Inter-rater variability is well documented, particularly in the verbal and abnormal-flexion categories.
Not designed as a prognostic instrument in isolation.

flashcards.a: Eye 4, Verbal 5, Motor 6 — total 15
5 = localises to pressure; 4 = normal flexion/withdrawal
3 — there is no zero
Motor 2 (extension)

checkboxes: Best response recorded for each component
Untestable components marked NT (not scored as 1)
Pupil size and reactivity recorded alongside
Trend recorded, not a single reading

curb_65_pneumonia_severity.title: CURB-65 — Pneumonia Severity
curb_65_pneumonia_severity.summary: Five equally weighted adverse features predicting 30-day death rate in community-acquired pneumonia. A severity aid, not an admission instruction.

inputs.label: Systolic BP <90 mmHg or diastolic ≤60 mmHg

bands.label: Low severity — outpatient management often appropriate
High severity — assess for critical care
bands.action: Urgent senior review

warnings: CURB-65 does not account for hypoxaemia, coillness and disability, social circumstances, or ability to take oral therapy — all of which may override the score.
Not validated in immunocompromised patients, hospital-acquired pneumonia, or children.
CRB-65 (omitting urea) is the version for settings without immediate biochemistry.
limitations: Derived in European populations; local death rate and resource context differ.

flashcards.a: Confusion, Urea >7, Respiratory rate ≥30, Blood pressure low, age ≥65
High severity — consider critical care assessment

wells_score_dvt.title: Wells Score — DVT
wells_score_dvt.summary: Pre-test probability for DVT. Determines whether D-dimer or immediate imaging is the appropriate next step.

terms: wells score for deep vein thrombosis

inputs.label: Active cancer (treatment within 6 months or palliative)
Paralysis, paresis, or recent plaster immobilisation of a leg
Recently bedridden ≥3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks
Localised tenderness along the deep venous system
Calf swelling >3 cm compared with the asymptomatic leg
Pitting oedema confined to the symptomatic leg
Alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT

bands.label: DVT unlikely
bands.action: D-dimer; if negative, DVT effectively excluded

bands.label: DVT likely
bands.action: Proceed to compression ultrasound

warnings: D-dimer is non-specific and rises in pregnancy, sepsis, malignancy, recent surgery and older age. A raised D-dimer alone never diagnoses DVT.
A negative D-dimer does not exclude DVT in the 'likely' group — image them.
limitations: Not validated in pregnancy or in patients already anticoagulated.

flashcards.a: DVT likely — proceed to compression ultrasound
An alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT

also_known_as: wells score for deep vein thrombosis

cha_ds_vasc_af_stroke_risk.title: CHA₂DS₂-VASc — AF Stroke Risk
cha_ds_vasc_af_stroke_risk.summary: Estimates annual thromboembolic risk in non-valvular atrial fibrillation, guiding the decision to anticoagulate.

terms: cha₂ds₂-vasc — stroke risk in atrial fibrillation

inputs.label: Vascular disease (prior MI, peripheral arterial disease, aortic plaque)

warnings: This score does NOT apply to moderate-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve — those patients require a vitamin K antagonist regardless of score.
Balance against bleeding risk (e.g. HAS-BLED). A high bleeding score is a prompt to correct modifiable risks, not an automatic reason to withhold anticoagulation.
Anticoagulant choice, dose and monitoring depend on renal function, weight, drug interactions and local availability.
limitations: Sex is a risk modifier rather than an independent risk factor in several contemporary guidelines.

flashcards.a: Age ≥75 and prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism

flashcards.q: Does CHA₂DS₂-VASc apply to mechanical valves?
flashcards.a: No — those need a VKA irrespective of score

also_known_as: cha₂ds₂-vasc — stroke risk in atrial fibrillation

has_bled_bleeding_risk.title: HAS-BLED — Bleeding Risk
has_bled_bleeding_risk.summary: Estimates 1-year major bleeding risk in anticoagulated atrial fibrillation. Its purpose is to identify and correct modifiable risk factors.

bands.label: High bleeding risk
bands.action: Address modifiable factors; review more frequently — this is not an instruction to stop anticoagulation

warnings: A high HAS-BLED score is not in itself a contraindication to anticoagulation. Many patients at high bleeding risk are also at high stroke risk and benefit more.

flashcards.a: Identifying and correcting modifiable bleeding risk factors — not for withholding anticoagulation

sepsis_screening_qsofa.title: Sepsis Screening (qSOFA)
sepsis_screening_qsofa.summary: Quick SOFA is a bedside prompt to consider sepsis in suspected infection. It is a screening trigger, not a diagnosis and not a substitute for clinical judgement.

sepsis3_definitions.sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection (SOFA rise ≥2 from baseline).
sepsis3_definitions.septic_shock: Sepsis with blood-pressure-raising drug (adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine) requirement to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg AND lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

immediate_bundle: Take blood cultures before antibiotics if this does not delay them
Give broad-spectrum antibiotics per local policy
body.source_control: Actively seek and control the source — abscess drainage, device removal, debridement, decompression.

bands.label: Lower immediate risk — does NOT exclude sepsis
Higher risk of poor outcome
bands.action: Escalate urgently; senior review; consider critical care

warnings: qSOFA has poor sensitivity for early sepsis. A score of 0 or 1 must never be used to rule sepsis out.
Do not delay antibiotics while waiting for a score, a lactate, or an imaging slot in a patient who looks septic.
Children, pregnant women and older adults deteriorate with atypical or muted signs.
limitations: Sepsis-3 criteria were derived in high-resource electronic-record populations; applicability in where staff, drugs or equipment are short settings is contested.

flashcards.a: RR ≥22, altered mentation, systolic BP ≤100
Vasopressor requirement for MAP ≥65 plus lactate >2 mmol/L despite fluid resuscitation
No — it has poor sensitivity and must never be used to rule out

checkboxes: Antibiotics given within the target window

sources: Singer M et al. The Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3). JAMA 2016;315(8):801-810.
governance.nigeria_overlay: Antibiotic choice must follow the facility antibiogram and the National Antimicrobial Stewardship guidance, not a generic regimen.

child_pugh_score.title: Child-Pugh Score
child_pugh_score.summary: Five variables graded 1–3 giving classes A, B and C. Used for prognosis and operative risk stratification in cirrhosis.

terms: child-pugh score for chronic liver disease

warnings: Bilirubin thresholds differ in primary biliary cholangitis and other cholestatic diseases.
Ascites and encephalopathy grading are subjective and are the main source of inter-rater disagreement.
limitations: MELD/MELD-Na is preferred for transplant allocation and short-term death rate prediction.

flashcards.a: Bilirubin, Albumin, INR, Ascites, Encephalopathy — 'A BIAE'

also_known_as: child-pugh score for chronic liver disease

hepatic_encephalopathy_west_haven_grades.title: Hepatic Encephalopathy — West Haven Grades
hepatic_encephalopathy_west_haven_grades.summary: Four clinical grades of hepatic encephalopathy, from subtle alteration to coma.

grades.features: Trivial lack of awareness, euphoria or anxiety, shortened attention span, impaired addition/subtraction
Lethargy or apathy, disorientation to time, obvious personality change, inappropriate behaviour, asterixis present
Somnolence to semi-stupor but responsive to stimuli, confusion, gross disorientation
Coma, unresponsive to verbal or noxious stimuli

precipitants: Electrolyte disturbance especially hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia
management_principles: Identify and treat the precipitant — this is the single most effective intervention
Lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools daily
Rifaximin as add-on where available and indicated
Protect the airway at grade III–IV
Avoid sedatives
Nutrition — do NOT protein-restrict long term
Correct electrolytes, especially potassium
Screen for and treat infection

warnings: Grade III–IV encephalopathy is an airway emergency.
Long-term protein restriction is harmful and is no longer recommended.
Always exclude hypoglycaemia, intracranial haemorrhage, sepsis and drug effect before attributing coma to encephalopathy alone.

flashcards.q: At which West Haven grade does asterixis typically appear?
flashcards.a: Grade II

flashcards.q: Most effective intervention in hepatic encephalopathy?
flashcards.a: Finding and treating the precipitant
2–3 soft stools per day

shock_types_and_how_to_tell_them_apart.title: Shock — Types and How To Tell Them Apart
shock_types_and_how_to_tell_them_apart.summary: Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery for metabolic demand. It is a physiological state, not a blood-pressure number — a normotensive patient can be profoundly shocked.

terms: shock — types and how to tell them apart

body.definition: A state in which oxygen delivery fails to meet cellular metabolic demand, producing cellular dysfunction and, if uncorrected, irreversible organ injury and death.
universal_signs: Tachycardia (may be absent in beta-blockade, neurogenic shock, or terminal bradycardia)
Cool, mottled or clammy peripheries (except warm distributive shock)
Hypotension — a LATE sign, especially in children and young adults

categories.causes: Haemorrhage (trauma, GI bleed, ruptured ectopic, ruptured AAA, postpartum), burns, severe diarrhoea/vomiting, DKA, third-space loss
categories.priority: Stop the bleeding and restore volume — in haemorrhage, blood is the resuscitation fluid, not crystalloid

categories.causes: Large myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, acute valvular failure, myocarditis, end-stage cardiomyopathy, drug toxicity
categories.priority: Do not fluid-load blindly — treat the cause; consider heart-squeeze drug (dobutamine, adrenaline)s, revascularisation, rhythm control

categories.mechanism: Mechanical obstruction to filling or ejection
categories.causes: Tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, massive pulmonary embolism, dynamic hyperinflation, aortic dissection with tamponade
categories.priority: Relieve the obstruction immediately — needle/finger decompression, pericardiocentesis, thrombolysis
Antibiotics, find where the infection is coming from and drain, remove or clean it out, fluids, blood-pressure-raising drug (adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine)s
Intramuscular adrenaline FIRST — before antihistamine or steroid

categories.mechanism: Loss of sympathetic tone below a cord lesion
categories.causes: Spinal cord injury above T6, high spinal anaesthesia
categories.priority: HYPOTENSION WITH BRADYCARDIA — the combination that distinguishes it. Exclude haemorrhage first; blood-pressure-raising drug (adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine), atropine for bradycardia

categories.mechanism: Hormone deficiency impairing vascular tone and volume
categories.causes: Adrenal crisis, myxoedema coma, thyroid storm
categories.priority: Give hydrocortisone on clinical suspicion of adrenal crisis — do not wait for cortisol result

bedside_discriminators: JVP low + cold = hypovolaemic. JVP high + cold = cardiogenic or obstructive.
Warm, vasodilated, wide pulse pressure = distributive.
Hypotension WITH bradycardia and warm dry skin = neurogenic until proven otherwise.
Unequal air entry + tracheal deviation + distended neck veins = tension pneumothorax; decompress before imaging.
Muffled heart sounds + raised JVP + hypotension (Beck's triad) = tamponade.
Shock in a woman of reproductive age = ruptured ectopic pregnancy until excluded.
shared_first_steps: Two large-bore cannulae; take bloods including group and save, lactate, glucose
Continuous monitoring — ECG, BP, SpO₂, urine output
Treat the treatable immediately (decompress, stop bleeding, give adrenaline, give hydrocortisone)

warnings: Shock is often present before the blood pressure falls. Children and healthy young adults compensate then crash.
In haemorrhagic shock, large-volume crystalloid worsens dilution, acidosis and coagulopathy — activate the massive haemorrhage protocol.
Do not give fluid boluses reflexively in cardiogenic or obstructive shock.
Multiple mechanisms coexist — a septic patient may also be bleeding, and a trauma patient may also be in neurogenic shock.
limitations: Classic haemodynamic profiles are teaching archetypes; real patients are frequently mixed or atypical.

flashcards.a: Hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, distributive

flashcards.q: Which shock gives hypotension WITH bradycardia?
flashcards.a: Neurogenic shock
Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds — cardiac tamponade

flashcards.q: Is hypotension an early or late sign of shock?
flashcards.a: Late — especially in children and young adults
Intramuscular adrenaline

checkboxes: Bloods including lactate and crossmatch sent
Immediately reversible cause excluded (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, anaphylaxis, adrenal crisis, hypoglycaemia)
Fluid strategy chosen appropriate to type

anaphylaxis_adrenaline_first.title: Anaphylaxis — Adrenaline First
anaphylaxis_adrenaline_first.summary: Acute, life-threatening, generalised hypersensitivity with airway, breathing or circulation compromise. Intramuscular adrenaline is the first and most important intervention.

body.recognition: Sudden onset and rapid progression of symptoms, with Airway and/or Breathing and/or Circulation problems, usually (but not always) with skin or mucosal changes.
immediate_sequence: Remove the trigger if possible (stop the infusion, remove the sting).
Call for help. Note the time.
Position: lie flat with legs raised if hypotensive; sit up if breathing is the dominant problem; left lateral in pregnancy. NEVER stand a patient up suddenly.
ADRENALINE INTRAMUSCULAR into the anterolateral thigh — repeat every 5 minutes if no improvement.
High-flow oxygen.
Large-volume intravenous fluid challenge.
Reassess. If not responding to treatment after two IM doses, senior/critical care help and consider an adrenaline infusion in a monitored setting.
second_line: Antihistamine and corticosteroid are SECOND LINE and must never delay adrenaline.
Consider glucagon in patients on beta-blockers with not responding to treatment hypotension.
after: Observe — biphasic reactions occur, so the observation period must follow local policy and reflect severity.
Serum mast cell tryptase: ideally as soon as feasible after resuscitation, a second sample 1–2 h after symptom onset, and a baseline sample later.
Document the trigger. Prescribe and demonstrate an adrenaline auto-injector where indicated.
Refer to allergy services. Provide written avoidance advice and an emergency plan.

warnings: ADRENALINE IS INTRAMUSCULAR INTO THE ANTEROLATERAL THIGH. Intravenous adrenaline in anaphylaxis is for trained practitioners with monitoring only — inadvertent IV bolus of 1:1000 has caused fatal arrhythmia and myocardial injury.
Never delay adrenaline for antihistamines, steroids, or to establish IV access.
Sudden postural change from lying to standing has precipitated cardiac arrest — keep the patient flat.
Absence of a rash does not exclude anaphylaxis — skin changes are absent in a significant minority.
limitations: Doses above follow widely used resuscitation-council conventions; confirm against local formulary and paediatric weight-based policy.

flashcards.q: Adult IM adrenaline dose in anaphylaxis?
flashcards.a: 500 micrograms of 1:1000 (0.5 mL) into the anterolateral thigh

flashcards.q: How often may IM adrenaline be repeated?
flashcards.a: Every 5 minutes if there is no improvement
No — they are second line and must never delay adrenaline

flashcards.q: Why must you not stand an anaphylaxis patient up?
flashcards.a: Sudden postural change has precipitated cardiac arrest

checkboxes: IM adrenaline given into anterolateral thigh
Repeat adrenaline at 5 min if needed

dka_diagnosis_2024_criteria.title: DKA — Diagnosis (2024 criteria)
dka_diagnosis_2024_criteria.summary: The 2024 international consensus redefined DKA around three criteria (D, K, A), replaced semi-quantitative ketones with beta-hydroxybutyrate, and removed the anion gap.

criteria_all_three_required.threshold: Plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL (≥11.1 mmol/L) OR a prior history of diabetes irrespective of glucose
criteria_all_three_required.why: The history alternative captures euglycaemic DKA, now more common with SGLT2 inhibitors.

Beta-hydroxybutyrate is the dominant ketone in DKA (ratio to acetoacetate rises from 1:1 to up to 10:1). The nitroprusside strip measures only acetoacetate, so it underestimates at presentation and overestimates during resolution.
Venous sampling is sufficient — the 2024 report removed the need for arterial blood gases for acid-base assessment.

what_changed_from_2009: Glucose threshold lowered from 250 to 200 mg/dL, with history of diabetes as an alternative.
Quantitative beta-hydroxybutyrate replaced semi-quantitative urine ketones as the preferred ketone measure.
The anion gap was REMOVED from the diagnostic criteria and from severity assessment.
Arterial sampling for acid-base assessment was eliminated.
Severity now determines the level of care, and mild DKA may be managed on a general ward.

warnings: Not all criteria must be met to assign a severity band — clinical judgement and resource availability decide the level of care.
Euglycaemic DKA is easily missed. A patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor with acidosis and ketosis has DKA even with a near-normal glucose.
Where beta-hydroxybutyrate is unavailable, urine ketones ≥2+ satisfies the K criterion, and normalisation of the anion gap remains an acceptable surrogate for resolution.
Captopril and valproate can cause false-positive urine ketone strips.
limitations: Beta-hydroxybutyrate done at the bedside, result in minutes testing is not universally available in where staff, drugs or equipment are short settings — a documented equity limitation of this guideline.

flashcards.a: D: glucose ≥200 mg/dL or known diabetes; K: BOHB ≥3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones ≥2+; A: pH <7.3 and/or HCO₃ <18

flashcards.q: Was the anion gap kept in the 2024 DKA criteria?
flashcards.a: No — it was removed

flashcards.q: Why is beta-hydroxybutyrate preferred over urine ketones?
flashcards.a: Urine strips detect only acetoacetate, underestimating ketosis at presentation and overestimating during resolution
>6 mmol/L

sources: Umpierrez GE, Davis GM, ElSayed NA, et al. Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report. Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275.
Rodriguez Alvarez P, San Martin VT, Morey-Vargas OL. Hyperglycemic crises in adults: A look at the 2024 consensus report. Cleve Clin J Med 2025;92(3):152-158.

dka_management.title: DKA — Management
dka_management.summary: Three pillars: fluid, insulin, potassium — plus treating the precipitant. Simplified in the 2024 consensus.

pillar_1_fluid: Isotonic saline or a balanced crystalloid at 500–1000 mL/hour for the first 2–4 hours in patients without cardiac or renal compromise.
Balanced crystalloids are now suggested where available — associated with faster recovery and less hyperchloraemic acidosis.
Once intravascular volume is restored, subsequent replacement depends on haemodynamics, fluid balance and sodium.
Smaller boluses (e.g. 250 mL) in older adults and in heart or kidney failure.
Add 5–10% dextrose once glucose falls below 250 mg/dL (≈14 mmol/L) so insulin can continue until ketonaemia clears.
pillar_2_insulin: Severe DKA: fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour, or a nurse-driven variable-rate protocol.
Adjust to keep glucose around 200 mg/dL (≈11 mmol/L) and continue until ketoacidosis resolves — glucose normalises long before ketosis does.
Mild and uncomplicated moderate DKA may be treated with subcutaneous rapid-acting analogue every 1–2 hours under close nursing supervision, avoiding ICU admission.
If the patient was already on basal insulin, continue it alongside the infusion — this reduces rebound hyperglycaemia and recurrent DKA.
Transition to subcutaneous: estimate total daily dose (0.3–0.6 units/kg/day, or preadmission dose, or in-hospital requirement). Give basal insulin 1–2 hours BEFORE stopping the infusion.
pillar_3_potassium: Measure potassium at baseline, 2 hours after starting insulin, then every 4 hours until resolution.
If potassium <3.5 mmol/L at presentation: START replacement at about 10 mmol/hour and POSTPONE insulin until potassium exceeds 3.5 mmol/L.
Begin replacement once potassium falls below 5.0 mmol/L, aiming to hold it between 4 and 5 mmol/L.
Total body potassium is depleted even when the serum level looks normal or high — insulin will drive it intracellularly.
not_routine: Bicarbonate: consider only in severe acidosis with pH <7.0.
Phosphate: consider only if <1.0 mmol/L, particularly with muscle weakness or cardiorespiratory compromise.
monitoring: Electrolytes, phosphate, creatinine, beta-hydroxybutyrate and venous pH every 4 hours until resolution.
Strict fluid balance and hourly urine output.
Continuous cardiac monitoring where potassium is being replaced at rate.
before_discharge: Written plan for what to do when unwell
Identify and address the reason this episode happened

warnings: POTASSIUM BEFORE INSULIN if K⁺ is below 3.5 mmol/L. Giving insulin first can precipitate fatal hypokalaemic arrhythmia.
Do not stop the insulin infusion when the glucose normalises — add dextrose and continue until the ketosis resolves.
Cerebral oedema is rare in adults but is the leading cause of death in paediatric DKA — paediatric DKA follows a different, slower protocol.
Recurrent DKA admissions carry markedly higher death rate; each episode warrants a serious look at the underlying cause.
limitations: Doses and rates above reflect the 2024 adult consensus. Paediatric, pregnant and dialysis patients require their own protocols.

flashcards.q: Potassium threshold that delays insulin in DKA?
flashcards.a: <3.5 mmol/L — replace potassium first

flashcards.q: When is dextrose added in DKA?
flashcards.a: When glucose falls below about 250 mg/dL (14 mmol/L)

flashcards.q: Initial fixed-rate insulin infusion in severe DKA?
flashcards.a: 0.1 units/kg/hour

flashcards.q: How long before stopping the infusion should basal insulin be given?
flashcards.a: 1–2 hours

checkboxes: Diagnosis confirmed against the three criteria
Severity assigned and level of care decided
Insulin regimen chosen (IV vs SC) and documented
Transition plan written with basal given 1–2 h before infusion stops

sources: Umpierrez GE et al. Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275.
governance.nigeria_overlay: Where beta-hydroxybutyrate assays are unavailable, document the use of urine ketones and anion-gap normalisation as surrogates, and record this substitution in the notes.

hhs_diagnosis_and_management.title: HHS — Diagnosis and Management
hhs_diagnosis_and_management.summary: Profound hyperglycaemia and hyperosmolality without significant ketosis or acidosis. Formal HHS resolution criteria were defined for the first time in 2024.

terms: hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar state (hhs) — 2024 criteria and management

criteria_all_four_required: Calculated EFFECTIVE serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg OR total serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg.
Absence of significant ketonaemia: beta-hydroxybutyrate <3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones ≤2+.
Absence of acidosis: pH ≥7.3 AND bicarbonate ≥15 mmol/L.
what_changed: Effective osmolality threshold lowered and total osmolality added as an alternative.
Impaired mental status is NO LONGER a diagnostic criterion — many very ill patients are alert.
Bicarbonate threshold lowered from 18 to 15 mmol/L.
management: Fluid is the dominant therapy — the water deficit is typically far larger than in DKA.
Insulin: fixed-rate infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour (HALF the DKA rate).
If mixed features (hyperosmolality WITH significant ketonaemia or acidosis), treat as DKA at 0.1 units/kg/hour.
Glucose should fall no faster than 90–120 mg/dL per hour.
Sodium should not fall by more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours.
Osmolality should fall no more than 3.0–8.0 mOsm/kg per hour.
Measure glucose, creatinine, electrolytes and osmolality every 4 hours.
Thromboprevention — HHS carries a high thrombotic risk.
seek_precipitant: Infection, especially pneumonia and urinary sepsis
Poor access to water in a dependent patient

warnings: Correct osmolality and sodium SLOWLY. Rapid correction risks cerebral oedema and osmotic demyelination.
death rate in HHS is substantially higher than in DKA — these are usually older, frailer patients with major coillness and disability.
Mixed DKA-HHS pictures are common and are managed on the DKA pathway.

flashcards.a: 0.05 units/kg/hour — half the DKA rate

flashcards.q: Is altered mental state still an HHS criterion?
flashcards.a: No — removed in 2024

flashcards.q: Maximum safe rate of glucose fall in HHS?
flashcards.a: 90–120 mg/dL per hour
≥600 mg/dL (≈33.3 mmol/L)

checkboxes: Insulin at 0.05 units/kg/h (or 0.1 if mixed picture)
Pressure areas and hydration needs addressed

sources: Umpierrez GE et al. Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275.

also_known_as: hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar state (hhs) — 2024 criteria and management

hypoglycaemia_recognise_and_treat.title: Hypoglycaemia — Recognise and Treat
hypoglycaemia_recognise_and_treat.summary: Low blood glucose causing symptoms. Treat immediately on suspicion; do not wait for laboratory confirmation.

body.definition: Commonly defined as blood glucose <70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) as an alert value, with clinically significant hypoglycaemia below 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L). Whipple's triad — symptoms, documented low glucose, and relief of symptoms on correction.

treatment_by_state.action: 15–20 g fast-acting oral carbohydrate (e.g. glucose tablets, 150–200 mL fruit juice or sugary drink, or 3–4 teaspoons of sugar in water). Recheck in 10–15 minutes. Repeat up to three times if still low.

treatment_by_state.state: Conscious but confused or uncooperative, swallow intact
treatment_by_state.action: Buccal glucose gel or the same oral carbohydrate with assistance; be alert to aspiration risk.

treatment_by_state.state: Unconscious, seizing, or unsafe swallow — IV access available
treatment_by_state.action: Intravenous glucose. Common regimens: 75–100 mL of 20% glucose or 150–200 mL of 10% glucose over 10–15 minutes. Higher concentrations are more sclerosant.
Intramuscular or subcutaneous glucagon. It will not work if hepatic glycogen is depleted — alcohol, starvation, liver failure, prolonged fasting.

after_recovery: Once glucose >70 mg/dL and the patient can swallow, give LONG-ACTING carbohydrate to prevent rebound.
Do NOT omit the next dose of insulin without a plan — review the regimen instead.
Recheck glucose after 15 minutes and again after the long-acting carbohydrate.
Find the reason: missed meal, wrong insulin dose or timing, sulfonylurea, renal impairment, alcohol, new illness, exercise, adrenal insufficiency.
special: SULFONYLUREA hypoglycaemia is prolonged and relapsing. Admit and observe; a single correction is not enough. Octreotide may be considered.
Neonatal hypoglycaemia has different thresholds and a different protocol.
Any patient with reduced consciousness must have glucose checked — hypoglycaemia mimics stroke, intoxication, psychosis and sepsis.

warnings: CHECK GLUCOSE IN EVERY PATIENT WITH ALTERED CONSCIOUSNESS, SEIZURE OR FOCAL DEFICIT. It is the single most reversible cause and is missed routinely.
Prolonged untreated hypoglycaemia causes permanent neurological injury and death.
Glucagon fails when glycogen stores are depleted — in alcohol, starvation or liver failure, give glucose.
Concentrated glucose extravasation causes severe tissue necrosis — confirm cannula patency.
limitations: Concentrations and volumes of IV glucose vary between national protocols; confirm against local policy.

flashcards.a: Symptoms of hypoglycaemia, documented low glucose, relief on correction

flashcards.q: Why does glucagon fail in alcoholics?
flashcards.a: Hepatic glycogen stores are depleted

flashcards.q: How much fast-acting carbohydrate for a conscious hypo?
flashcards.a: 15–20 g, repeat after 10–15 minutes if still low
To prevent rebound hypoglycaemia

checkboxes: Fast-acting carbohydrate or IV glucose given
Sulfonylurea involvement considered and admission arranged if so

thyroid_storm_burch_wartofsky_score.title: Thyroid Storm — Burch-Wartofsky Score
thyroid_storm_burch_wartofsky_score.summary: Weighted clinical scoring for thyroid storm. It quantifies clinical suspicion of decompensated thyrotoxicosis; it does not replace judgement, and treatment starts on suspicion.

domains.scoring: Absent = 0; Mild (agitation) = 10; Moderate (delirium, psychosis, extreme lethargy) = 20; Severe (seizure, coma) = 30
Absent = 0; Moderate (diarrhoea, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain) = 10; Severe (unexplained jaundice) = 20
Absent = 0; Mild (pedal oedema) = 5; Moderate (bibasal crackles) = 10; Severe (pulmonary oedema) = 15

management_principles: Beta-blockade to control adrenergic symptoms (propranolol traditionally preferred; caution in decompensated heart failure).
Thionamide to block new hormone synthesis — propylthiouracil is often preferred acutely because it also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion.
Iodine (e.g. Lugol's or potassium iodide) to block hormone RELEASE — give at least one hour AFTER the thionamide, never before.
Corticosteroid to reduce T4→T3 conversion and treat possible relative adrenal insufficiency.
Cooling and supportive care; avoid aspirin, which displaces thyroid hormone from binding proteins.
Identify and treat the precipitant — infection, surgery, trauma, iodinated contrast, childbirth, thionamide withdrawal, DKA.
Bile acid sequestrant may be considered to interrupt enterohepatic recirculation in not responding to treatment cases.

warnings: GIVE IODINE ONLY AFTER THE THIONAMIDE, with at least an hour between them. Iodine before thionamide can fuel further hormone synthesis.
Avoid aspirin — it displaces thyroid hormone from thyroxine-binding globulin and raises free hormone.
Treat on clinical suspicion; do not wait for thyroid function results.
The score is a decision aid with recognised over-diagnosis; correlate with the whole clinical picture.
limitations: The BWPS has never been prospectively validated against a criterion standard; alternative Japanese Thyroid Association criteria exist and disagree in some cases.

flashcards.q: Why must iodine follow the thionamide?
flashcards.a: Iodine given first can be used as substrate for further hormone synthesis

flashcards.q: Why is propylthiouracil often preferred acutely?
flashcards.a: It also blocks peripheral conversion of T4 to T3

flashcards.q: Which analgesic is avoided in thyroid storm?
flashcards.a: Aspirin — it displaces thyroid hormone from binding proteins

checkboxes: Temperature, heart rate and rhythm recorded

adrenal_crisis_give_hydrocortisone_now.title: Adrenal Crisis — Give Hydrocortisone Now
adrenal_crisis_give_hydrocortisone_now.summary: Acute glucocorticoid deficiency causing hypotension unresponsive to fluid. Hydrocortisone is given on clinical suspicion; confirmation follows treatment.

recognition: Hypotension or shock disproportionate to the apparent illness and not responding to treatment to fluid
Vomiting, abdominal pain that can mimic an acute abdomen
History of steroid use recently stopped or not increased during illness
immediate_management: Take blood for cortisol, ACTH, glucose, electrolytes — but DO NOT DELAY TREATMENT for results.
Rapid intravenous fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline.
Identify and treat the precipitant — most often infection.
Continue hydrocortisone by infusion or regular divided doses until stable.
Mineralocorticoid replacement is not needed while high-dose hydrocortisone is running.
precipitants: Surgery, trauma, or anaesthesia without steroid cover
Vomiting or diarrhoea preventing oral absorption
Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage (including Waterhouse-Friderichsen with meningococcaemia)
prevention_sick_day_rules: Double the usual oral glucocorticoid during fever or intercurrent illness.
Switch to injection if vomiting or unable to absorb.
Carry a steroid emergency card and an emergency injection kit.
Patient and family trained to give intramuscular hydrocortisone.
Additional cover for surgery, dental procedures and labour.

warnings: GIVE HYDROCORTISONE ON SUSPICION. Waiting for a cortisol result has killed patients. A single dose does no harm if the diagnosis proves wrong.
Adrenal crisis is repeatedly misdiagnosed as gastroenteritis, sepsis, or an acute surgical abdomen.
Any patient on long-term steroids who becomes acutely unwell needs increased steroid, not the usual dose.
Secondary (pituitary) insufficiency spares the mineralocorticoid axis, so hyperkalaemia may be absent — its absence does not exclude crisis.
limitations: Specific hydrocortisone doses vary by age, weight and national protocol; confirm against local formulary.

flashcards.q: Electrolyte pattern of primary adrenal crisis?
flashcards.a: Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia (and often hypoglycaemia)

flashcards.q: Do you wait for cortisol before treating?
flashcards.a: No — give hydrocortisone immediately on suspicion
Double the usual dose during fever or acute illness; switch to injection if vomiting

flashcards.q: Why may hyperkalaemia be absent in secondary insufficiency?
flashcards.a: The mineralocorticoid axis is preserved

checkboxes: Hydrocortisone given WITHOUT waiting for results
Emergency injection kit supplied and technique demonstrated

status_epilepticus_timed_pathway.title: Status Epilepticus — Timed Pathway
status_epilepticus_timed_pathway.summary: A seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or recurrent seizures without recovery between them. Treatment is time-driven, and the commonest failure is under-dosing the benzodiazepine.

body.definition: Convulsive status epilepticus: a generalised convulsive seizure ≥5 minutes, or two or more seizures without full recovery of consciousness between them.

actions: Airway, breathing, circulation; recovery position; suction
High-flow oxygen
CHECK GLUCOSE — treat hypoglycaemia immediately
IV access; take bloods (glucose, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, FBC, toxicology, anticonvulsant levels)
Note the time the seizure started
Protect from injury; do not force anything into the mouth
Give an adequate benzodiazepine dose by an appropriate route.
Common options: IV lorazepam, IV diazepam, IM midazolam, buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam where there is no IV access.
MAY BE REPEATED ONCE. Under-dosing is the commonest error in status.
Monitor for respiratory depression; have airway support ready.
Load with a second-line agent: levetiracetam, valproate, phenytoin/fosphenytoin, or phenobarbital, per local protocol.
Give as a loading infusion at the protocol rate — phenytoin requires cardiac monitoring and must not be given fast or in glucose-containing fluid.
If seizures continue, a different second-line agent may be tried.

phases.time: 40+ min — not responding to treatment status
actions: Call anaesthesia/critical care. Rapid sequence induction and ventilation.
Continuous infusion of midazolam, propofol or thiopentone with EEG monitoring where available.
Treat the cause aggressively.
Consider non-convulsive status if consciousness does not recover after clinical seizures stop.

always_seek_cause: CNS infection — meningitis, encephalitis, cerebral malaria
Drug withdrawal — alcohol, benzodiazepine, anticonvulsant non-adherence
Fever in a young child (febrile convulsion)
body.eclampsia_exception: In pregnancy or up to 6 weeks postpartum, seizures are eclampsia until proven otherwise. MAGNESIUM SULFATE is the first-line agent, not a benzodiazepine.

warnings: ECLAMPSIA IS THE EXCEPTION — magnesium sulfate, not benzodiazepine, is first line in pregnancy and the postpartum period.
CHECK GLUCOSE FIRST IN EVERY SEIZING PATIENT.
Under-dosing benzodiazepines is the most frequent and most consequential error.
Phenytoin must not be mixed with glucose-containing fluids and must be infused slowly with cardiac monitoring — rapid infusion causes hypotension and arrhythmia.
If the patient does not wake up after the convulsions stop, consider non-convulsive status.
limitations: Specific drug doses and rates vary by national protocol, age and weight — this artifact deliberately omits them and points to the local protocol.

flashcards.a: Seizure ≥5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery between them
Magnesium sulfate — not a benzodiazepine
Under-dosing the benzodiazepine

flashcards.q: Why must phenytoin not be given in glucose fluid?
flashcards.a: It precipitates — use sodium chloride, with cardiac monitoring and slow infusion

checkboxes: IV access obtained and bloods sent
First-line benzodiazepine given at full dose
Pregnancy status established — magnesium if eclampsia
Non-convulsive status considered if not waking

governance.nigeria_overlay: Confirm first- and second-line agents and doses against the National Standard Treatment Guidelines and the facility's paediatric and adult seizure protocols.

stroke_first_hours.title: Stroke — First Hours
stroke_first_hours.summary: Sudden focal neurological deficit of vascular origin. Imaging must distinguish ischaemic from haemorrhagic before any antithrombotic decision.

terms: acute stroke — recognition and hyperacute pathway

recognition.community_tool: FAST — Face, Arm, Speech, Time to call for help.
recognition.extended: BE-FAST adds Balance and Eyes (sudden visual loss or diplopia), improving detection of posterior circulation stroke.
recognition.caution: Posterior circulation strokes present with vertigo, ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria and reduced consciousness and are frequently missed.

immediate_actions: Note the time last known well — this drives every treatment decision.
Airway, breathing, circulation. Nil by mouth until a swallow screen is done.
CHECK GLUCOSE — hypoglycaemia is the classic stroke mimic.
Urgent non-contrast CT head to distinguish ischaemia from haemorrhage.
ECG (atrial fibrillation), bloods including FBC, clotting, glucose, electrolytes.
Assess with a validated severity scale (e.g. NIHSS) where trained.
Refer immediately to the stroke service — reperfusion decisions are time-critical.
ischaemic_principles: Reperfusion — intravenous thrombolysis and/or mechanical thrombectomy for eligible patients within licensed time windows and after haemorrhage is excluded.
Antiplatelet therapy once haemorrhage is excluded and after any thrombolysis interval has elapsed.
Admit to a stroke unit — organised stroke unit care is one of the most robust survival interventions in stroke medicine.
Do not lower blood pressure aggressively in the hyperacute ischaemic phase unless thrombolysis is planned or there is another indication.
Manage glucose, temperature and oxygenation; treat fever and hyperglycaemia.
haemorrhagic_principles: Neurosurgical referral for selected haematomas, hydrocephalus, or posterior fossa bleeds.
always_after: Swallow screen BEFORE any oral intake, including medication — aspiration pneumonia is a leading cause of death.
Early mobilisation and doctors, nurses and other staff working together rehabilitation.
Venous thromboembolism prevention appropriate to stroke type.
Secondary prevention — blood pressure, lipids, glucose, atrial fibrillation, smoking, carotid assessment.
Screen for post-stroke depression, spasticity, pain and cognitive impairment.

warnings: NEVER give an antiplatelet or anticoagulant before imaging has excluded haemorrhage.
CHECK GLUCOSE IN EVERY SUSPECTED STROKE — hypoglycaemia is fully reversible and mimics stroke exactly.
Keep the patient nil by mouth until a formal swallow screen is completed.
An early CT can look normal in ischaemic stroke — a normal scan does not exclude infarction; it excludes bleeding.
limitations: Availability of thrombolysis and thrombectomy varies enormously by setting; the pathway must be adapted to what the facility can actually deliver.

flashcards.q: What does BE-FAST add to FAST?
flashcards.a: Balance and Eyes — improving detection of posterior circulation stroke

flashcards.q: Single most important number in acute stroke?
flashcards.a: Time last known well

flashcards.q: What must be excluded before antiplatelet therapy?
flashcards.a: Intracranial haemorrhage, by CT

flashcards.q: Classic stroke mimic that must always be excluded?
flashcards.a: Hypoglycaemia

checkboxes: Nil by mouth until swallow screen
Blood pressure managed per stroke type

governance.nigeria_overlay: Where CT is not immediately available, transfer decisions and the risks of empirical treatment without imaging must follow an explicit written facility protocol. Antiplatelet therapy without imaging is not endorsed here.

also_known_as: acute stroke — recognition and hyperacute pathway

tetanus_principles_of_management.title: Tetanus — Principles of Management
tetanus_principles_of_management.summary: Toxin-mediated disease treated by neutralising unbound toxin, eliminating the source, controlling spasm, and supporting respiration in a low-stimulus environment.

generalised: Generalised reflex spasms provoked by light, noise or touch, with preserved consciousness (agonising)
Autonomic instability — labile blood pressure, tachycardia, arrhythmia, sweating, fever
neonatal: Presents in the first two weeks of life
Failure to suck after an initially normal feeding period
Almost always follows unclean cord practice
localised_and_cephalic: Spasm confined to the region of the wound
Cephalic tetanus follows head/facial wounds and may involve cranial nerve palsies

principles_of_management.detail: Human tetanus immunoglobulin where available (equine antitetanus serum with test dosing where it is not). Toxin already fixed to nerve terminals CANNOT be neutralised — this is why early administration matters and why recovery takes weeks.
Thorough wound debridement and removal of foreign material. LEAVE THE WOUND OPEN — do not close it primarily. Delayed closure only once healthy.
Antibiotic to eradicate vegetative Clostridium tetani; metronidazole is widely preferred over penicillin in current practice.
Benzodiazepines are the mainstay. Magnesium sulfate is used adjunctively. Severe cases require neuromuscular blockade with mechanical ventilation.
Nurse in a quiet, darkened, low-stimulus room. Cluster nursing interventions. Every touch, light and sound can trigger a spasm.
Laryngeal spasm and respiratory muscle involvement kill. Early tracheostomy is often required in generalised tetanus.
Labile cardiovascular state; magnesium and careful sedation; avoid abrupt stimulation.
Very high metabolic demand. feeding through the gut — by mouth or through a tube via nasogastric tube; meticulous fluid balance.
Thromboprevention, pressure area care, physiotherapy, fracture risk from severe spasm, aspiration prevention.
Natural infection does NOT confer immunity. A full primary vaccination course must be given during convalescence.

prevention: Routine childhood immunisation and maternal tetanus-toxoid-containing vaccine to prevent neonatal tetanus.
Clean delivery and clean cord care.
Wound management: assess tetanus-prone wounds and give toxoid and/or immunoglobulin per national schedule.
A tetanus-prone wound includes: >6 hours old, deep, contaminated with soil/manure, puncture, devitalised tissue, burns, retained foreign body, compound fracture.

warnings: DO NOT CLOSE THE WOUND PRIMARILY. Clostridium tetani is an anaerobe — closure creates the exact conditions it needs.
Surviving tetanus does NOT confer immunity. The patient must be fully immunised before discharge or they can get it again.
Consciousness is fully preserved during spasms. pain relief and sedation are not optional.
Sudden autonomic surges cause cardiac arrest — this is a leading cause of death even in patients whose spasms are controlled.
limitations: Immunoglobulin availability, antibiotic choice and sedation protocols vary by country and by facility resource level.

flashcards.q: First clinical sign of generalised tetanus?
flashcards.a: Trismus (lockjaw)

flashcards.q: Why must the tetanus wound be left open?
flashcards.a: Clostridium tetani is an anaerobe — closure favours it
No — a full primary vaccination course is required
Metronidazole (over penicillin)

flashcards.q: Why nurse in a dark quiet room?
flashcards.a: Light, noise and touch trigger reflex spasms

checkboxes: Airway plan made; tracheostomy considered early
Thromboprophylaxis and pressure care in place
Primary immunisation course started before discharge

governance.nigeria_overlay: Confirm the tetanus-toxoid schedule and the availability of human tetanus immunoglobulin versus equine antitetanus serum against the National Programme on Immunization and the facility formulary. Where equine serum is used, follow the local desensitisation/test-dose protocol.

acute_abdomen_approach.title: Acute Abdomen — Approach
acute_abdomen_approach.summary: A systematic approach to abdominal pain requiring urgent decision: is this a surgical emergency, and does the patient need theatre, imaging, or observation?

red_flags: Board-like rigidity or generalised guarding — perforation until proven otherwise
Pain out of proportion to findings — think mesenteric ischaemia
Absolute constipation with distension and vomiting — obstruction
Pain with shock in a woman of reproductive age — ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Bilious vomiting in a neonate — malrotation with volvulus until excluded

pain_pattern_logic.meaning: Stretch or ischaemia of a hollow viscus; localises to foregut (epigastric), midgut (periumbilical), hindgut (suprapubic)

pain_pattern_logic.character: Sharp, well localised, worse on movement
pain_pattern_logic.meaning: Parietal peritoneum irritated — the shift of appendicitis pain from periumbilical to right iliac fossa is this transition
Shared dermatomes — diaphragmatic irritation to the shoulder tip (Kehr's sign), ureteric colic to the groin

core_workup: Full history including menstrual and sexual history
Abdominal examination including hernial orifices and external genitalia — NEVER omit these
Pregnancy test in every woman of reproductive age
FBC, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, glucose, amylase/lipase, liver function, group and save, clotting
Erect chest radiograph for free air; supine abdominal film for obstruction where CT is unavailable
Ultrasound — first line for biliary, gynaecological and paediatric problems, and for free fluid
CT where available and where it will change management
ECG in older patients and epigastric pain
resuscitation_first: Wide-bore intravenous access and fluid resuscitation
pain relief — adequate pain relief does NOT mask the diagnosis and must not be withheld
Nasogastric tube if obstructed or vomiting
Antibiotics where perforation or sepsis is suspected
Consent and mark if going to theatre

warnings: ALWAYS DO A PREGNANCY TEST in a woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain. Ruptured ectopic pregnancy kills quickly and presents atypically.
ALWAYS EXAMINE THE HERNIAL ORIFICES AND SCROTUM. An obstructed hernia and a torted testis are both missed by an abdomen-only examination.
Withholding pain relief to 'preserve signs' is outdated and harmful.
Older adults, people with diabetes, immunosuppressed patients and those on steroids may have catastrophic pathology with unimpressive signs.
Pain grossly out of proportion to abdominal findings suggests mesenteric ischaemia — a diagnosis usually made too late.

flashcards.q: Why does appendicitis pain shift from umbilicus to RIF?
flashcards.a: Visceral pain from midgut foregut innervation gives way to parietal peritoneal irritation once inflammation reaches the parietal layer
Referred left shoulder tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation — classically splenic rupture or free blood

flashcards.q: Which examination is most often omitted in the acute abdomen?
flashcards.a: Hernial orifices and external genitalia

flashcards.q: Which single test must never be forgotten in a woman of reproductive age?
flashcards.a: Pregnancy test

checkboxes: Bloods including group and save sent
Consent and site marking if for theatre

governance.nigeria_overlay: Typhoid ileal perforation is a leading cause of generalised peritonitis in endemic settings and must be high on the differential for a young patient with prolonged fever followed by sudden abdominal pain.

appendicitis_alvarado_score.title: Appendicitis — Alvarado Score
appendicitis_alvarado_score.summary: Eight clinical and laboratory features supporting a diagnosis of acute appendicitis. It stratifies probability; it does not decide the operation.

body.mnemonic: MANTRELS — Migration, Anorexia, Nausea, Tenderness RIF, Rebound, Elevated temperature, Leucocytosis, Shift.

eponymous_signs.elicit: Palpation of the left iliac fossa produces pain in the right iliac fossa
Pain on passive extension of the right hip — suggests a retrocaecal appendix
Pain on passive internal rotation of the flexed right hip — suggests a pelvic appendix
Maximal tenderness one third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus

atypical_groups: Pregnancy — the appendix is displaced upwards, and pain may be right upper quadrant
Children — rapid progression to perforation; higher perforation rate
Older adults — muted signs, later presentation, higher illness and disability
Retrocaecal appendix — flank pain, minimal anterior tenderness, psoas sign positive

inputs.label: Migration of pain to the right iliac fossa
Tenderness in the right iliac fossa

bands.label: Appendicitis unlikely
bands.action: Consider alternative diagnoses; discharge with safety-net only if the patient is well and can return

bands.label: Equivocal
bands.action: Observe with serial examination, or image

bands.label: Probable appendicitis
bands.action: Surgical review

bands.label: Very probable appendicitis
bands.action: Surgical review

warnings: The score performs less well in women of reproductive age, where gynaecological pathology overlaps heavily. Always exclude pregnancy and consider ovarian torsion and pelvic inflammatory disease.
A low score does not exclude appendicitis, especially early in the course or in a retrocaecal appendix.
Serial examination by the same clinician remains one of the most valuable diagnostic tools.

flashcards.a: RIF tenderness and leucocytosis
Left iliac fossa palpation producing right iliac fossa pain

flashcards.q: Psoas sign suggests which appendix position?
flashcards.a: Retrocaecal
Migration, Anorexia, Nausea, Tenderness, Rebound, Elevated temperature, Leucocytosis, Shift

bowel_obstruction_assess_and_manage.title: Bowel Obstruction — Assess and Manage
bowel_obstruction_assess_and_manage.summary: Mechanical blockage of bowel. The core questions: small or large bowel, complete or partial, and is the bowel strangulated?

small_bowel: Bolus obstruction — ascaris, bezoar, gallstone ileus

strangulation_warning_signs: Tachycardia and fever out of keeping
Rising white cell count and lactate
Failure to improve on conservative management
initial_management: Nasogastric tube on free drainage — 'drip and suck'
Urinary catheter and strict fluid balance chart
Erect chest radiograph (free air) and abdominal radiograph or CT
Group and save; antibiotics if strangulation or perforation suspected
when_to_operate: Signs of strangulation or perforation — immediate
Obstructed hernia that will not reduce
Complete large bowel obstruction with a competent ileocaecal valve (risk of caecal blowout)
Failure of conservative management in adhesive small bowel obstruction after an agreed trial period
Sigmoid volvulus that fails endoscopic detorsion or shows gangrene
radiology_pearls: Small bowel: central loops, valvulae conniventes crossing the full width, >3 cm diameter
Large bowel: peripheral, haustra not crossing the full width, >6 cm (caecum >9 cm)
Sigmoid volvulus: 'coffee bean' or 'bent inner tube' sign pointing to the right upper quadrant
Free subdiaphragmatic gas on an erect film means perforation
Duodenal atresia: 'double bubble' with no distal gas

warnings: An irreducible, tense, tender hernia is a surgical emergency — do not persist with attempts at reduction.
Caecal diameter above about 9–12 cm in large bowel obstruction signals imminent perforation.
Vomiting in bowel obstruction causes profound hypovolaemia, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis — resuscitate properly before theatre.
In children, intussusception classically presents with intermittent inconsolable crying, drawing up the legs, and redcurrant jelly stool — a late sign.
Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise, and it is a true emergency.

flashcards.q: Four cardinal features of intestinal obstruction?
flashcards.a: Colicky pain, vomiting, distension, absolute constipation

flashcards.q: Valvulae conniventes vs haustra on X-ray?
flashcards.a: Valvulae cross the full bowel width (small bowel); haustra do not (large bowel)

flashcards.q: Commonest cause of small bowel obstruction in an operated abdomen?
flashcards.a: Adhesions

flashcards.q: Bilious vomiting in a neonate means what until proven otherwise?
flashcards.a: Malrotation with midgut volvulus

checkboxes: NG tube passed and on free drainage

typhoid_perforation.title: Typhoid Perforation
typhoid_perforation.summary: Perforation of a Peyer's patch ulcer in the terminal ileum during enteric fever. A major cause of peritonitis in endemic regions with high death rate if surgery is delayed.

body.typical_history: Prolonged fever (often 2–3 weeks) with abdominal discomfort, then SUDDEN severe abdominal pain, rapid deterioration and signs of generalised peritonitis. Often in a young patient.
body.why_it_happens: Salmonella Typhi proliferates in Peyer's patches of the terminal ileum, producing ulceration that can perforate — typically in the third week of illness.
clinical_findings: Generalised abdominal tenderness with guarding and rigidity
Signs of shock in late presentation
investigations: Erect chest radiograph — free subdiaphragmatic gas (may be absent in a significant minority)
FBC — leucopenia is classic in typhoid but leucocytosis appears with perforation
Electrolytes, urea, creatinine — usually markedly deranged
Blood culture
Widal test (limited value — see the Widal artifact)
Group and crossmatch
management_principles: Aggressive resuscitation FIRST — these patients are profoundly hypovolaemic and septic
Broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-negatives and anaerobes, plus specific anti-typhoid therapy
Nasogastric decompression, urinary catheter, strict fluid balance
Correct electrolytes and anaemia
EARLY LAPAROTOMY — delay is the strongest predictor of death
At operation: peritoneal lavage, identify ALL perforations (they are frequently multiple), and choose the procedure:
• Simple closure in two layers for a single small perforation with healthy edges
• Wedge excision and closure for unhealthy edges
• Segmental resection with anastomosis or stoma for multiple or extensive perforations
• Ileostomy where the patient is unstable or the bowel is very unhealthy
Consider leaving the skin open or delayed primary closure given the high wound infection rate
Post-operative critical care, nutrition, and stoma education where relevant
prevention: Early and adequate treatment of enteric fever
Public health case finding and carrier identification

warnings: ALWAYS LOOK FOR MULTIPLE PERFORATIONS. Missing a second perforation is a well-recognised cause of post-operative death.
Absence of free gas on an erect film does NOT exclude perforation.
Delay to surgery is the single most important modifiable predictor of death rate — but operating on an unresuscitated patient is equally lethal. Resuscitate rapidly and then operate.
Leucopenia is typical of typhoid itself; do not be falsely reassured by a normal or low white cell count.

flashcards.q: Where does typhoid perforation classically occur?
flashcards.a: Terminal ileum, at a Peyer's patch, typically in the third week

flashcards.q: Most important intra-operative caution in typhoid perforation?
flashcards.a: Look for multiple perforations

flashcards.q: Typical white cell picture in typhoid before perforation?
flashcards.a: Leucopenia
Delay to surgery

checkboxes: Antibiotics given covering Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms

governance.nigeria_overlay: Antibiotic selection must reflect local Salmonella Typhi resistance patterns, including the burden of multidrug-resistant and fluoroquinolone-non-susceptible strains. Follow the facility antibiogram and national guidance.

hernia_types_and_management.title: Hernia — Types and Management
hernia_types_and_management.summary: A protrusion of a viscus or part of a viscus through a defect in the wall that normally contains it. Classified by site and by clinical state.

by_clinical_state.meaning: Contents return to the abdomen spontaneously or with manipulation
Contents cannot be reduced but remain viable
Bowel lumen occluded, causing intestinal obstruction
Blood supply compromised — ischaemia then gangrene
Contents inflamed (e.g. appendix in the sac)

by_site.anatomy: Through the deep ring, LATERAL to the inferior epigastric vessels, along the inguinal canal
by_site.notes: Commonest overall; congenital patent processus vaginalis; may reach the scrotum

by_site.anatomy: Through Hesselbach's triangle, MEDIAL to the inferior epigastric vessels
by_site.notes: Acquired weakness; rarely enters the scrotum; lower strangulation risk

by_site.anatomy: Through the femoral canal, BELOW and LATERAL to the pubic tubercle
by_site.notes: Commoner in women; HIGH risk of strangulation; narrow rigid neck

by_site.anatomy: Through or beside the umbilical cicatrix
by_site.notes: Common in infants (usually resolves), and in adults with raised intra-abdominal pressure
Risk factors: infection, obesity, steroids, poor technique, cough, malnutrition

by_site.anatomy: Through the linea alba above the umbilicus
by_site.notes: Often small, contains extraperitoneal fat, disproportionately painful
