Elderly thin women; Howship-Romberg sign — medial thigh pain on internal rotation
Sliding vs rolling (paraoesophageal); managed medically or by fundoplication

named_special_types.name: Richter
named_special_types.description: Only part of the bowel circumference is in the sac — can strangulate WITHOUT causing obstruction

named_special_types.name: Maydl
named_special_types.description: 'W' loop; the strangulated segment lies inside the abdomen, not in the sac

named_special_types.name: Sliding
named_special_types.description: Part of the sac wall is formed by a viscus (e.g. caecum, bladder)

body.landmark_discrimination: The PUBIC TUBERCLE is the key landmark. Inguinal hernias emerge ABOVE and MEDIAL to it; femoral hernias below and lateral.
management_principles: Elective repair for symptomatic reducible hernias, weighing operative risk
Emergency exploration for strangulation — do not delay for imaging
Assess and resect non-viable bowel
Tension-free mesh repair where the field is clean
Avoid mesh in a contaminated field — use tissue repair
Address precipitating factors: chronic cough, constipation, prostatism, obesity, ascites
In infants, umbilical hernias usually close spontaneously by 3–5 years; inguinal hernias in infants should be repaired because of strangulation risk

warnings: A RICHTER'S HERNIA CAN STRANGULATE WITHOUT BOWEL OBSTRUCTION. The absence of obstruction does not exclude ischaemia.
Do not force reduction of a tender irreducible hernia — reduction en masse can return gangrenous bowel to the abdomen.
Femoral hernias have a high strangulation rate and should generally be repaired promptly even when small.
Always examine hernial orifices in any patient with abdominal pain or obstruction.

flashcards.q: Key landmark distinguishing inguinal from femoral hernia?
flashcards.a: The pubic tubercle — inguinal above and medial, femoral below and lateral

flashcards.q: Indirect vs direct inguinal hernia relative to inferior epigastric vessels?
flashcards.a: Indirect is lateral; direct is medial
Richter's hernia

flashcards.q: Which hernia contains a Meckel diverticulum?
flashcards.a: Littre's hernia
Medial thigh pain on internal rotation — obturator hernia

checkboxes: Site determined relative to the pubic tubercle
Bowel sounds over the hernia checked
Consent and side marking if operating
Mesh vs tissue repair decision documented

trauma_primary_survey_abcde.title: Trauma Primary Survey (ABCDE)
trauma_primary_survey_abcde.summary: A prioritised sequence that finds and treats what kills first. Each step is completed and any problem treated before moving on.

actions: Direct pressure, haemostatic dressing, tourniquet for compressible exsanguinating limb bleeding
Pelvic binder for suspected pelvic fracture
This precedes airway in exsanguinating external bleeding

sequence.step: A — Airway with cervical spine protection
actions: Assess patency: talk to the patient; a normal voice implies a patent airway
Look for blood, vomit, teeth, foreign body, facial or laryngeal injury, burns to the airway
Chin lift/jaw thrust; suction; airway adjuncts
a tube in the trachea with the cuff up if GCS ≤8, airway burn, unable to protect, or persistent obstruction
Manual in-line stabilisation of the cervical spine throughout
Expose the chest; look, listen, feel; count the respiratory rate; pulse oximetry
High-flow oxygen
Identify and treat immediately life-threatening chest injuries: tension pneumothorax, open pneumothorax, massive haemothorax, flail chest with pulmonary contusion, cardiac tamponade
Needle or finger decompression for tension pneumothorax — clinical diagnosis, do NOT wait for a radiograph
Pulse, blood pressure, capillary refill, skin colour and temperature, conscious level
Two large-bore cannulae; take bloods including crossmatch, gas and lactate
Control external bleeding
Identify the five places blood hides: chest, abdomen, pelvis/retroperitoneum, long bones, and 'on the floor'
Blood products for haemorrhagic shock; activate the massive haemorrhage protocol
Tranexamic acid early where indicated
Consider FAST/eFAST scan and pelvic binder
GCS (E, V, M recorded separately)
Pupil size, symmetry and reactivity
Lateralising signs and gross limb movement
CHECK GLUCOSE
Consider raised intracranial pressure and impending herniation
Fully expose to examine, then cover immediately
Log roll with adequate help to inspect the back and perform a rectal examination if indicated
PREVENT HYPOTHERMIA — warm fluids, warming blankets, raise ambient temperature
Remove wet clothing

adjuncts: Continuous monitoring: ECG, blood pressure, SpO₂, capnography if intubated
Urinary catheter (contraindicated if urethral injury suspected — blood at meatus, high-riding prostate, perineal bruising)
Nasogastric tube (use orogastric if a basal skull fracture is suspected)
Arterial or venous blood gas and lactate
body.secondary_survey: Only after the primary survey is complete and the patient is stabilising: a full head-to-toe examination with AMPLE history (Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last meal, Events).
body.lethal_triad: Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy reinforce each other. Damage control resuscitation aims to interrupt this cycle: stop the bleeding, give blood products in balanced ratios, keep the patient warm, and limit crystalloid.

warnings: TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX IS A CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS. Decompress before requesting a chest radiograph.
Do not pass a urethral catheter if there is blood at the meatus, a high-riding prostate, or perineal bruising.
Do not pass a nasogastric tube through the nose if a basal skull fracture is suspected — use the oral route.
Large-volume crystalloid in haemorrhagic shock worsens dilutional coagulopathy — give blood.
Hypothermia in trauma is a killer, not a comfort issue. Cover the patient at every opportunity.
Reassess from the beginning whenever the patient deteriorates.

flashcards.q: Five places blood hides in trauma?
flashcards.a: Chest, abdomen, pelvis/retroperitoneum, long bones, and on the floor

flashcards.q: What does the <C> before ABCDE stand for?
flashcards.a: Catastrophic external haemorrhage
Hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy

flashcards.q: Do you X-ray before decompressing a tension pneumothorax?
flashcards.a: No — it is a clinical diagnosis, decompress immediately
Allergies, Medications, Past history, Last meal, Events

checkboxes: Airway assessed and secured; C-spine protected
Chest exposed and examined; life-threats excluded
Two large-bore cannulae; bloods and crossmatch sent
Log roll performed with adequate staff

gunshot_and_stab_wound_how_to_clerk.title: Gunshot and Stab Wound — How To Clerk
gunshot_and_stab_wound_how_to_clerk.summary: Penetrating trauma history determines the likely tract, the energy transferred, and therefore what must be excluded. The mechanism is clinical information, not curiosity.

terms: gunshot and penetrating injury — specialist clerking
gunshot and stab wound — how to clerk

mechanism_questions: What weapon? Handgun, rifle, shotgun, blade, arrow, machete, industrial nail gun?
How many shots or blows were heard or felt?
Approximate distance from the weapon? Close range causes more tissue damage and may leave powder tattooing.
What was the victim's position and posture at the time? This determines the internal tract, which may not be a straight line between wounds.
What happened afterwards — did they walk, collapse, lose consciousness, or have a seizure?
How were they transported, and how long did it take? Was any pre-hospital care given?
Any tourniquet applied, and at what time? (Tourniquet time must be recorded.)
Estimated blood loss at the scene and en route.
examination_priorities: Full exposure — count EVERY wound, including axillae, perineum, scalp, back, and between skin folds
Do NOT label wounds 'entry' and 'exit' in the clinical record — that is a forensic determination. Describe location, size and shape objectively.
Mark wounds with radio-opaque markers before imaging where protocol allows
Neurovascular assessment distal to every wound — pulses, capillary refill, motor and sensory function
Peripheral nerve examination documented by named nerve
Perineal and rectal examination for pelvic or low abdominal wounds

specific_complications_to_seek.risks: Airway injury, vascular injury (carotid, vertebral, jugular), oesophageal injury, cord injury. Zones I–III determine investigation.
Tension or open pneumothorax, haemothorax, cardiac injury and tamponade, great vessel injury, tracheobronchial and oesophageal injury, diaphragmatic injury.
Hollow viscus perforation, solid organ injury, retroperitoneal vascular injury, diaphragmatic injury. Any wound between the nipples and the groin may involve the abdomen.
Rectal injury, bladder and urethral injury, major venous plexus bleeding, EXTERNAL GENITALIA and ERECTILE function — ask about and document.
Cord transection, incomplete syndromes, autonomic dysreflexia later, neurogenic shock.
Vascular injury requiring urgent repair, nerve injury with permanent weakness or paralysis, fracture, compartment syndrome, limb-threatening ischaemia.

counselling_and_documentation: Discuss realistically the possibility of permanent weakness, paralysis, sensory loss, bowel or bladder dysfunction, and sexual/erectile dysfunction where the injury pattern makes these plausible.
Preserve clothing and any recovered projectile per local forensic policy — hand over with a documented chain of custody.
Complete any legally mandated report (police notification requirements vary by jurisdiction).
Offer psychological support and, where relevant, violence-intervention services.

warnings: COUNT EVERY WOUND AND EXAMINE EVERY BODY SURFACE. Missed posterior and axillary wounds are a classic and lethal error.
Do not document wounds as 'entry' or 'exit' — that is a forensic conclusion and misdocumentation has legal consequences.
The internal tract is often not a straight line between two skin wounds; the body may have been in a different posture.
Tourniquet application time must be recorded and communicated at every handover.
Do not probe wounds blindly in the emergency department — this can dislodge clot and cause catastrophic bleeding.

flashcards.q: Why must you not label wounds entry and exit?
flashcards.a: It is a forensic determination, not a clinical one, and misdocumentation has legal consequences

flashcards.q: Why does posture at the time of injury matter?
flashcards.a: The internal tract depends on body position and is often not a straight line between wounds

flashcards.q: What must always be recorded about a tourniquet?
flashcards.a: The time it was applied

checkboxes: Time of injury and time of arrival recorded
Fully exposed; ALL wounds counted and mapped
Wounds described objectively, not labelled entry/exit
Distal neurovascular status documented for each limb
Named peripheral nerves tested and recorded
Spinal assessment and log roll done
Clothing and projectile preserved with chain of custody
Counselling on possible long-term deficits documented
also_known_as: gunshot and penetrating injury — specialist clerking

burns_tbsa_and_fluid_rule_of_nines_parkl.title: Burns — TBSA and Fluid (Rule of Nines, Parkland)
burns_tbsa_and_fluid_rule_of_nines_parkl.summary: Wallace Rule of Nines with Parkland-type fluid estimation. The formula is a STARTING POINT that is titrated to urine output, never a fixed prescription.

terms: burns — tbsa and fluid (rule of nines, parkland)
burns — total body surface area and fluid resuscitation

body.rule_of_nines_child: Children have a proportionally larger head and smaller legs. Use the Lund and Browder chart, which is age-adjusted and far more accurate. A rough paediatric adjustment: head 18%, each leg 14%.
body.palmar_rule: The patient's whole palm including fingers is approximately 1% of their body surface area — useful for scattered or irregular burns.

depth.appearance: Erythema, no blisters, brisk capillary refill
Blotchy red or white, less blanching
White, waxy, leathery, charred; thrombosed vessels

inhalation_injury_red_flags: Facial burns, singed nasal hairs, soot in mouth or sputum
Consider early intubation — airway oedema progresses rapidly and a delayed airway may be impossible
body.titration: Adjust the rate to achieve urine output of approximately 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults and 1 mL/kg/h in children. Urine output, not the formula, is the guide.
other_priorities: Stop the burning process; remove clothing and jewellery
Cool the burn with running water for about 20 minutes; do NOT use ice
Cover with clean non-adherent dressing or cling film (lengthwise, not circumferentially)
pain relief — burns are extremely painful
Consider escharotomy for circumferential full-thickness burns compromising ventilation or limb perfusion
Consider carbon monoxide and cyanide exposure in enclosed-space fires
Early nutrition — burns cause extreme catabolism
Refer to a burns unit per national criteria
Non-accidental injury must be actively considered in children with burns

inputs.label: Total body surface area burned (partial thickness and deeper)

outputs.label: Estimated total crystalloid in first 24 hours
Give in first 8 hours FROM TIME OF BURN

warnings: THE CLOCK STARTS AT THE TIME OF THE BURN, NOT AT ARRIVAL. Subtract fluid already given and time already elapsed.
DO NOT include superficial (epidermal) erythema in the TBSA calculation — this is the commonest cause of over-resuscitation.
Over-resuscitation causes abdominal compartment syndrome, pulmonary oedema and compartment syndrome. Titrate to urine output.
Airway compromise from inhalation injury progresses quickly. If in doubt, get a tube in early — later may be impossible.
Circumferential full-thickness burns of the chest or a limb can cause ventilatory failure or limb loss and may need escharotomy.
In children, always consider non-accidental injury and assess the pattern against the history.
limitations: Parkland (4 mL/kg/%TBSA), modified Brooke (2 mL) and other formulae differ; follow the receiving burns unit's protocol.
TBSA estimation by eye is notoriously inaccurate — use a Lund and Browder chart.

flashcards.q: Adult Rule of Nines — anterior trunk?

flashcards.a: The patient's whole palm including fingers ≈ 1% TBSA

flashcards.q: When does the Parkland clock start?
flashcards.a: At the time of the burn, not at hospital arrival

flashcards.q: Which burn depth is excluded from TBSA?
flashcards.a: Superficial epidermal erythema

flashcards.q: Urine output target in adult burns resuscitation?
flashcards.a: About 0.5 mL/kg/hour

checkboxes: Cooled with running water ~20 min (not ice)
TBSA estimated using a chart, superficial erythema EXCLUDED
Fluid calculated from time of BURN
Two large-bore cannulae (through unburned skin where possible)
Urine output target set and charted hourly
also_known_as: burns — total body surface area and fluid resuscitation

compartment_syndrome_spot_it_early.title: Compartment Syndrome — Spot It Early
compartment_syndrome_spot_it_early.summary: Raised pressure within a closed fascial compartment causing ischaemia. It is a clinical diagnosis and a surgical emergency; waiting for pulselessness means waiting too long.

the_six_ps_with_a_warning.sign: Pain on PASSIVE STRETCH of the compartment muscles
the_six_ps_with_a_warning.value: EARLIEST and MOST RELIABLE — the key clinical test
Early-intermediate; sensory nerves are affected before motor
LATE — irreversible damage may already have occurred
VERY LATE — pulses are usually PRESENT in compartment syndrome. Their presence does NOT exclude it.

causes: Fractures, especially tibial shaft and forearm
Reperfusion after vascular repair or prolonged ischaemia
immediate_actions: Remove ALL circumferential dressings, casts and splints down to skin
Position the limb at the level of the heart — do NOT elevate above heart level (this reduces perfusion pressure)
Adequate pain relief; but escalating opioid requirement is itself a warning sign
Correct hypotension — systemic hypotension worsens compartment perfusion
Compartment pressure measurement where available and where the patient cannot be assessed clinically (drowsy and hard to rouse, regional block, child)
EMERGENCY FASCIOTOMY is the definitive treatment
special_populations: drowsy and hard to rouse, intubated or anaesthetised patients cannot report pain — maintain a high index of suspicion and consider pressure monitoring
Regional anaesthesia and dense pain relief can mask the cardinal symptom — this is a recognised diagnostic hazard
Children may present only with increasing pain relief requirement, agitation and anxiety ('the three As')

warnings: PULSES ARE USUALLY PRESENT IN COMPARTMENT SYNDROME. Do not use a palpable pulse to exclude the diagnosis.
Do not elevate the limb above heart level — this reduces arterial inflow and perfusion pressure.
Pain on passive stretch is the earliest reliable sign. If you elicit it, escalate immediately.
Escalating opioid requirement after a fracture is compartment syndrome until proven otherwise.
Regional blocks can mask the diagnosis — document this risk when siting a block in a high-risk limb.

flashcards.q: Earliest reliable sign of compartment syndrome?
flashcards.a: Pain on passive stretch of the compartment muscles

flashcards.q: Does a present pulse exclude compartment syndrome?
flashcards.a: No — pulses are usually present
No — keep it at heart level; elevation reduces perfusion pressure
Emergency fasciotomy

checkboxes: Pain assessed and compared with expected level
Passive stretch test performed and documented
All circumferential dressings/casts removed to skin
Limb positioned at heart level, not elevated
Compartment pressures measured if patient cannot be assessed clinically

fracture_principles_of_management.title: Fracture — Principles of Management
fracture_principles_of_management.summary: The organising framework for any fracture: reduce, hold, rehabilitate — within a wider sequence of resuscitation, assessment and definitive care.

the_four_rs: RESUSCITATE — fractures may be part of major trauma; ABCDE first
REDUCE — restore alignment, length and rotation
RETAIN (HOLD) — maintain reduction with cast, traction, external or internal fixation
REHABILITATE — restore function; early movement where the fixation allows
description_checklist: Which bone, and which part (proximal, shaft, distal third)
Pattern: transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted, segmental, greenstick, buckle, avulsion
Skin condition and soft tissue envelope
open_fracture_priorities: Remove gross contamination; photograph the wound if policy allows, then cover with a saline-soaked dressing
Antibiotics as soon as possible — time to antibiotics matters
Gustilo-Anderson classification guides prognosis and management

gustilo_anderson.description: Wound <1 cm, clean, minimal soft tissue damage
Wound >1 cm, moderate soft tissue damage, no extensive stripping
Extensive soft tissue damage but adequate coverage of bone
Extensive soft tissue loss with periosteal stripping; requires flap coverage
Any open fracture with arterial injury requiring repair

special_paediatric_points: Physeal (growth plate) injuries — Salter-Harris classification I–V
Greenstick and buckle (torus) fractures reflect the plasticity of immature bone
Greater remodelling potential, so more angulation may be accepted
ALWAYS consider non-accidental injury: unexplained fractures, fractures inconsistent with the stated mechanism, multiple fractures of different ages, fractures in non-ambulant infants

warnings: Document distal neurovascular status BEFORE and AFTER every reduction or manipulation, and after applying any cast.
A tight cast can cause compartment syndrome — teach the patient the warning signs and how to seek help.
Suspected non-accidental injury in a child is a safeguarding emergency requiring escalation, not a diagnosis to be deferred.
An open fracture is a surgical emergency: antibiotics early, debridement urgently.

flashcards.q: The four Rs of fracture management?
flashcards.a: Resuscitate, Reduce, Retain (hold), Rehabilitate
Open fracture with arterial injury requiring repair
Physeal (growth plate) injuries in children

flashcards.q: What must be documented before AND after every reduction?
flashcards.a: Distal neurovascular status

checkboxes: Immobilisation applied and checked for tightness
Antibiotics and tetanus for open fracture
Compartment syndrome risk discussed with patient

acute_scrotum_torsion_or_infection.title: Acute Scrotum — Torsion or Infection?
acute_scrotum_torsion_or_infection.summary: Sudden scrotal pain is testicular torsion until proven otherwise. The testis is salvageable for only a few hours — imaging must not delay exploration.

discriminators.torsion: Sudden, often waking from sleep or after minor trauma/exertion
Neonates and 12–18 years, but occurs at any age
discriminators.epididymo_orchitis: Sexually active adults and older men

discriminators.torsion: High-riding, horizontal (Angell's sign on the other side)

other_causes: Torsion of the appendix testis — 'blue dot sign', more localised upper pole tenderness
management: Nil by mouth immediately
pain relief
Urgent urology/surgical review
IMMEDIATE SCROTAL EXPLORATION where torsion is suspected — do NOT delay for Doppler ultrasound
At exploration: detorse, assess viability, orchidopexy of BOTH testes (the bell-clapper anomaly is bilateral) or orchidectomy if non-viable
For epididymo-orchitis: antibiotics guided by likely organism and age, scrotal support, pain relief, sexual health screening and partner notification where relevant
body.salvage_and_time: Salvage rates fall sharply with time from onset. Within roughly 6 hours salvage is high; beyond about 12–24 hours it becomes poor. Time from onset must be documented explicitly.

warnings: A NORMAL DOPPLER ULTRASOUND DOES NOT EXCLUDE TORSION. If clinical suspicion is high, explore.
Do not delay theatre to obtain imaging — the testis is lost while you wait.
Torsion occurs in neonates and in adults, not only in teenagers. Age is not a reason to dismiss it.
Always examine the scrotum in a boy or man presenting with abdominal pain — referred pain from torsion is a classic missed presentation.
Fournier's gangrene (necrotising fasciitis of the perineum) is a separate, immediately life-threatening emergency requiring urgent radical debridement.

flashcards.q: Most useful single clinical sign in torsion?
flashcards.a: Absent cremasteric reflex

flashcards.q: Does a normal Doppler exclude torsion?
flashcards.a: No — explore if clinical suspicion is high

flashcards.q: Why fix both testes at exploration?
flashcards.a: The bell-clapper anomaly is bilateral
No relief on elevating the testis

checkboxes: Time of symptom onset documented explicitly
Cremasteric reflex tested on both sides
Consent for exploration and possible orchidectomy discussed
Bilateral orchidopexy planned if torsion confirmed

urinary_retention_and_catheter.title: Urinary Retention and Catheter
urinary_retention_and_catheter.summary: Painful inability to pass urine with a palpable bladder. Decompression relieves it; the important work is finding the cause and anticipating post-obstructive diuresis.

obstructive: Pelvic mass, including gravid uterus and fibroids
neurological: Spinal cord compression — CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME must be excluded

catheter_indications: Accurate urine output monitoring in critical illness
Facilitating healing of sacral wounds in incontinence
catheter_contraindications_and_cautions: SUSPECTED URETHRAL INJURY — blood at the meatus, high-riding or impalpable prostate, perineal or scrotal bruising. Do NOT catheterise; call urology.
Known complex stricture — do not force
Recent urethral or prostatic surgery — discuss with the operating team

suprapubic_catheter.when: Urethral route impossible or contraindicated (stricture, urethral injury, failed urethral attempt), or long-term drainage preferred
suprapubic_catheter.absolute_caution: Do NOT insert blind if the bladder is not palpable or ultrasonically confirmed, if there is a history of lower abdominal surgery with possible adherent bowel, or if there is known bladder cancer
suprapubic_catheter.technique_note: Insert about 2 cm above the pubic symphysis in the midline, with ultrasound guidance where available

post_obstructive_diuresis: After decompressing a chronically obstructed bladder, urine output can be massive.
Monitor hourly urine output, blood pressure and electrolytes.
Replace fluid and electrolytes as guided; watch for hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia and hypovolaemia.
Also watch for haematuria ex vacuo after rapid decompression.
after_catheterisation: Send urine for analysis and culture
Consider imaging for hydronephrosis if renal function is impaired
Start an alpha-blocker before a trial without catheter in men with likely BPH

warnings: EXCLUDE CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME. Retention with back pain, saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg symptoms or altered anal tone is a neurosurgical emergency requiring urgent MRI.
Do not catheterise if urethral injury is suspected — blood at the meatus, high-riding prostate, or perineal bruising.
Never force a catheter. Repeated forced attempts create false passages and strictures.
Anticipate post-obstructive diuresis after decompressing chronic retention; unmonitored, it causes profound hypovolaemia and electrolyte disturbance.

flashcards.q: Three signs suggesting urethral injury that contraindicate catheterisation?
flashcards.a: Blood at the meatus, high-riding prostate, perineal/scrotal bruising

flashcards.q: What must always be excluded in retention with back pain?
flashcards.a: Cauda equina syndrome

flashcards.q: What follows decompression of chronic retention?
flashcards.a: Post-obstructive diuresis — monitor output and electrolytes

checkboxes: Appropriate catheter size and material chosen
Anaesthetic lubricant instilled and given time to work
Urine sent for analysis and culture
Hourly urine output monitored for post-obstructive diuresis

antenatal_booking_what_to_check.title: Antenatal Booking — What To Check
antenatal_booking_what_to_check.summary: The first antenatal contact establishes dates, baseline health, and risk. Everything later in the pregnancy is interpreted against what is recorded here.

terms: antenatal booking visit — parameters and checks

history: Confirm the pregnancy and establish dates: LMP, cycle regularity, contraception use, earliest ultrasound
Gravidity and parity — record the full obstetric history pregnancy by pregnancy
Previous pregnancy outcomes: mode of delivery, birth weights, gestation at delivery, complications, perinatal losses
Previous caesarean — indication, type of uterine incision, any complications
Medical history: hypertension, diabetes, cardiac disease, sickle cell disease, epilepsy, thyroid disease, mental health, HIV, TB, hepatitis
Surgical history including myomectomy or uterine surgery
Drug history and allergies; folic acid use
Family history: diabetes, hypertension, multiple pregnancy, genetic conditions, haemoglobinopathy
Social history: support, occupation, smoking, alcohol, substance use, intimate partner violence screening, nutrition, financial access to care

dating.naegele_rule: EDD = first day of LMP + 1 year − 3 months + 7 days (assumes a regular 28-day cycle with ovulation on day 14).
dating.caveat: Adjust for cycle length. Early ultrasound (before 14 weeks) is more accurate than LMP and should override it when they disagree by more than the accepted margin.
dating.gestational_age: Record in completed weeks and days.

examination: Blood pressure — record the baseline carefully; later hypertension is defined against it
General examination including pallor, jaundice, oedema, thyroid
Abdominal examination: symphysio-fundal height (from about 20 weeks), lie, presentation, fetal heart
Assess for scars from previous surgery
baseline_investigations: Blood group and Rhesus status, antibody screen
Hepatitis B surface antigen; hepatitis C where indicated
Urinalysis and midstream urine for asymptomatic bacteriuria
Random or fasting glucose; formal screening for gestational diabetes at the appropriate gestation
Malaria screening and intermittent preventive treatment where endemic
Ultrasound for dating and later anomaly scan
interventions_and_counselling: Folic acid (ideally started preconception) and iron supplementation per protocol
Insecticide-treated bed net and malaria prevention where endemic
Danger signs education — see the obstetric danger signs artifact
Birth preparedness and complication readiness plan
Where to deliver and transport plan
Discuss and document a plan for previous caesarean
risk_stratification_flags: Previous stillbirth, neonatal death, or preterm birth
Pre-existing hypertension, diabetes, cardiac or renal disease

warnings: Record the BOOKING blood pressure and protein status carefully — the diagnosis of pre-eclampsia later depends on this baseline.
A woman with a previous caesarean needs an explicit, documented plan for mode of delivery and place of birth.
Rhesus-negative women need a documented anti-D plan.
Screening for intimate partner violence should be conducted privately, without a partner present.

flashcards.a: LMP + 1 year − 3 months + 7 days

flashcards.q: Why is the booking blood pressure so important?
flashcards.a: Later diagnosis of gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia is made against this baseline

flashcards.q: Which dating method takes precedence when LMP and early scan disagree?
flashcards.a: Early ultrasound before 14 weeks

checkboxes: Full obstetric history taken pregnancy by pregnancy
Booking bloods sent including genotype and Rhesus
Birth plan and transport plan documented
Risk flags identified and plan made

governance.nigeria_overlay: Follow the National Guidelines for Antenatal Care and the National Malaria Control Programme schedule for intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) and insecticide-treated nets.

also_known_as: antenatal booking visit — parameters and checks

pre_eclampsia_and_eclampsia.title: Pre-eclampsia and Eclampsia
pre_eclampsia_and_eclampsia.summary: A multisystem hypertensive disorder of pregnancy. Magnesium sulfate prevents and treats eclamptic seizures; delivery is the definitive treatment.

terms: pre-eclampsia and eclampsia — assessment and management

definitions.definition: New hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria or other features
New hypertension after 20 weeks WITH proteinuria OR with maternal organ dysfunction or uteroplacental dysfunction (fetal growth restriction), even without proteinuria
Severe hypertension, symptoms of imminent eclampsia, thrombocytopenia, impaired liver function, renal insufficiency, pulmonary oedema, or new visual/cerebral disturbance
Generalised seizure in a woman with pre-eclampsia, not attributable to another cause
Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets — may occur with only modest hypertension

symptoms_of_imminent_eclampsia: Severe frontal or occipital headache not relieved by simple pain relief
Visual disturbance — blurring, flashing lights, scotomata
Epigastric or right upper quadrant pain
investigations: Blood pressure measured correctly with an appropriate cuff, repeated
Urinalysis for protein; quantify (protein:creatinine ratio or 24-hour)
Full blood count including platelets
Liver function tests
Urea, creatinine, electrolytes, uric acid
Coagulation screen if platelets low or HELLP suspected
Group and save
Fetal assessment: fetal heart, growth, liquor, umbilical artery Doppler, cardiotocography
management_principles: CONTROL SEIZURES: magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for both preventing and treating eclamptic seizures — superior to diazepam and phenytoin. Give a a bigger first dose to get the level up quickly then maintenance per protocol.
CONTROL BLOOD PRESSURE: antihypertensive therapy for severe hypertension to prevent maternal stroke. Avoid precipitous falls that compromise placental perfusion.
FLUID CAUTION: restrict fluids. Pulmonary oedema is a leading cause of death in pre-eclampsia; these women are intravascularly depleted but leak.
DELIVER: delivery is the only definitive treatment. Timing balances maternal risk against fetal maturity. In eclampsia, deliver once the mother is stabilised — not before.
Corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity where preterm delivery is anticipated and time allows.
Continue vigilance for at least 24–48 hours postpartum — a substantial proportion of eclampsia occurs AFTER delivery.
Left lateral position, airway protection and oxygen during a seizure. Do not restrain.
magnesium_toxicity_monitoring: Deep tendon (patellar) reflexes — LOSS OF REFLEXES IS THE EARLIEST WARNING
Respiratory rate — must remain above the protocol threshold
Urine output — magnesium is renally excreted, so oliguria causes accumulation
Antidote: calcium gluconate must be immediately available at the bedside whenever magnesium is running

warnings: MAGNESIUM SULFATE, NOT DIAZEPAM, IS FIRST LINE FOR ECLAMPTIC SEIZURES.
Calcium gluconate must be physically at the bedside before magnesium is started.
Loss of patellar reflexes is the earliest sign of magnesium toxicity — check them regularly and chart them.
Pre-eclampsia can occur without proteinuria, and HELLP can occur with unimpressive blood pressure. Do not exclude the diagnosis on one parameter.
Eclampsia occurs postpartum in a large minority of cases — monitoring must continue after delivery.
Do NOT fluid-load. Pulmonary oedema is a major cause of maternal death in this condition.

flashcards.a: Magnesium sulfate
Loss of deep tendon (patellar) reflexes
Calcium gluconate — must be at the bedside
Yes — organ dysfunction or fetal growth restriction can establish the diagnosis
Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets

checkboxes: Blood pressure measured correctly and repeated
Urinalysis for protein done and quantified
Symptoms of imminent eclampsia specifically asked about
Bloods including platelets and LFTs sent
Reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output charted
Steroids for fetal lung maturity if preterm

governance.nigeria_overlay: Confirm the magnesium sulfate loading and maintenance regimen (including whether the Pritchard intramuscular or Zuspan intravenous regimen is in use) against the National Standard Treatment Guidelines and the facility protocol.

also_known_as: pre-eclampsia and eclampsia — assessment and management

postpartum_bleeding_pph_stop_the_bleedin.title: Postpartum Bleeding (PPH) — Stop The Bleeding
postpartum_bleeding_pph_stop_the_bleedin.summary: Excessive bleeding after delivery. The four Ts organise the causes; uterine massage, uterotonics and rapid escalation save lives.

definitions.primary: Bleeding within 24 hours of delivery — traditionally ≥500 mL after vaginal birth or ≥1000 mL after caesarean, but ANY bleeding causing failing circulation — low BP, fast pulse, cold peripheries qualifies.
definitions.secondary: Abnormal bleeding from 24 hours to 12 weeks postpartum.

four_ts.action: Rub up a contraction with fundal massage, empty the bladder, uterotonics, bimanual compression, balloon tamponade

four_ts.meaning: Genital tract laceration, episiotomy, uterine rupture, uterine inversion, haematoma
four_ts.assessment: Well-contracted uterus but continued bleeding — inspect the cervix, vagina and perineum under good light
four_ts.action: Repair the tear; explore under anaesthesia if needed

four_ts.meaning: Retained placenta or placental fragments; morbidly adherent placenta
four_ts.assessment: Inspect the placenta and membranes for completeness
four_ts.action: Controlled cord traction, manual removal under anaesthesia, examination and evacuation of the uterus

four_ts.meaning: Coagulopathy — pre-existing, HELLP, DIC, amniotic fluid embolism, dilutional
four_ts.assessment: Oozing from puncture sites, non-clotting blood
four_ts.action: Correct with blood products guided by coagulation results and the massive haemorrhage protocol

immediate_sequence: CALL FOR HELP — this is a team emergency. Assign roles including a timekeeper and a scribe.
ABC. High-flow oxygen. Lie flat, keep warm.
Two large-bore cannulae; take FBC, coagulation, crossmatch (at least 4 units), fibrinogen.
Rub up a contraction by fundal massage.
Empty the bladder — catheterise.
Uterotonics per protocol: oxytocin first line; add ergometrine (avoid in hypertension), misoprostol, or carboprost (avoid in asthma) as escalation.
TRANEXAMIC ACID early — give as soon as PPH is diagnosed; benefit falls with delay.
Bimanual uterine compression while preparing definitive measures.
Aortic compression as a temporising measure in extremis.
Warm fluid and blood products; activate the massive haemorrhage protocol.
Examine under anaesthesia; repair trauma; remove retained tissue.
Intrauterine balloon tamponade.
Non-pneumatic anti-shock garment for stabilisation and transfer where available.
Surgical escalation: uterine compression sutures (e.g. B-Lynch), stepwise devascularisation (uterine and internal iliac artery ligation), and finally HYSTERECTOMY.
Do not delay hysterectomy in exsanguinating haemorrhage — delay costs lives.
prevention: Active management of the third stage of labour: prophylactic uterotonic, controlled cord traction, uterine massage
Identify and plan for risk factors: previous PPH, multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios, grand multiparity, prolonged or augmented labour, chorioamnionitis, placenta praevia or accreta spectrum, anaemia
Correct antenatal anaemia — anaemic women tolerate blood loss far less well
Deliver high-risk women where blood and surgery are available

warnings: Blood loss is systematically UNDERESTIMATED by eye. Weigh swabs and use calibrated drapes; trust the physiology (pulse, blood pressure, conscious level, urine output) over the estimate.
Young, healthy, anaemic women compensate well and then decompensate suddenly. Tachycardia and narrow pulse pressure precede hypotension.
Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia. Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma. Check before giving.
A well-contracted uterus with continuing bleeding means TRAUMA — inspect the genital tract thoroughly.
Do not delay definitive surgery, including hysterectomy, in a woman who is exsanguinating.

flashcards.a: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin
Uterine atony (tone) — about 70%

flashcards.q: When should tranexamic acid be given in PPH?
flashcards.a: As soon as PPH is diagnosed — benefit falls with delay

flashcards.q: Well-contracted uterus but still bleeding — what does that suggest?
flashcards.a: Genital tract trauma
Carboprost

checkboxes: Help called; roles assigned; timekeeper appointed
Genital tract inspected under good light
Placenta and membranes inspected for completeness
Hysterectomy considered without delay if exsanguinating

governance.nigeria_overlay: Confirm uterotonic availability, cold-chain status for oxytocin (heat-stable carbetocin may be an option), and the facility blood availability pathway. Where blood is scarce, early referral decisions must be protocolised.

pregnancy_danger_signs.title: Pregnancy Danger Signs
pregnancy_danger_signs.summary: The signs every pregnant or recently delivered woman and her family must be taught to recognise and act on immediately.

terms: when to come to hospital pregnancy

antenatal: Severe headache with or without visual disturbance
Swelling of the face and hands
postnatal_mother: Heavy bleeding or passage of large clots
Severe low mood, inability to care for the baby, or thoughts of harming self or baby
newborn: Not feeding or unable to suck
Jaundice on day 1 or extending to palms and soles
body.teaching_note: Danger-signs education is only effective when paired with a concrete plan: where to go, how to get there, who will accompany, and how it will be paid for.

warnings: Danger-signs counselling without a transport and funding plan does not change outcomes. Birth preparedness must be concrete.

flashcards.a: Vaginal bleeding, severe headache with visual disturbance, convulsions, severe abdominal pain

flashcards.q: Why is danger-signs teaching alone insufficient?
flashcards.a: Without a transport and funding plan, recognition does not translate into timely care

checkboxes: Danger signs taught to the woman
Taught to an accompanying family member

apgar_score.title: APGAR Score
apgar_score.summary: Five signs scored 0–2 at 1 and 5 minutes to describe the newborn's condition and response to resuscitation. It is a description, not a trigger — resuscitation starts before the score is assigned.

components.2: Cry, cough or sneeze; active withdrawal

body.timing: Assign at 1 and 5 minutes. If the 5-minute score is below 7, continue assigning every 5 minutes up to 20 minutes.

bands.label: Severely depressed
bands.action: Continue full resuscitation

bands.label: Moderately depressed
bands.action: Continue support and reassess

warnings: DO NOT WAIT FOR THE 1-MINUTE APGAR TO START RESUSCITATION. Drying, stimulation, airway positioning and ventilation begin immediately if the baby is not breathing.
The APGAR is not a measure of asphyxia and does not by itself predict long-term neurological outcome.
Prematurity, maternal sedation, congenital anomalies and neuromuscular disease all lower the score independently of asphyxia.
Heart rate and respiratory effort are the two components that actually drive resuscitation decisions.
limitations: Poor inter-observer reliability, particularly for colour and grimace.
Was never designed or validated as a prognostic tool.

flashcards.a: Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration
1 and 5 minutes; continue 5-minutely to 20 minutes if the 5-minute score is <7

flashcards.q: Do you delay resuscitation to score the APGAR?
flashcards.a: No — never
Heart rate and respiratory effort

child_dehydration_plan_a_b_c.title: Child Dehydration — Plan A, B, C
child_dehydration_plan_a_b_c.summary: Classify dehydration by clinical signs and choose plan A, B or C. Oral rehydration is the default; intravenous fluid is for shock and failed oral therapy.

terms: child dehydration — plan a, b, c
paediatric dehydration — assessment and fluid plan

classification.signs: Alert; eyes normal; drinks normally; skin pinch goes back immediately
Restless or irritable; sunken eyes; drinks eagerly, thirsty; skin pinch goes back slowly
Lethargic or unconscious; sunken eyes; drinks poorly or unable to drink; skin pinch goes back very slowly

plan_a: Give extra fluid: ORS, clean water, soups, breast milk. Continue breastfeeding.
Give zinc supplementation daily for 10–14 days — reduces duration and severity, and future episodes.
Continue feeding — do not starve the child.
Teach the mother the danger signs and when to return immediately.
Show her how to prepare and give ORS.
plan_b: Give ORS over 4 hours under supervision at the facility, in small frequent sips or by cup and spoon.
If vomiting, pause 10 minutes then continue more slowly.
plan_c: Start intravenous fluid IMMEDIATELY with an isotonic solution per the national protocol, in staged volumes.
Reassess frequently — pulse, perfusion, conscious level, urine output.
Start ORS by mouth or nasogastric tube as soon as the child can drink.
If IV access is impossible, use intraosseous access or nasogastric ORS while arranging transfer.
Give zinc once able to take oral therapy.
body.critical_exception_sam: A child with SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION must NOT receive standard rehydration. Use ReSoMal (reduced sodium, higher potassium) and give it slowly, because these children are at high risk of fluid overload and heart failure. Standard IV fluids in SAM without shock have caused deaths.
always: Look for and treat the cause: cholera, rotavirus, dysentery, malaria, sepsis, urinary infection, surgical abdomen
Check for blood in stool (dysentery) — requires antibiotic treatment
Assess nutritional status including MUAC and oedema
Weigh the child and use the weight to guide fluids

warnings: A CHILD WITH SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION FOLLOWS A DIFFERENT PROTOCOL. Standard fluid volumes can cause fatal fluid overload — use ReSoMal, given slowly.
Skin pinch is unreliable in marasmus (loss of subcutaneous fat) and in kwashiorkor (oedema masks it).
Do not use antidiarrhoeal or antimotility drugs in children.
Zinc is a core, evidence-based part of childhood diarrhoea management and is frequently omitted.
Weigh the child — fluid volumes are weight-based, and estimating weight is a common source of error.

flashcards.a: No dehydration, some dehydration, severe dehydration
Urgent intravenous rehydration for severe dehydration

flashcards.q: Which rehydration solution is used in severe acute malnutrition?
flashcards.a: ReSoMal — reduced sodium, higher potassium, given slowly

flashcards.q: How long is zinc given in childhood diarrhoea?
flashcards.a: 10–14 days

checkboxes: Dehydration category assigned using standard signs
SAM specifically excluded before choosing the fluid plan
Plan A, B or C selected and documented

governance.nigeria_overlay: Follow the National IMCI (Integrated Management of Childhood Illness) chart booklet for exact ORS and IV volumes and staging by age.

also_known_as: paediatric dehydration — assessment and fluid plan

severe_malnutrition_sam_ward_management.title: Severe Malnutrition (SAM) — Ward Management
severe_malnutrition_sam_ward_management.summary: Complicated SAM is managed in two phases — stabilisation then rehabilitation — with the WHO ten steps. The physiology is abnormal, so ordinary paediatric rules do not apply.

admission_criteria_6_59_months: Bilateral pitting oedema of nutritional origin
PLUS medical complications, failed appetite test, or no appetite → INPATIENT care
Without complications and with good appetite → OUTPATIENT therapeutic care with RUTF

oedema_grading.description: Bilateral pitting oedema of both feet
Oedema of feet, legs and arms
Oedema of feet, legs, arms and face/body — severe

ten_steps.note: Feed immediately and frequently, including at night. Check glucose.
Keep warm, cover head, kangaroo care, avoid draughts. Hypothermia and hypoglycaemia usually occur together and both signal infection.
Use ReSoMal, given SLOWLY. Assessing dehydration clinically is unreliable in SAM. IV fluids only for shock.
All have excess body sodium and deficient potassium and magnesium. DO NOT give sodium-rich fluids or treat oedema with a diuretic.
Classic signs of infection are usually ABSENT. Give broad-spectrum antibiotics routinely on admission per protocol.
Vitamin A, folic acid, zinc, multivitamin. WITHHOLD IRON during the stabilisation phase — iron worsens infection and oxidative stress; add it only in the rehabilitation phase.
F-75 (low protein, low energy, low sodium) in small frequent feeds, including overnight. The aim is to maintain, not to gain.

Transition to RUTF or F-100 over 2–3 days once stabilised, appetite has returned and oedema is reducing. WHO 2023 recommends transitioning from F-75 to RUTF over 2–3 days as tolerated, with energy intake of about 100–135 kcal/kg/day during the transition.

ten_steps.action: Provide SENSORY STIMULATION and emotional support
ten_steps.note: Play, tender loving care, maternal involvement. Developmental delay is part of the illness.
Discharge criteria, outpatient linkage, caregiver education, household food security, immunisation catch-up.

refeeding_syndrome: The lethal risk of feeding too much too fast.
Insulin surge drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells.
Presents with cardiac failure, arrhythmia, respiratory failure, confusion, seizures and sudden death.
Prevention: start low and slow (F-75), monitor and replace electrolytes, watch for a rising respiratory rate and pulse, and for increasing oedema or hepatomegaly.
body.danger_of_over_transfusion: If transfusion is needed for severe anaemia, use a small volume slowly with a diuretic per protocol — these children develop heart failure easily.

warnings: DO NOT GIVE IRON DURING THE STABILISATION PHASE. It increases infection risk and oxidative injury.
DO NOT GIVE A DIURETIC FOR NUTRITIONAL OEDEMA. The oedema is not from fluid overload and diuretics are harmful.
DO NOT USE STANDARD ORS. Use ReSoMal, given slowly. Standard ORS has too much sodium and too little potassium for these children.
Signs of infection are usually absent — treat presumptively with antibiotics on admission.
A rising respiratory rate or pulse, or increasing oedema or liver size, during feeding suggests fluid overload or refeeding syndrome. Stop and reassess.
Hypoglycaemia and hypothermia in a child with SAM signal serious infection and carry high death rate.
limitations: Energy targets and RUTF quantities have been debated in the literature since the 2023 WHO guideline. Follow the national CMAM protocol.
Infants under 6 months with SAM require a separate protocol focused on re-establishing breastfeeding.

flashcards.q: Why is iron withheld in the stabilisation phase of SAM?
flashcards.a: It increases infection risk and oxidative stress
ReSoMal — reduced sodium, higher potassium, given slowly

flashcards.q: Should nutritional oedema be treated with a diuretic?
flashcards.a: No — never; it is not from fluid overload
F-75 is for stabilisation (maintain); F-100/RUTF is for rehabilitation (catch-up growth)

flashcards.q: Two conditions that signal serious infection in SAM?
flashcards.a: Hypoglycaemia and hypothermia
Excess total body sodium, deficient potassium and magnesium

checkboxes: Bilateral pitting oedema assessed and graded
Complications assessed to decide inpatient vs outpatient
Vitamin A, folic acid, zinc given
F-75 started in small frequent feeds including at night
Respiratory rate and pulse charted for overload
Transition to RUTF/F-100 only when criteria met

sources: WHO guideline on the prevention and management of wasting and nutritional oedema (acute malnutrition) in infants and children under 5 years. Geneva: WHO; 2023.
WHO. Transition feeding of children 6–59 months of age with severe acute malnutrition (eLENA).
governance.nigeria_overlay: Follow the National Guidelines for Community Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM), Federal Ministry of Health, for admission criteria, feed volumes, antibiotic choice and discharge criteria.

newborn_jaundice_assess.title: Newborn Jaundice — Assess
newborn_jaundice_assess.summary: Jaundice is common and usually physiological, but the dangerous causes present early, rise fast, or persist. Kernicterus is preventable and devastating.

red_flags_never_physiological: Jaundice in the FIRST 24 HOURS of life — always pathological
Jaundice extending to the palms and soles
Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia at any age — think biliary atresia, and time matters
Jaundice persisting beyond 14 days in a term baby (21 days if preterm)
Pale stools and dark urine — obstructive picture
Signs of sepsis, poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, high-pitched cry

day_1: Haemolysis: Rhesus or ABO incompatibility, G6PD deficiency, spherocytosis

clinical_assessment: Examine in bright natural light, blanching the skin
Kramer's rule gives a rough cephalocaudal progression estimate but is unreliable — it must not replace bilirubin measurement
Assess tone, cry, feeding and alertness for acute bilirubin encephalopathy
investigations: Total AND conjugated (direct) bilirubin — the split is essential
Blood group of mother and baby; direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test
Full blood count, reticulocyte count, blood film
G6PD assay where prevalent
Sepsis screen if unwell
Thyroid function if prolonged
Urine culture if prolonged
Liver function and ultrasound if conjugated
management_principles: Plot bilirubin against gestational age and postnatal age on the appropriate treatment threshold chart
Ensure adequate feeding and hydration — poor intake worsens jaundice
Phototherapy per chart thresholds
Exchange transfusion for very high levels or signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy
Intravenous immunoglobulin may be used in isoimmune haemolytic disease per protocol
Treat the underlying cause: sepsis, hypothyroidism, urinary infection
CONJUGATED hyperbilirubinaemia requires urgent investigation for biliary atresia — surgical outcomes deteriorate sharply with delay
acute_bilirubin_encephalopathy: Intermediate: irritability, high-pitched cry, hypertonia with retrocollis and opisthotonus, fever
Chronic (kernicterus): athetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, gaze palsy, dental dysplasia

warnings: JAUNDICE IN THE FIRST 24 HOURS IS ALWAYS PATHOLOGICAL. Investigate urgently.
ALWAYS SPLIT THE BILIRUBIN. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is never physiological and biliary atresia is time-critical.
Visual estimation of jaundice severity is unreliable, especially in darker skin. Measure the bilirubin.

G6PD deficiency is common in many African populations and can cause severe rapid haemolysis — ask about family history and avoid precipitants including naphthalene mothballs (camphor balls), which are a well-documented cause in West Africa.
Phototherapy thresholds depend on gestational age, postnatal age and risk factors — use the chart, not a single number.

flashcards.q: Jaundice in the first 24 hours means?
flashcards.a: Always pathological — usually haemolysis or sepsis

flashcards.q: Why must bilirubin always be split?
flashcards.a: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is never physiological and may be biliary atresia, which is time-critical

flashcards.q: How long may physiological jaundice persist in a term baby?
flashcards.a: Up to 14 days; beyond that requires investigation

flashcards.q: Local precipitant of G6PD haemolysis to counsel against?
flashcards.a: Naphthalene/camphor mothballs used to store baby clothes

checkboxes: Plotted on the correct treatment threshold chart
Mother and baby blood group and Coombs done
Naphthalene/mothball exposure asked about and counselled

governance.nigeria_overlay: G6PD deficiency and exposure to naphthalene mothballs are important local causes of severe neonatal jaundice. Counsel explicitly against storing baby clothes with camphor/naphthalene balls.

mental_state_examination_mse.title: Mental State Examination (MSE)
mental_state_examination_mse.summary: A structured description of the patient's mental state at the time of interview. It records observation and phenomenology, not interpretation or diagnosis.

record: Apparent age, build, self-care and grooming, clothing appropriateness
Physical signs: injuries, tremor, sweating, needle marks, weight loss, pallor
Level of consciousness and alertness
Eye contact, rapport, facial expression
Psychomotor activity: retardation, agitation, restlessness, stupor
Abnormal movements: tremor, tics, dystonia, tardive dyskinesia, catatonic signs (waxy flexibility, posturing, negativism, echopraxia)
Attitude to the interviewer: cooperative, guarded, hostile, seductive, perplexed
Rate: pressured, slow
Volume: loud, soft, inaudible
Quantity: poverty of speech, over-talkative
Fluency and rhythm; dysarthria, stuttering
Spontaneity
NOTE: speech describes FORM; content belongs under thought
MOOD — the patient's own subjective description, ideally in quotation of their own words
AFFECT — your objective observation: range (full, restricted, blunted, flat), reactivity, congruence with stated mood, lability, appropriateness
Flight of ideas, loosening of associations, tangentiality, circumstantiality
Thought block, perseveration, neologism, clang association, word salad
Poverty of thought
Preoccupations, ruminations, obsessions, phobias
Overvalued ideas

DELUSIONS: describe the belief, its fixity, and whether it is bizarre. Types: persecutory, grandiose, referential, nihilistic, guilt, jealousy, control, thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcasting, somatic
Suicidal and homicidal ideation — ALWAYS asked directly and recorded explicitly
Hallucinations: modality (auditory, visual, olfactory, gustatory, tactile), content, second vs third person, command hallucinations
Illusions
Depersonalisation and derealisation
Note: visual hallucinations raise the probability of an organic cause
Orientation to time, place and person
Attention and concentration (e.g. serial sevens, months backwards)
Registration and short-term memory
Long-term memory
Language, praxis, executive function
Use a formal tool (e.g. MMSE, MoCA) where indicated, noting its limitations by education and language
Does the patient recognise that something is wrong?
Do they attribute it to a mental illness?
Do they accept the need for treatment?
Insight is a spectrum, not a yes/no
Capacity to reason about consequences and make decisions in their own interest
Risk to SELF: suicidal ideation, plan, means, intent, preparatory acts, protective factors, previous attempts
Risk to OTHERS: thoughts, targets, means, history of violence
Risk FROM others: exploitation, abuse, neglect
Risk of SELF-NEGLECT: nutrition, hygiene, medical non-adherence
Record what was asked and the answers given, not just a conclusion

body.organic_screen: Always consider and exclude organic causes: delirium, infection, metabolic disturbance, hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, drug intoxication or withdrawal, medication effect, head injury, epilepsy, thyroid disease, HIV, neurosyphilis, B12 deficiency, space-occupying lesion.
body.documentation_principle: Record what you observed and what the patient said, in descriptive terms. 'Patient stated: I hear my neighbour's voice telling me to leave the house' is a finding. 'Patient is psychotic' is a conclusion and belongs in the formulation, not the MSE.

warnings: ALWAYS ASK DIRECTLY ABOUT SUICIDAL IDEATION. Asking does not plant the idea; not asking leaves risk undetected.
Visual hallucinations, fluctuating consciousness and disorientation point strongly towards an organic cause — screen physically before attributing symptoms to primary mental illness.
Cognitive screening tools are affected by education, literacy and language. Interpret them in that context and record which language was used.
The MSE describes the present moment. Repeat it — the mental state changes.

flashcards.a: Mood is the patient's subjective report; affect is your objective observation

flashcards.q: Which hallucination modality most suggests an organic cause?
flashcards.a: Visual

flashcards.q: Does asking about suicide increase risk?
flashcards.a: No — asking directly is essential and does not plant the idea

flashcards.q: Where does 'thought block' belong — form or content?
flashcards.a: Form

checkboxes: Mood recorded in the patient's own words
Suicidal ideation asked about DIRECTLY and documented
Organic causes considered and physical examination done

delirium_or_dementia.title: Delirium or Dementia?
delirium_or_dementia.summary: Two syndromes of cognitive impairment that are constantly confused. Delirium is acute, fluctuating and usually reversible; missing it is dangerous.

comparison.dementia: Progressive, relatively stable day to day

comparison.delirium: IMPAIRED — this is the cardinal feature

comparison.dementia: Less common early (except Lewy body dementia)

comparison.delirium: Usually reversible if the cause is treated

body.critical_point: HYPOACTIVE DELIRIUM IS THE COMMONEST TYPE AND THE MOST OFTEN MISSED. The quiet, withdrawn, drowsy patient is easily labelled 'just tired' or 'depressed'. It carries the worse prognosis.
delirium_causes_pinch_me: plus: hypoxia, electrolyte disturbance, hypoglycaemia, urinary retention, alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal, stroke, head injury, sepsis, myocardial infarction, thyroid disease, B12 deficiency
delirium_management: Identify and treat the underlying cause — this is the treatment
Review and stop deliriogenic drugs (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids, steroids)
Optimise environment: good lighting, day-night orientation, clock and calendar, familiar objects, family presence
Ensure glasses and hearing aids are worn
Mobilise; avoid catheters and lines where possible
Address pain, constipation, urinary retention, hydration and nutrition
Antipsychotics only for severe distress or danger, at the lowest dose for the shortest time — AVOID in Lewy body dementia and Parkinson disease, where they can cause severe reactions

dementia_types.features: Insidious memory-led decline, amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles
Stepwise decline, focal signs, vascular risk factors
Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behaviour disorder, severe antipsychotic sensitivity
Early personality and behavioural change or language impairment, younger onset
Hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, HIV, normal pressure hydrocephalus, depression (pseudodementia), subdural haematoma

warnings: DELIRIUM AND DEMENTIA FREQUENTLY COEXIST. Dementia is the biggest risk factor for delirium — a sudden change in a person with dementia is delirium until proven otherwise.
Hypoactive delirium is missed routinely and has the worst outcomes.
AVOID ANTIPSYCHOTICS IN LEWY BODY DEMENTIA AND PARKINSON DISEASE — severe sensitivity reactions can occur.
Always check glucose, oxygenation and for urinary retention and constipation in acute confusion.
Delirium is associated with increased death rate, longer stay and higher rates of institutionalisation — it is not benign.

flashcards.a: Impaired attention and altered consciousness with acute fluctuating onset

flashcards.q: Which delirium subtype is most often missed?
flashcards.a: Hypoactive

flashcards.q: PINCH ME mnemonic for delirium causes?
flashcards.a: Pain, INfection, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment

flashcards.q: Which dementia has severe antipsychotic sensitivity?
flashcards.a: Lewy body dementia

checkboxes: Time course established from a collateral history
Glasses and hearing aids in place
Lewy body/Parkinson sensitivity checked before any antipsychotic
Follow-up cognitive assessment planned once acute illness resolves

tb_treatment_regimens_and_drug_resistanc.title: TB Treatment — Regimens and Drug Resistance
tb_treatment_regimens_and_drug_resistanc.summary: Regimen families for drug-susceptible TB and for MDR/RR-TB, including the 6-month all-oral BPaLM and BDLLfxC regimens. Drug choice depends on susceptibility testing and national programme policy.

terms: tb treatment — regimens and drug resistance
tuberculosis treatment — drug-susceptible and drug-resistant regimens

drug_susceptible_adult.standard: Intensive phase of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, followed by a continuation phase of isoniazid and rifampicin — conventionally written 2RHZE / 4RH.
drug_susceptible_adult.shorter_option: A 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin-containing regimen is recommended by WHO for eligible patients with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB where rifapentine is available.
drug_susceptible_adult.paediatric_note: WHO recommends a 4-month regimen for selected children and adolescents with non-severe drug-susceptible TB. Paediatric dosing uses weight bands and dispersible fixed-dose combinations.
drug_susceptible_adult.extrapulmonary: TB meningitis and osteoarticular TB require longer continuation phases; TB meningitis also requires adjunctive corticosteroid.

first_line_drug_notes.key_toxicity: Peripheral neuropathy (give pyridoxine), hepatitis, drug-induced lupus
first_line_drug_notes.note: Pyridoxine is essential in pregnancy, HIV, malnutrition, diabetes, alcohol use and renal failure

first_line_drug_notes.key_toxicity: Hepatitis, orange discolouration of urine, tears and contact lenses, flu-like syndrome
first_line_drug_notes.note: POTENT CYP450 INDUCER — reduces the effect of oral contraceptives, warfarin, many antiretrovirals, azoles, corticosteroids and others. Always screen interactions.
Dose-reduced or avoided in significant renal impairment

first_line_drug_notes.key_toxicity: OPTIC NEURITIS — loss of visual acuity and red-green colour discrimination
first_line_drug_notes.note: Baseline and periodic visual acuity and colour vision checks; warn the patient to report visual change immediately
Injectable; largely displaced by all-oral regimens

definitions.meaning: Resistant to at least isoniazid AND rifampicin
MDR/RR-TB with additional resistance to any fluoroquinolone
MDR/RR-TB with fluoroquinolone resistance plus resistance to at least one other Group A drug

bpalm.regimen: Bedaquiline, Pretomanid, Linezolid, Moxifloxacin for 6 months
bpalm.linezolid_dose: 600 mg once daily for both BPaLM and BPaL
bpalm.evidence: TB-PRACTECAL stage 2 showed treatment success of about 89% with BPaLM versus about 52% with the standard of care regimens of the time
bpalm.exclusions: Not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding because of limited pretomanid safety data. Caution where there has been more than one month of previous exposure to bedaquiline, linezolid, pretomanid or delamanid unless resistance to those agents has been excluded.
bpalm.fluoroquinolone_dst: Fluoroquinolone susceptibility testing is strongly encouraged but must not delay starting BPaLM; the result decides whether moxifloxacin is retained (BPaLM) or dropped (BPaL).

bdllfxc.regimen: Bedaquiline, Delamanid, Linezolid, Levofloxacin, Clofazimine for 6 months
bdllfxc.indication: MDR/RR-TB with or without additional fluoroquinolone resistance (pre-XDR-TB)
bdllfxc.status: A newer all-oral 6-month option introduced in the WHO consolidated guidelines, Module 4: treatment and care (2025 consolidation).

drug_resistant.nine_month: Modified all-oral 9-month regimens remain recommended for MDR/RR-TB where fluoroquinolone resistance has been excluded.
drug_resistant.longer_regimens: Individualised longer all-oral regimens built from Group A, B and C drugs for patients not eligible for shorter regimens.

key_toxicity_monitoring_dr_tb.monitor: ECG for QT prolongation; liver function
ECG for QT prolongation; tendinopathy; dysglycaemia
QT prolongation; skin and conjunctival discolouration

MYELOSUPPRESSION (full blood count), PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY, OPTIC NEURITIS. Dose may be reduced to 300 mg or interrupted for significant toxicity, but dose modification should be avoided in the first 9 weeks if possible.
Liver function; combined QT effect with other agents

cross_cutting_care: HIV testing for every person with TB; start antiretroviral therapy per national timing guidance
Contact tracing and TB preventive treatment for eligible contacts
Baseline and periodic monitoring: weight, sputum, liver function, renal function, visual acuity, ECG where QT-prolonging drugs are used
Manage drug interactions, especially rifampicin with antiretrovirals and hormonal contraception

warnings: NEVER ADD A SINGLE DRUG TO A FAILING TB REGIMEN — this generates further resistance.
Regimen selection and dosing must follow the National TB Programme. This artifact describes regimen families, not a prescription.
Multiple QT-prolonging agents are combined in DR-TB regimens; ECG monitoring and electrolyte correction (potassium, magnesium, calcium) are mandatory.
Warn every patient on ethambutol to report any visual change immediately.
Rifampicin failure of hormonal contraception is a common and avoidable harm — counsel and offer alternative contraception.
Pretomanid-containing regimens are not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
limitations: Exact doses, weight bands and durations are deliberately not reproduced here — they change with guideline revisions and differ by national programme.
Drug availability, especially pretomanid and delamanid, varies markedly by country.

flashcards.a: Bedaquiline, Pretomanid, Linezolid, Moxifloxacin — 6 months for MDR/RR and pre-XDR TB
600 mg once daily
Bedaquiline, Delamanid, Linezolid, Levofloxacin, Clofazimine
Optic neuritis — loss of acuity and red-green colour discrimination

flashcards.q: Why must you never add one drug to a failing regimen?
flashcards.a: It amplifies resistance

flashcards.q: Which first-line TB drug is a potent CYP450 inducer?
flashcards.a: Rifampicin
Myelosuppression, peripheral neuropathy, optic neuritis

checkboxes: Bacteriological confirmation and rapid molecular DST obtained
HIV test done and result documented
Baseline visual acuity and colour vision if on ethambutol
Baseline ECG if QT-prolonging drugs used
Potassium, magnesium and calcium checked and corrected
Notification to the national programme completed

sources: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis. Module 4: treatment — drug-resistant tuberculosis treatment, 2022 update.
WHO. Consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 4: treatment and care (2025 consolidation), introducing BDLLfxC.
WHO news release, 15 April 2025: WHO announces landmark changes in treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis.
WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2025, section 2.4.
governance.nigeria_overlay: Follow the National Tuberculosis, Leprosy and Buruli Ulcer Control Programme (NTBLCP) guidelines for regimen selection, weight-band dosing, drug availability and reporting.

malaria_diagnosis_severity_and_treatment.title: Malaria — Diagnosis, Severity and Treatment
malaria_diagnosis_severity_and_treatment.summary: Parasitological confirmation before treatment, artemisinin-based combination therapy for uncomplicated disease, and by injection or drip, not by mouth artesunate for severe malaria.

terms: malaria — diagnosis, severity and treatment principles

species.note: Causes almost all severe disease and death; no hypnozoite stage; can sequester in the microvasculature
Hypnozoites cause relapse; needs radical cure with an 8-aminoquinoline after G6PD testing
Quartan fever; may cause chronic low-grade parasitaemia and nephrotic syndrome
Zoonotic, Southeast Asia; can be rapidly severe

diagnosis: Parasitological confirmation before treatment wherever possible — rapid diagnostic test or microscopy
Thick film for detection and parasite density; thin film for species identification
A negative RDT does not exclude malaria in a very ill patient — repeat and use microscopy
Some RDTs miss falciparum with hrp2/hrp3 gene deletions
Quantify parasitaemia where possible — it informs severity
severe_malaria_criteria: Prostration — inability to sit, stand or feed
Abnormal bleeding or disseminated intravascular coagulation
Jaundice with another sign of organ dysfunction

treatment_principles.uncomplicated: Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), chosen and dosed according to the national malaria treatment guideline. Complete the full course even when symptoms resolve.
treatment_principles.severe: by injection or drip, not by mouth ARTESUNATE is the treatment of choice for severe malaria in adults and children, and is superior to quinine. Give at least 24 hours of by injection or drip, not by mouth therapy and until oral medication is tolerated, then complete a full course of ACT.
treatment_principles.pre_referral: Where by injection or drip, not by mouth treatment cannot be given immediately, rectal artesunate is recommended as pre-referral treatment in children under 6 years, followed by immediate referral.
treatment_principles.vivax_radical_cure: An 8-aminoquinoline is needed to clear hypnozoites — G6PD status must be assessed first because of haemolysis risk.
treatment_principles.delayed_haemolysis: Post-artesunate delayed haemolysis can occur one to three weeks after treatment — check haemoglobin at follow-up.

supportive_care_severe: Check and treat HYPOGLYCAEMIA repeatedly — it is common, especially in children, pregnancy and with quinine
Cautious fluid management — avoid aggressive bolus fluid in children with impaired perfusion, which increased death rate in the FEAST trial
Transfuse for severe anaemia per protocol
Monitor renal function and urine output
Exclude and treat concurrent bacterial sepsis, especially in children and pregnancy
Nurse unconscious patients carefully; airway protection
prevention: Perennial malaria chemoprevention in infants where applicable
Malaria vaccination in eligible children where implemented
malaria_in_pregnancy: Higher risk of severe disease, anaemia, low birth weight, stillbirth and maternal death
Placental sequestration means peripheral films may be negative despite significant infection
Treat promptly; drug choice by trimester follows national guidance

warnings: ALWAYS CHECK GLUCOSE in severe malaria — hypoglycaemia is common, recurrent and easily fatal, particularly in children and pregnancy.
by injection or drip, not by mouth artesunate is superior to quinine for severe malaria and should be first line where available.
Aggressive fluid bolus therapy in African children with severe febrile illness and impaired perfusion increased death rate in the FEAST trial — fluid resuscitation must be cautious and protocolised.
Do not exclude malaria on a single negative rapid test in a severely ill patient in an endemic area.
Concurrent bacterial sepsis is common in severe malaria — consider empirical antibiotics.
Warn about post-artesunate delayed haemolysis and arrange a follow-up haemoglobin.
limitations: Specific ACT choice, dosing and second-line agents differ by country and change with resistance surveillance.

flashcards.a: Parenteral artesunate — superior to quinine
P. vivax and P. ovale

flashcards.q: What must always be checked and rechecked in severe malaria?
flashcards.a: Blood glucose

flashcards.q: What did the FEAST trial show?
flashcards.a: Fluid bolus therapy increased mortality in African children with severe febrile illness and impaired perfusion
Delayed haemolysis — check haemoglobin at follow-up

checkboxes: Renal function and acid-base assessed in severe disease
Parenteral artesunate started for severe malaria
Pre-referral rectal artesunate given if transfer needed
Full oral ACT course completed after parenteral therapy
Follow-up haemoglobin arranged for delayed haemolysis
Bed net and prevention counselling given

sources: WHO Guidelines for malaria (regularly updated).
governance.nigeria_overlay: Follow the National Malaria Elimination Programme (NMEP) treatment guidelines for first- and second-line ACT selection, severe malaria protocols, IPTp schedule and case management in pregnancy.
