antibiotics_classes_cover_and_side_effec.title: Antibiotics — Classes, Cover and Side Effects
antibiotics_classes_cover_and_side_effec.summary: Structural map of antibacterial classes: how they work, what they cover, and their signature toxicities. Empirical choice must follow the local antibiogram.

terms: antibiotic classes, mechanism and spectrum — reference
antibiotics — classes, cover and side effects

classes.mechanism: Inhibit cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins
classes.spectrum_note: Narrow to very broad depending on agent; cloxacillin class for staphylococci; piperacillin-tazobactam broad including Pseudomonas
classes.toxicity: Hypersensitivity including anaphylaxis, rash, diarrhoea, interstitial nephritis, seizures at high dose

classes.spectrum_note: Gram-negative cover broadens with generation; ceftazidime covers Pseudomonas; poor enterococcal cover throughout
classes.toxicity: Hypersensitivity, Clostridioides difficile, biliary sludging with ceftriaxone; ceftriaxone incompatible with calcium-containing fluids in neonates

classes.mechanism: Cell wall synthesis inhibition, stable to most beta-lactamases
classes.spectrum_note: Very broad; reserve agents; ertapenem lacks Pseudomonas cover
classes.toxicity: Seizures (especially imipenem), C. difficile; strong stewardship restriction

classes.mechanism: Bind D-Ala-D-Ala, blocking cell wall cross-linking
classes.toxicity: Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, infusion reaction ('red man' syndrome) if given too fast; requires therapeutic drug monitoring

classes.mechanism: Bind 30S ribosomal subunit, irreversible; concentration-dependent killing
classes.spectrum_note: Aerobic Gram-negatives; synergy with beta-lactams for enterococci and staphylococci; NO anaerobic activity
classes.toxicity: NEPHROTOXICITY and OTOTOXICITY (vestibular and cochlear, often irreversible), neuromuscular blockade; requires level monitoring

classes.spectrum_note: Atypicals (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydia), some Gram-positives, Campylobacter
classes.toxicity: QT prolongation, gastrointestinal upset, hepatitis, many CYP interactions (less with azithromycin)

classes.mechanism: Inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
classes.spectrum_note: Broad Gram-negative; moxifloxacin better Gram-positive and anaerobic; ciprofloxacin covers Pseudomonas
classes.toxicity: TENDINOPATHY AND TENDON RUPTURE, peripheral neuropathy, QT prolongation, aortic aneurysm risk, CNS effects, dysglycaemia, C. difficile; avoid with divalent cations

classes.spectrum_note: Atypicals, rickettsiae, Brucella, some MRSA, malaria prevention adjunct
classes.toxicity: Photosensitivity, oesophageal ulceration (take upright with water), dental staining and effects on growing bone — avoid in pregnancy and young children

classes.mechanism: Reduced intracellularly to reactive intermediates that damage DNA
classes.spectrum_note: Anaerobes and protozoa (amoebiasis, giardiasis, trichomoniasis); preferred in tetanus
classes.toxicity: Metallic taste, disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use

classes.spectrum_note: Broad; Pneumocystis prevention and treatment; nocardia; some MRSA
classes.toxicity: Rash including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, hyperkalaemia, marrow suppression, raised creatinine without true GFR change, kernicterus risk in neonates

classes.spectrum_note: Gram-positives and anaerobes; toxin suppression in necrotising soft tissue infection
classes.toxicity: Strongly associated with C. difficile colitis

classes.spectrum_note: Very broad; used for typhoid and meningitis where alternatives are unavailable
classes.toxicity: APLASTIC ANAEMIA (unpredictable, not dose-related, dose-independent), dose-related marrow suppression, GREY BABY SYNDROME in neonates

classes.spectrum_note: Gram-positive including MRSA and VRE; also used in DR-TB
classes.toxicity: Myelosuppression, peripheral and optic neuropathy, serotonin syndrome risk with serotonergic drugs, lactic acidosis

stewardship_principles: Take cultures before antibiotics wherever this does not delay treatment in sepsis
Start empirically based on the LOCAL antibiogram, likely source and patient factors
Review at 48–72 hours: step down to a narrower or lower-dose treatment, switch intravenous to oral, or stop
Document indication, dose, route, planned duration and review date on the chart
Verify allergy history properly — most reported penicillin allergy is not true allergy
Consider drug interactions and QT-prolonging combinations

warnings: This is a class reference, not a prescribing authority. Empirical antibiotic choice must follow the facility antibiogram and national antimicrobial stewardship policy.
Verify allergy histories carefully — an unverified penicillin allergy label drives use of broader, more toxic, more expensive agents.
Aminoglycosides and vancomycin require therapeutic drug monitoring and renal dose adjustment.
Fluoroquinolone tendon rupture and neuropathy may be permanent — counsel patients and avoid where a safer option exists.
Chloramphenicol's aplastic anaemia is unpredictable, not dose-related and not dose-related.

flashcards.a: Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity (vestibular and cochlear)

flashcards.q: Which antibiotic class causes tendon rupture?
flashcards.a: Fluoroquinolones
Dose-related suppression and idiosyncratic aplastic anaemia; plus grey baby syndrome in neonates
Metronidazole

flashcards.q: Why does vancomycin need slow infusion?
flashcards.a: To avoid the infusion-related 'red man' reaction

checkboxes: Cultures taken before antibiotics where feasible

governance.nigeria_overlay: Align with the Nigeria National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance and the facility antibiogram. Rising resistance in Salmonella Typhi, Klebsiella and Staphylococcus aureus makes local data essential.

also_known_as: antibiotic classes, mechanism and spectrum — reference

brand_names_what_drug_is_this.title: Brand Names — What Drug Is This?
brand_names_what_drug_is_this.summary: Locally encountered brand names mapped to their generic ingredients. Brand names are unregulated across markets and the same brand can contain different drugs in different countries.

terms: brand name to generic — governed alias register
brand names — what drug is this?

aliases.caution: Respiratory depression; dependence; interacts with other CNS depressants
Systemic ketoconazole carries significant hepatotoxicity and interaction risk and is restricted in many countries — confirm the exact formulation
Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol
Cholestatic hepatitis; diarrhoea
QT prolongation
Tendinopathy; avoid with divalent cations
Take with fat-containing food for absorption
As above
Hepatotoxicity in overdose; check for paracetamol in combination products
Tremor, tachycardia, hypokalaemia at high dose
Hypokalaemia, hypovolaemia, ototoxicity at high dose
Prolonged hypoglycaemia
Withhold in significant renal impairment and around iodinated contrast per protocol
High risk of prolonged hypoglycaemia, especially in older adults and renal impairment
Cough, hyperkalaemia, angio-oedema; contraindicated in pregnancy
Ankle oedema, flushing
Sedation, anticholinergic effects in older adults
Avoid in glaucoma, myasthenia, bowel obstruction with paralytic ileus
Avoid in first trimester per local guidance
Rash, hyperkalaemia, marrow suppression

body.governance_rule: Every alias must be reviewed and approved by pharmacy against the actual product registered in the jurisdiction of use. Aliases are jurisdiction-scoped and must never be applied globally.

warnings: THE SAME BRAND NAME CAN CONTAIN DIFFERENT ACTIVE INGREDIENTS IN DIFFERENT COUNTRIES. Always verify against the physical pack and the national registration.
Combination products frequently hide a second active ingredient — paracetamol-containing combinations are a common cause of inadvertent overdose.
Prescribe by generic name. Brand aliases exist here for RECOGNITION when a patient reports what they have been taking, not for prescribing.
Substandard and falsified medicines are a documented problem in several markets — consider product quality when a patient fails to respond.

flashcards.a: Dihydrocodeine

flashcards.q: Why must brand aliases be jurisdiction-scoped?
flashcards.a: The same brand name may contain different active ingredients in different countries
Artemether-lumefantrine

heart_failure_the_four_pillars.title: Heart Failure — The Four Pillars
heart_failure_the_four_pillars.summary: The four pillars of prognostic therapy in HFrEF, plus symptomatic and adjunctive agents. Diuretics relieve symptoms; the four pillars change survival.

terms: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction — disease-modifying therapy

four_pillars.agents: ARNI (sacubitril-valsartan) preferred where available and tolerated; otherwise ACE inhibitor; ARB if ACE inhibitor not tolerated because of cough
four_pillars.monitoring: Renal function and potassium before and after each titration; blood pressure
four_pillars.cautions: Hyperkalaemia, renal impairment, angio-oedema (never combine ARNI with an ACE inhibitor — leave a 36-hour washout), contraindicated in pregnancy, avoid with bilateral renal artery stenosis

four_pillars.agents: Evidence-based agents only: bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, nebivolol
four_pillars.monitoring: Heart rate, blood pressure, symptoms of decompensation
four_pillars.cautions: START LOW, GO SLOW. Do not start during acute decompensation with fluid overload. Symptoms may transiently worsen before improving. Caution in severe asthma and high-grade heart block

four_pillars.monitoring: POTASSIUM AND RENAL FUNCTION before starting, at 1 and 4 weeks, then regularly
four_pillars.cautions: Hyperkalaemia, especially with ACE inhibitor/ARNI and in renal impairment; gynaecomastia with spironolactone

four_pillars.agents: Dapagliflozin or empagliflozin — benefit is independent of diabetes status
four_pillars.monitoring: Renal function, volume status, glucose in people with diabetes
four_pillars.cautions: Genital mycotic infection, volume depletion, EUGLYCAEMIC DKA (withhold during acute illness, fasting and around surgery), rare necrotising fasciitis of the perineum

additional_agents.role: Symptom and congestion control — improves symptoms but is not a death rate-reducing therapy
additional_agents.monitoring: Weight, renal function, electrolytes, volume status

additional_agents.role: Sinus rhythm with heart rate above target despite maximal tolerated beta-blockade
Where RAS blockade is not tolerated; additional benefit demonstrated in self-identified Black patients
Symptom and hospitalisation reduction; rate control in atrial fibrillation — see the digoxin artifact
Selected patients after a worsening heart failure event
Intravenous iron for iron deficiency improves symptoms and function
Only if there is a specific indication such as atrial fibrillation or thrombus — not routine in HFrEF alone

device_and_other: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator and cardiac resynchronisation therapy for selected patients
Salt and fluid advice, daily weights and a self-management plan
Treat the cause: ischaemia, valve disease, hypertension, arrhythmia, alcohol, thyroid disease, anaemia, peripartum cardiomyopathy
body.titration_principle: Start all four pillars early at low dose and titrate up, rather than maximising one drug before starting the next. Prognostic benefit appears early and at low doses.

warnings: NEVER COMBINE AN ARNI WITH AN ACE INHIBITOR. A 36-hour washout is required when switching, because of angio-oedema risk.
Do not start or up-titrate a beta-blocker during acute decompensation with fluid overload.
Hyperkalaemia is the main hazard of combined RAS blockade and MRA — monitor potassium rigorously.
SGLT2 inhibitors can cause euglycaemic DKA. Withhold during acute illness, prolonged fasting and around surgery, and counsel patients.
Only specific beta-blockers have death rate evidence in heart failure — atenolol is not one of them.
These are class-level principles. Doses, thresholds and sequencing must follow current guidelines and the local formulary.

flashcards.a: RAS blockade (ARNI/ACEi/ARB), beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor

flashcards.q: Washout needed when switching ACE inhibitor to ARNI?
flashcards.a: 36 hours

flashcards.q: Which four beta-blockers have HFrEF mortality evidence?
flashcards.a: Bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, nebivolol

flashcards.q: Is a loop diuretic a mortality-reducing drug in HFrEF?
flashcards.a: No — it treats congestion and symptoms

flashcards.q: Key SGLT2 inhibitor hazard to counsel about?
flashcards.a: Euglycaemic DKA — withhold during acute illness or fasting

digoxin_use_cautions_and_toxicity.title: Digoxin — Use, Cautions and Toxicity
digoxin_use_cautions_and_toxicity.summary: A cardiac glycoside with a small gap between the dose that works and the dose that harms. Useful in selected patients, dangerous when electrolytes or renal function change.

body.mechanism: Inhibits the sodium-potassium ATPase, raising intracellular sodium and thereby intracellular calcium via the sodium-calcium exchanger — makes the heart squeeze harder. Also increases vagal tone, slowing atrioventricular conduction.
indications: Rate control in atrial fibrillation, particularly with coexisting heart failure or in sedentary patients
Symptom control and reduction of hospitalisation in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, as an add-on
contraindications_and_cautions: Second- or third-degree heart block without a pacemaker
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (may worsen outflow obstruction)
Wolff-Parkinson-White with atrial fibrillation — can accelerate conduction down the accessory pathway and precipitate ventricular fibrillation
Significant renal impairment — dose reduction required
Electrolyte disturbance, especially hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypercalcaemia
advantages: Does not lower blood pressure, so useful when hypotension limits beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers
makes the heart squeeze harder in heart failure
disadvantages: small gap between the dose that works and the dose that harms

precipitants: HYPOKALAEMIA (the most important — potentiates digoxin binding)
Advanced age and low lean body mass
Interacting drugs: amiodarone, verapamil, diltiazem, quinidine, macrolides, itraconazole, spironolactone, and diuretics causing potassium loss

features.gastrointestinal: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain — often the earliest symptoms
features.visual: XANTHOPSIA — yellow-green vision, halos around lights, blurred vision
features.cardiac: Almost any arrhythmia. Classically bradyarrhythmias, atrioventricular block, atrial tachycardia with block, bidirectional ventricular tachycardia, ventricular ectopy.

toxicity.ecg_note: The 'reverse tick' or sagging ST depression is a sign of digoxin EFFECT at therapeutic levels — it does NOT indicate toxicity.
management: Stop digoxin
Correct potassium and magnesium — but be cautious with potassium in the presence of significant hyperkalaemia from massive overdose
Continuous cardiac monitoring
Treat arrhythmias; atropine for symptomatic bradycardia
Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Fab) for life-threatening arrhythmia, significant hyperkalaemia in acute overdose, or haemodynamic instability
AVOID calcium in digoxin toxicity with hyperkalaemia — historically associated with 'stone heart'; follow local toxicology advice
Digoxin is not effectively removed by dialysis

warnings: HYPOKALAEMIA IS THE COMMONEST PRECIPITANT OF DIGOXIN TOXICITY. Any patient on digoxin and a loop diuretic needs potassium monitoring.
Digoxin effect on the ECG is not the same as digoxin toxicity — do not stop the drug on ECG appearance alone.
Digoxin is contraindicated in atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White.
Renal function determines the dose. A fall in renal function will cause accumulation without any change in the prescription.
Levels must be taken at least 6 hours after a dose; earlier sampling gives a falsely high result.

flashcards.a: Hypokalaemia

flashcards.q: Classic visual symptom of digoxin toxicity?
flashcards.a: Xanthopsia — yellow-green vision with halos

flashcards.q: Is the reverse tick sign a sign of toxicity?
flashcards.a: No — it indicates digoxin effect at therapeutic levels

flashcards.q: Which arrhythmia is characteristic of digoxin toxicity?
flashcards.a: Bidirectional ventricular tachycardia; also atrial tachycardia with block

flashcards.q: Minimum interval before sampling a digoxin level?
flashcards.a: 6 hours after the dose

Loading and maintenance dose appropriate to renal function and lean body weight

Patient counselled on nausea and visual symptoms

insulin_types_regimens_and_doses.title: Insulin — Types, Regimens and Doses
insulin_types_regimens_and_doses.summary: Insulin classes by pharmacokinetics, and how basal, prandial and correction components fit together.

terms: insulin types, regimens and basal-bolus principles

types.role: Meal cover; the insulin used in intravenous infusions
Basal cover; has a distinct peak, which creates nocturnal hypoglycaemia risk
Basal cover with greater dosing flexibility
Simpler twice-daily regimens; less flexible, requires consistent meal timing

regimens.structure: One long-acting injection, usually with continued oral agents
Long-acting basal plus rapid-acting before each meal, with correction doses. Most physiological and most flexible.

regimens.use: Where simplicity and adherence matter more than flexibility
regimens.structure: Fixed ratio before breakfast and evening meal
Continuous basal rate with meal boluses

basal_bolus_logic: BASAL insulin covers hepatic glucose output between meals and overnight. It is judged by the FASTING and pre-meal glucose, and by whether glucose stays stable when a meal is skipped.
PRANDIAL (bolus) insulin covers the carbohydrate in a meal. It is judged by the rise from pre-meal to about 2 hours after the meal.
CORRECTION insulin brings a high glucose back towards target and is added to the prandial dose.
A common starting point for total daily dose is around 0.3–0.5 units/kg/day, split roughly half basal and half prandial, then titrated. Requirements vary enormously.
Never fix a dose and leave it — insulin regimens require iterative titration against recorded glucose patterns.
practical_safety: Insulin is a high-alert medication and a leading cause of serious medication error.
Write UNITS in full. Never abbreviate to 'U' — misread as a zero, this has caused ten-fold overdoses.
Use an insulin syringe or pen, never a standard syringe, for subcutaneous insulin.
Rotate injection sites to prevent lipohypertrophy, which causes erratic absorption.
Check insulin CONCENTRATION — 100 units/mL is standard but concentrated preparations exist.
Sick-day rules: do NOT stop basal insulin during illness in type 1 diabetes; monitor glucose and ketones more frequently.
In hospital, sliding-scale-only regimens without basal insulin are associated with poor control and should be avoided in insulin-deficient patients.

warnings: NEVER OMIT BASAL INSULIN IN TYPE 1 DIABETES, EVEN IF THE PATIENT IS NIL BY MOUTH. Omission precipitates DKA.
Write 'units' in full on every prescription. The abbreviation 'U' misread as a zero has caused fatal ten-fold overdoses.
Never draw up insulin with a non-insulin syringe.
Correction-scale-only ('sliding scale') management without basal insulin is poor practice in insulin-deficient patients.
Doses stated here are illustrative starting points only — all insulin prescribing must follow local protocol and be individualised.

flashcards.q: Which insulin is used in intravenous infusions?
flashcards.a: Short-acting regular (soluble) human insulin
Fasting and between-meal glucose, from hepatic glucose output

flashcards.q: Why must 'units' be written in full?
flashcards.a: 'U' misread as a zero has caused fatal ten-fold overdoses

flashcards.q: Can basal insulin be stopped when a type 1 patient is nil by mouth?
flashcards.a: No — omission precipitates DKA

flashcards.q: Which basal insulin has a distinct peak?
flashcards.a: NPH (isophane) — hence nocturnal hypoglycaemia risk

general_examination_head_to_toe.title: General Examination — Head to Toe
general_examination_head_to_toe.summary: The survey performed before any system examination: end of the bed, then hands, arms, face, neck and legs, looking for the signs that point to systemic disease.

preparation: Introduce yourself: name and role.
Confirm the patient's identity — name and date of birth.
Explain what you propose to do and why, in language they understand.
Obtain and document CONSENT.
Ask about pain before touching.
Wash hands / apply alcohol gel; don gloves if indicated.
Ensure privacy, adequate warmth and good lighting.
Offer a chaperone for any intimate examination and record who was present.
Expose adequately but preserve dignity — expose only what you are examining, when you examine it.
Position the patient correctly for the system being examined.
Stand on the patient's RIGHT side by convention.
end_of_bed: Respiratory distress — rate, accessory muscles, pursed lips, tripod position
Around the bed: oxygen, nebuliser, inhalers, drains, catheters, infusions, monitors, mobility aids, sputum pot, vomit bowl, feeding tube, insulin, glucose chart
hands: Colour of palms — palmar pallor (crease pallor suggests significant anaemia), palmar erythema
Nails: CLUBBING, koilonychia (spoon nails — iron deficiency), leukonychia (white nails — hypoalbuminaemia), splinter haemorrhages, nail-fold infarcts, onycholysis
Wasting of the small muscles of the hand
Tremor: fine (beta-agonist, thyrotoxicosis), coarse, flapping (asterixis — CO₂ retention, hepatic or uraemic encephalopathy)
pulse_and_arms: Radial pulse: rate, rhythm, character, volume
Collapsing pulse (raise the arm — feel for a water-hammer impulse)
Blood pressure, both arms if indicated
Bruising, purpura, needle marks, arteriovenous fistula
face_and_neck: Eyes: CONJUNCTIVAL PALLOR (lower lid), SCLERAL ICTERUS (best seen in natural light), xanthelasma, corneal arcus, subconjunctival haemorrhage, exophthalmos
Mouth: central cyanosis (under the tongue), hydration of mucous membranes, oral candidiasis, ulcers, angular stomatitis, glossitis, dental hygiene, gum hypertrophy
Face: moon facies, acromegalic features, malar flush, butterfly rash, parotid swelling, facial oedema

Neck: JVP, lymph nodes (systematically — submental, submandibular, pre- and post-auricular, occipital, anterior and posterior cervical chains, supraclavicular), thyroid (ask the patient to swallow), tracheal position, carotid pulse and bruits
legs_and_general: Pitting oedema — press for at least 15 seconds over a bony prominence and state the level reached
Sacral oedema in a bedbound patient
Skin: ulcers, cellulitis, rashes, purpura, scars, injection sites
Nutritional status; weight and BMI where relevant
closing: Cover the patient and restore their clothing and dignity.
State that you would complete the examination with the relevant additional assessments.
Summarise your findings, including relevant negatives.
Document findings contemporaneously, with the date, time and your signature.

warnings: Consent and a chaperone are required for intimate examinations, and both must be documented.

Pallor, cyanosis and jaundice are harder to assess in darker skin. Use the conjunctivae, palms, soles, oral mucosa, tongue undersurface and nail beds, and compare with the patient's own unaffected areas.
Pitting oedema requires sustained pressure for at least 15 seconds — brief pressure misses it.

preparation: Introduce yourself: name and role.

peripheral: Hands: temperature, clubbing, splinter haemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, tar staining, peripheral cyanosis, xanthomata
Pulse: rate, rhythm, character (slow-rising in aortic stenosis, collapsing in aortic regurgitation), volume; radio-radial and radio-femoral delay

palpate: APEX BEAT: locate and describe position (normally 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line) and character (tapping, heaving/sustained, thrusting/volume-loaded, double impulse)
Parasternal HEAVE with the heel of the hand — right ventricular hypertrophy
THRILLS over each auscultation area — a palpable murmur
auscultate: Four classic areas: AORTIC (2nd right intercostal space), PULMONARY (2nd left intercostal space), TRICUSPID (4th–5th left parasternal), MITRAL (apex, 5th space mid-clavicular line)
Use the DIAPHRAGM for high-pitched sounds and the BELL for low-pitched sounds (mitral stenosis murmur, third heart sound)
Identify S1 and S2 while palpating the carotid to time the cycle
Listen for added sounds: S3, S4, opening snap, ejection click, prosthetic clicks, pericardial rub
For any murmur describe: TIMING (systolic/diastolic), SITE of maximal intensity, RADIATION, CHARACTER, PITCH, GRADE (Levine 1–6), and effect of dynamic manoeuvres
MANOEUVRES: left lateral position with the bell at the apex on expiration for mitral stenosis; sitting forward, breath held in expiration, at the left sternal edge for aortic regurgitation
Radiation: aortic stenosis to the carotids; mitral regurgitation to the axilla
Right-sided murmurs increase on INSPIRATION; left-sided murmurs increase on EXPIRATION
complete: Lung bases for crackles and effusions
Liver for pulsatile hepatomegaly and hepatojugular reflux

A quiet diastolic murmur will be missed without the correct manoeuvre and a quiet room.
Never diagnose a murmur as innocent without considering age, symptoms and associated findings.

cranial_nerves_1_12_test_and_lesion.title: Cranial Nerves 1–12 — Test and Lesion
cranial_nerves_1_12_test_and_lesion.summary: Each cranial nerve, its modality, what it supplies, how to test it, and what a lesion looks like.

preparation: Introduce yourself: name and role.
Confirm the patient's identity — name and date of birth.
Explain what you propose to do and why, in language they understand.
Obtain and document CONSENT.
Ask about pain before touching.
Wash hands / apply alcohol gel; don gloves if indicated.
Ensure privacy, adequate warmth and good lighting.
Offer a chaperone for any intimate examination and record who was present.
Expose adequately but preserve dignity — expose only what you are examining, when you examine it.
Position the patient correctly for the system being examined.
Stand on the patient's RIGHT side by convention.
Sit facing the patient at eye level, about an arm's length away.
Have to hand: pen torch, Snellen chart, ophthalmoscope, cotton wool, neurotip, tuning fork (512 Hz), tongue depressor, and a smell source.

nerves.test: Ask about any change in smell or taste. Test each nostril separately with a familiar non-irritant odour, the other nostril occluded and eyes closed.
nerves.lesion: Anosmia — head injury with cribriform plate fracture, frontal tumour (olfactory groove meningioma), Parkinson disease, upper respiratory infection, ageing.

nerves.function: Vision, afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex
nerves.test: Visual ACUITY (Snellen, each eye, with correction). Visual FIELDS by confrontation, quadrant by quadrant, plus assessment for inattention. Pupillary reflexes — direct, consensual, and SWINGING TORCH TEST for a relative afferent pupillary defect. Colour vision (Ishihara). FUNDOSCOPY.
nerves.lesion: Field defect localises the lesion: monocular loss (optic nerve), bitemporal hemianopia (chiasm — pituitary), homonymous hemianopia (tract/radiation), macular sparing (occipital cortex). RAPD indicates optic nerve disease.

nerves.function: Superior, inferior and medial recti, inferior oblique, levator palpebrae superioris; pupillary constriction and accommodation
nerves.test: Eye movements in an H pattern. Look for ptosis, and pupil size and reactivity.
nerves.lesion: 'Down and out' eye, ptosis, dilated unreactive pupil. A PAINFUL third nerve palsy WITH pupil involvement is a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise — a surgical emergency. Pupil-sparing palsies are more typical of microvascular (diabetic) causes.

nerves.function: Superior oblique — depresses and intorts the adducted eye
nerves.test: Ask the patient to look down and in.
nerves.lesion: Vertical diplopia worse on looking down and inward — patients tilt the head away from the affected side. Classically troublesome on descending stairs or reading.

nerves.function: Sensation to the face in three divisions (ophthalmic V1, maxillary V2, mandibular V3); motor to the muscles of mastication; afferent limb of the corneal reflex
nerves.test: Light touch and pin-prick in all three divisions bilaterally. Motor: clench the teeth and palpate masseter and temporalis; open the jaw against resistance (jaw deviates TOWARDS a weak side). Corneal reflex with a wisp of cotton wool. Jaw jerk.
nerves.lesion: Sensory loss by division, weak mastication, absent corneal reflex. Brisk jaw jerk suggests an upper motor neurone lesion above the pons.

nerves.test: Ask the patient to look laterally.
nerves.lesion: Failure of abduction with horizontal diplopia worse on looking to that side. A FALSE LOCALISING SIGN in raised intracranial pressure because of its long intracranial course.

nerves.function: Muscles of facial expression; taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; lacrimation and salivation; stapedius
nerves.test: Raise the eyebrows, screw the eyes shut against resistance, blow out the cheeks, show the teeth, purse the lips. Ask about taste and hyperacusis.
nerves.lesion: UPPER MOTOR NEURONE lesion SPARES THE FOREHEAD (bilateral cortical innervation of the upper face) — think stroke. LOWER MOTOR NEURONE lesion involves the forehead — think Bell palsy, Ramsay Hunt syndrome, parotid tumour, otitis media. This distinction is the single highest-yield point in cranial nerve examination.

nerves.test: Gross hearing (whisper test) each ear. RINNE (tuning fork on mastoid, then beside the ear) and WEBER (fork on the vertex). Assess for nystagmus; Dix-Hallpike where indicated.
nerves.lesion: Conductive loss: Rinne negative (bone > air) on the affected side, Weber lateralises TO the affected ear. Sensorineural loss: Rinne positive bilaterally, Weber lateralises AWAY from the affected ear.

nerves.function: Sensation to the posterior third of the tongue and pharynx, taste posterior third, stylopharyngeus; afferent limb of the gag reflex
nerves.test: Ask about swallowing. Gag reflex (afferent IX). Assess palatal sensation.
nerves.lesion: Reduced gag, impaired taste posteriorly, dysphagia.

nerves.function: Palate, pharynx and larynx motor; parasympathetic to thorax and abdomen; efferent limb of the gag reflex
nerves.test: Say 'aah' and watch the uvula and soft palate. Assess voice quality and cough.
nerves.lesion: UVULA DEVIATES AWAY FROM THE SIDE OF THE LESION. Hoarse or bovine cough with recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement; nasal regurgitation.

nerves.test: Shrug the shoulders against resistance (trapezius). Turn the head against resistance — the sternocleidomastoid tested is on the side OPPOSITE the direction of turning.
nerves.lesion: Weak shoulder shrug, weak head turning to the opposite side, winging of the scapula in some lesions.

nerves.test: Inspect the tongue in the floor of the mouth for wasting and fasciculation, then ask the patient to protrude it and move it side to side.
nerves.lesion: TONGUE DEVIATES TOWARDS THE SIDE OF THE LESION in a lower motor neurone lesion (the intact genioglossus pushes it across). Wasting and fasciculation indicate a lower motor neurone lesion.

closing: Cover the patient and restore their clothing and dignity.
State that you would complete the examination with the relevant additional assessments.
Summarise your findings, including relevant negatives.
Document findings contemporaneously, with the date, time and your signature.

memory_aids.names: Oh Oh Oh To Touch And Feel Very Good Velvet — Ah Heaven
memory_aids.modality: Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most (S = sensory, M = motor, B = both)
memory_aids.deviation_rules: UVULA AWAY from the lesion; TONGUE TOWARDS the lesion; JAW TOWARDS the weak side.

warnings: A PAINFUL THIRD NERVE PALSY WITH PUPIL INVOLVEMENT IS A POSTERIOR COMMUNICATING ARTERY ANEURYSM UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. Image urgently.
Forehead sparing distinguishes an upper from a lower motor neurone facial palsy — this determines whether you are managing a stroke or a Bell palsy.
A sixth nerve palsy can be a false localising sign of raised intracranial pressure.
In lower motor neurone facial palsy the eye cannot close — corneal protection with lubricants and taping at night is essential to prevent exposure keratopathy.

power_tone_and_reflexes_grading_and_tech.title: Power, Tone and Reflexes — Grading and Technique
power_tone_and_reflexes_grading_and_tech.summary: The standard grading scales for motor power, tone, reflexes and plantar response, and the technique for eliciting each.

terms: neurological power, tone and reflex grading
power, tone and reflexes — grading and technique

mrc_power_scale.finding: Active movement against gravity and resistance (subdivided 4−, 4, 4+)

power_technique: Test each muscle group individually, comparing sides.
Isolate the joint — stabilise the limb proximally.
Record the myotome and the named muscle, not just 'weak arm'.

Key myotomes: C5 shoulder abduction, C6 elbow flexion/wrist extension, C7 elbow extension, C8 finger flexion, T1 finger abduction, L2 hip flexion, L3 knee extension, L4 ankle dorsiflexion, L5 great toe extension, S1 ankle plantarflexion

tone.description: Reduced resistance, floppy limb — lower motor neurone, cerebellar, acute upper motor neurone lesion ('spinal shock')
VELOCITY-DEPENDENT increase in tone with a 'clasp-knife' give-way — pyramidal (upper motor neurone) lesion
Increase in tone that is NOT velocity-dependent, present throughout the range — 'lead-pipe', or 'cogwheel' when combined with tremor — extrapyramidal (Parkinsonian)
Variable resistance that increases with the examiner's effort — frontal lobe disease, dementia, delirium

body.tone_technique: Ask the patient to relax completely. Move each joint passively at varying speeds — spasticity is only revealed at speed. Assess for CLONUS by rapid dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee slightly flexed; more than a few beats of sustained clonus is pathological.

reflex_grading.finding: Brisk — may be normal in an anxious patient

reflex_technique: Position the limb so the tendon is slightly stretched and the patient is relaxed.
Strike the TENDON, not the muscle belly, with a swinging tendon hammer using gravity.
If a reflex appears absent, use REINFORCEMENT (Jendrassik manoeuvre — clench the teeth or interlock and pull the fingers) before declaring it absent.

plantar_response.technique: Run a blunt object along the LATERAL border of the sole from heel towards the little toe, then curve medially across the ball of the foot. Watch the GREAT TOE.
plantar_response.normal: Flexor — the great toe moves downwards
plantar_response.abnormal: EXTENSOR (Babinski sign) — the great toe moves upwards, often with fanning of the other toes; indicates an upper motor neurone lesion
plantar_response.note: The extensor plantar response is normal in infants up to about 1–2 years, before myelination is complete.

umn_vs_lmn.umn: Pyramidal — extensors weak in the arm, flexors weak in the leg
umn_vs_lmn.lmn: Follows the nerve or root distribution

warnings: Never record a reflex as absent without attempting reinforcement.
Spasticity is velocity-dependent; rigidity is not. Move the limb at different speeds or you will miss the distinction.
An extensor plantar response is normal in infants up to about 1–2 years.
In acute upper motor neurone lesions (spinal shock, acute stroke), tone and reflexes may initially be REDUCED — the classic upper motor neurone picture develops over days.

flashcards.a: Active movement against gravity but not against resistance
Spasticity is velocity-dependent with a clasp-knife give; rigidity is not velocity-dependent (lead-pipe or cogwheel)

flashcards.a: S1, S2

flashcards.q: Where do you stroke to elicit the plantar response?
flashcards.a: Lateral border of the sole, curving medially across the ball of the foot

clerking_presenting_complaint_and_histor.title: Clerking — Presenting Complaint and History
clerking_presenting_complaint_and_histor.summary: The universal structure for taking a history, with the symptom-analysis frameworks and the red-flag layer.

terms: presenting complaint and history of presenting complaint — master template

structure: Identifying data: name, age, sex, occupation, place of residence, source and reliability of the history
PRESENTING COMPLAINT — in the patient's own words, with duration, listed in order of the patient's priority
HISTORY OF PRESENTING COMPLAINT — the detailed chronological narrative
for women: GYNAECOLOGICAL AND OBSTETRIC HISTORY
for children: BIRTH, DEVELOPMENTAL, FEEDING AND IMMUNISATION HISTORY

SOCRATES_for_pain: Onset — sudden or gradual, what the patient was doing
Character — sharp, dull, burning, colicky, crushing
general_symptom: When did it start and what were you doing?
Is it getting better, worse, or staying the same?
What makes it better or worse?
What do you think is causing it?
How is it affecting your daily life, work and sleep?
What have you already taken or done for it?

must_ask: Risk factors: smoking, hypertension, diabetes, lipids, family history, cocaine use
Exercise tolerance quantified in metres or stairs
Bowel habit change, blood or mucus per rectum, melaena
LAST MENSTRUAL PERIOD and possibility of pregnancy
Sudden or gradual onset — thunderclap suggests subarachnoid haemorrhage
Worse on waking, coughing or straining
Jaw claudication and scalp tenderness in older patients (giant cell arteritis)
TRAVEL HISTORY with dates and prevention
Contact with unwell people, animals, or a TB case
Last menstrual period and cycle pattern
Quantity — pads per day, clots, flooding
Volume and appearance — fresh, coffee ground
NSAID, steroid, anticoagulant and alcohol use
Halos around lights and nausea (acute angle-closure glaucoma)
Description of the event including duration
Sleep deprivation, alcohol, drug use, missed medication

red_flag_layer: New back pain with neurological signs or sphincter disturbance
Chest pain with exertion or at rest
Change in bowel habit over 6 weeks in an older adult
social_history_depth: Occupation — current and previous, with specific exposures (dust, asbestos, chemicals, noise, animals)
Smoking in pack-years; alcohol in units per week and pattern; recreational drug use including route
Living arrangements, housing, water and sanitation
Who else is at home; caring responsibilities
Functional status and activities of daily living
Financial ability to access care and medicines
Sexual history where relevant, taken sensitively
Intimate partner violence screening in private
body.documentation_rule: Record what the patient said and what you found. Distinguish clearly between the history (reported), examination (observed), and your assessment (interpreted). Never document a finding you did not elicit.

warnings: A prompt is not a finding. A template may prompt 'assess for pallor', but only the examiner can record whether pallor was present. Never pre-populate or auto-complete clinical findings.
An eyewitness account is essential in seizure, collapse and confusion. A history from the patient alone is often insufficient.
Always ask the last menstrual period in a woman of reproductive age with any acute presentation.
Take the sexual history and intimate partner violence screening in private, without family members present.

flashcards.a: Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associated symptoms, Timing, Exacerbating/relieving factors, Severity

flashcards.q: What must never be auto-populated in a clerking template?
flashcards.a: Clinical findings — a prompt is not a finding

flashcards.q: Which history is essential in a seizure presentation?
flashcards.a: An eyewitness account

sample_bottle_colours_which_bottle_for_w.title: Sample Bottle Colours — Which Bottle For Which Test
sample_bottle_colours_which_bottle_for_w.summary: Tube stopper colour indicates the additive, which determines which tests the sample can be used for and the order in which tubes must be filled.

terms: blood collection tubes — colour code reference
sample bottle colours — which bottle for which test

tubes.critical_note: MUST BE FILLED TO THE MARK — the blood-to-citrate ratio is fixed at 9:1. Under-filling gives falsely prolonged clotting times.

tubes.colour: Red (plain) / Gold or Yellow (SST with gel)
tubes.additive: None, or clot activator with separator gel
tubes.typical_tests: Biochemistry, serology, hormones, drug levels, group and save in some systems
tubes.critical_note: Allow adequate clotting time before centrifugation

tubes.typical_tests: Plasma biochemistry, ammonia, some special assays, chromosomes
Full blood count, ESR, HbA1c, blood film, reticulocytes, blood group and crossmatch (many systems), sickling test
tubes.critical_note: MIX BY GENTLE INVERSION IMMEDIATELY — clotted EDTA samples are the commonest cause of rejected haematology specimens. EDTA contaminates and falsely lowers calcium and raises potassium in other tubes.
Essential for accurate glucose — without fluoride, red cells continue to consume glucose in the tube and the result falls

tubes.typical_tests: Blood group, crossmatch, direct antiglobulin test in systems using a dedicated tube
tubes.critical_note: Labelling requirements for transfusion samples are stricter — hand-write at the bedside, at the time of draw

tubes.typical_tests: Trace elements, heavy metals, zinc, copper, lead
tubes.critical_note: Ordinary tubes leach trace elements and invalidate the result

tubes.typical_tests: ESR in systems using a dedicated tube
tubes.critical_note: Different ratio to the light blue coagulation tube — not interchangeable

tubes.typical_tests: HLA typing, DNA studies, paternity testing
tubes.critical_note: Distinct from the gold SST tube despite similar appearance in some systems

body.order_of_draw_principle: A standard order of draw exists to prevent additive carryover between tubes. The conventional sequence is: blood culture bottles first, then citrate (light blue), then serum (red/gold), then heparin (green), then EDTA (purple), then fluoride oxalate (grey). CONFIRM THE EXACT ORDER AND TUBE COLOURS WITH YOUR OWN LABORATORY — colour conventions differ between manufacturers and countries.
carryover_examples: EDTA carried into a biochemistry tube causes a spuriously LOW calcium and spuriously HIGH potassium — a classic cause of a phone call about a 'critical' result that is an artefact.
Heparin carryover interferes with coagulation studies.
Fluoride carryover inhibits enzymes in biochemistry assays.
labelling_rules: Label at the BEDSIDE, at the time of collection, never in advance and never afterwards.
Minimum: full name, hospital or unique identifier, date of birth, date and time of collection, and the collector's identity.
Transfusion samples have additional mandatory requirements and are rejected for any discrepancy — this is a deliberate safety control, not bureaucracy.
Request form and tube must match exactly.

warnings: TUBE COLOUR CONVENTIONS ARE NOT UNIVERSAL. They differ between manufacturers and countries. This artifact must be overlaid with your own laboratory's chart before use.
Under-filled citrate tubes give falsely prolonged clotting times and have led to inappropriate treatment decisions.
EDTA carryover causes spuriously low calcium and high potassium.
Label transfusion samples at the bedside by hand. Pre-labelled or ward-labelled samples are the mechanism by which patients receive the wrong blood.

flashcards.q: Which tube for a full blood count?
flashcards.a: EDTA — purple/lavender top

flashcards.q: Which tube for glucose, and why?
flashcards.a: Grey top with sodium fluoride — it inhibits glycolysis so the glucose does not fall in the tube

flashcards.q: Why must a citrate tube be filled to the mark?
flashcards.a: The 9:1 blood-to-citrate ratio is fixed; under-filling falsely prolongs clotting times

flashcards.q: What does EDTA carryover do to calcium and potassium?
flashcards.a: Falsely lowers calcium and falsely raises potassium

flashcards.q: When and where must a transfusion sample be labelled?
flashcards.a: By hand, at the bedside, at the time of collection

tubes_and_catheters_sizes_when_to_use_wh.title: Tubes and Catheters — Sizes, When To Use, When Not To
tubes_and_catheters_sizes_when_to_use_wh.summary: The commonly used tubes and catheters: what each looks like, what it is for, how it is sized, and when it must not be used.

terms: airway, tubes and catheters — identification, sizing and indications
tubes and catheters — sizes, when to use, when not to

devices.sizing: Measured from the incisors to the angle of the jaw
devices.indications: Airway obstruction from tongue in an UNCONSCIOUS patient without a gag reflex
devices.contraindications: Intact gag reflex — will induce vomiting and laryngospasm
devices.note: Colour-coded by size in most systems; a temporary measure only, never a a tube in the trachea with the cuff up

devices.sizing: Length from nostril to tragus; diameter roughly matching the patient's little finger
devices.indications: Airway support where the gag reflex is intact or the mouth cannot be opened (trismus, clenched jaw, seizure)
devices.contraindications: SUSPECTED BASE OF SKULL FRACTURE — risk of intracranial placement. Also coagulopathy and nasal obstruction
devices.note: Better tolerated than a Guedel in a semi-conscious patient

devices.contraindications: High aspiration risk, unfasted patient, poor lung compliance
devices.note: Does not definitively protect against aspiration

devices.sizing: Internal diameter in mm. Adults approximately 7.0–8.0 for women and 8.0–9.0 for men. Paediatric size is estimated by formula (for example uncuffed internal diameter ≈ age/4 + 4) and must be cross-checked against a length-based tape.
devices.indications: a tube in the trachea with the cuff up protection, controlled ventilation, GCS ≤8, airway burn, apnoea, failure to oxygenate or ventilate
devices.contraindications: Relative: severe airway distortion. Never delay oxygenation for intubation attempts
devices.note: CONFIRM PLACEMENT WITH WAVEFORM CAPNOGRAPHY — this is the standard of care. Auscultation and chest rise alone are not sufficient. Record the depth at the teeth and secure the tube.

devices.sizing: Internal diameter; cuffed or uncuffed; fenestrated or non-fenestrated
devices.indications: Prolonged ventilation, upper airway obstruction, secretion management, protection in bulbar dysfunction
devices.contraindications: Relative: coagulopathy, local infection, unstable cervical spine
devices.note: Emergency algorithms differ for a patent versus an absent upper airway (laryngectomy). The bed-head sign stating which is present is a critical safety control.

devices.sizing: French gauge — fine-bore for feeding, wide-bore (e.g. Ryle's) for drainage and aspiration
devices.indications: Gastric decompression in obstruction or ileus, aspiration of contents, feeding through the gut — by mouth or through a tube, gastric lavage in specific poisonings
devices.contraindications: BASE OF SKULL FRACTURE (use the oral route), oesophageal stricture or recent oesophageal surgery, severe coagulopathy, oesophageal varices (relative — discuss)
devices.note: POSITION MUST BE CONFIRMED BEFORE ANY FEED OR MEDICATION. Aspirate pH testing is first line; a chest radiograph interpreted by a competent person is the definitive check. Feeding into a misplaced nasogastric tube is a recognised never event.

devices.sizing: French gauge; small-bore Seldinger for air and free fluid, large-bore for blood, pus and thick fluid
devices.indications: Pneumothorax (tension after needle decompression, large or symptomatic), haemothorax, empyema, large or symptomatic pleural effusion, post-thoracotomy
devices.contraindications: Relative: coagulopathy, adhesions. Never delay decompression of a tension pneumothorax
devices.note: Insert within the SAFE TRIANGLE — bordered by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi, a line at the level of the nipple (about the 5th intercostal space), with the apex below the axilla. Pass the tube over the SUPERIOR border of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle running beneath each rib.

devices.sizing: French/Charrière gauge; typically 12–16 Fr in adults, larger three-way for irrigation
devices.indications: Retention, accurate output monitoring, perioperative, neuropathic bladder, clot irrigation, comfort in end-of-life care
devices.contraindications: SUSPECTED URETHRAL INJURY — blood at the meatus, high-riding prostate, perineal bruising
devices.note: Inflate the balloon ONLY once urine is flowing. Inflating in the urethra causes serious injury. Record the residual volume.

devices.indications: Urethral route impossible or contraindicated; long-term drainage preference
devices.contraindications: Impalpable and unscanned bladder, previous lower abdominal surgery with possible adherent bowel, known bladder cancer, uncorrected coagulopathy

devices.sizing: Gauge — the LARGER the gauge number, the SMALLER the bore. Colour-coded internationally.
devices.contraindications: Infection or injury at the site, limb with lymphoedema or an arteriovenous fistula
devices.note: Flow rate depends on the fourth power of the radius and inversely on length — a SHORT WIDE cannula delivers far more than a long narrow one. In haemorrhagic shock, two short wide-bore cannulae beat any central line.

warnings: NEVER PASS A NASOGASTRIC OR NASOPHARYNGEAL TUBE THROUGH THE NOSE IF A BASE OF SKULL FRACTURE IS SUSPECTED — intracranial placement has occurred. Use the oral route.
CONFIRM NASOGASTRIC TUBE POSITION BEFORE ANY FEED OR MEDICATION. Feeding into the lung is a never event.
Confirm endotracheal tube placement with waveform capnography. Auscultation alone is insufficient.
Never inflate a urinary catheter balloon until urine is flowing.
Insert chest drains within the safe triangle and pass the tube over the superior border of the rib.
Larger gauge number means smaller cannula. This inversion causes errors under pressure.

flashcards.a: Orange — the largest commonly used, for massive transfusion

flashcards.q: Does a larger gauge number mean a bigger or smaller cannula?
flashcards.a: Smaller

flashcards.q: Borders of the safe triangle for chest drain insertion?
flashcards.a: Lateral border of pectoralis major, anterior border of latissimus dorsi, the 5th intercostal space, with the apex below the axilla

flashcards.q: Why is the chest tube passed over the top of the rib?
flashcards.a: The neurovascular bundle runs in the subcostal groove beneath each rib

flashcards.q: Which airway is contraindicated with an intact gag reflex?
flashcards.a: Oropharyngeal (Guedel) airway

flashcards.q: Gold standard for confirming ETT placement?
flashcards.a: Waveform capnography

theatre_instruments_name_it_and_know_its.title: Theatre Instruments — Name It and Know Its Use
theatre_instruments_name_it_and_know_its.summary: Core theatre instruments grouped by what they do, with the visual features that distinguish similar-looking instruments.

terms: surgical instruments — recognition and use by function
theatre instruments — name it and know its use

instruments.name: Scalpel handle with blade
instruments.note: No. 3 handle with No. 10/11/15 blades for fine work; No. 4 handle with No. 20–24 blades for larger incisions. No. 11 is the pointed stab blade used for abscess incision.

instruments.name: Mayo scissors
instruments.note: Heavier, straight or curved, blunt tips — for cutting TISSUE and suture. Straight Mayo is conventionally the 'suture scissors'.

instruments.name: Metzenbaum scissors
instruments.note: Longer, finer, more delicate — for DELICATE DISSECTION. The shank is noticeably longer than the blade.

instruments.name: Diathermy pencil
instruments.note: Cutting and coagulation; requires a correctly applied patient return electrode

instruments.name: Toothed (rat-tooth) dissecting forceps
instruments.note: Interlocking teeth — for TOUGH tissue such as skin and fascia; will damage bowel

instruments.name: Non-toothed (plain) dissecting forceps
instruments.note: Serrated flat tips — for DELICATE tissue

instruments.name: DeBakey forceps
instruments.note: Atraumatic longitudinal rows of fine teeth — for vascular and bowel tissue

instruments.name: Allis tissue forceps
instruments.note: Short interdigitating TEETH at the tip — grips tissue that will be excised; traumatic

instruments.name: Babcock tissue forceps
instruments.note: Broad, FENESTRATED, atraumatic curved jaws with NO teeth — for delicate tubular structures such as bowel, appendix, fallopian tube

instruments.name: Kocher (Ochsner) forceps
instruments.note: Heavy clamp with transverse serrations AND a single interlocking TOOTH at the tip — very secure, traumatic grip; used for fascia and pedicles

instruments.name: Sponge-holding (Rampley) forceps
instruments.note: Ring-ended, for skin preparation and swab holding

instruments.name: Halsted mosquito forceps
instruments.note: Small, fine, curved or straight — for small vessels

instruments.name: Spencer Wells / Crile artery forceps
instruments.note: Medium, transverse serrations along the full jaw

instruments.name: Right-angled (Lahey/Mixter) forceps
instruments.note: For passing ligatures behind structures

instruments.name: Langenbeck retractor
instruments.note: Small L-shaped hand-held; superficial wounds

instruments.name: Deaver retractor
instruments.note: Long curved blade; deep abdominal retraction

instruments.name: Morris retractor
instruments.note: Broad right-angled blade for abdominal wall

instruments.name: Doyen retractor
instruments.note: Curved blade often used in pelvic and obstetric surgery

instruments.name: Self-retaining retractors (Balfour, Travers, Weitlaner, Norfolk and Norwich)
instruments.note: Hold themselves open, freeing hands

instruments.name: Needle holder (Mayo-Hegar, Crile-Wood)
instruments.note: Short heavy jaws with fine cross-hatching; hold the needle at the junction of the middle and posterior thirds

instruments.name: Gillies needle holder
instruments.note: Combined needle holder and scissors, asymmetric handles

instruments.name: Yankauer sucker
instruments.note: Rigid, bulbous, fenestrated tip for oropharynx and open cavities

instruments.name: Poole sucker
instruments.note: Multi-fenestrated guard preventing tissue occlusion — for large volumes of free fluid

instruments.name: Towel clips (Backhaus)
instruments.note: Secure drapes

instruments.name: Kidney dish, gallipot, receiver
instruments.note: Basic theatre containers

commonly_confused_pairs.discriminator: Allis has TEETH and is traumatic (for tissue to be removed). Babcock is FENESTRATED and atraumatic (for bowel and tubes).
Metzenbaum has a much LONGER SHANK relative to a short fine blade; Mayo is heavier with a blade-to-shank ratio closer to 1:1.
Kocher has an interlocking TOOTH at the tip; Spencer Wells does not.
Look at the tip — interlocking teeth versus flat serrations.

count_and_safety: The surgical count of swabs, needles and instruments before, during and at closure is a mandatory safety control.
The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist has three phases: SIGN IN (before induction), TIME OUT (before skin incision), SIGN OUT (before the patient leaves theatre).
Sharps must be passed via a neutral zone or hands-free technique.
Retained foreign object is a never event — a discrepant count must be resolved before the patient leaves theatre, including by radiograph.

warnings: Never use toothed forceps or Allis forceps on bowel — they crush and perforate. Use Babcock or DeBakey.
A discrepant surgical count must be resolved before the patient leaves theatre. Retained foreign object is a never event.
Instrument names vary between countries and institutions. Learn the LOCAL names used in your theatre alongside these.

chest_x_ray_how_to_read_it.title: Chest X-ray — How To Read It
chest_x_ray_how_to_read_it.summary: A reproducible reading order for the chest radiograph, plus the quality assessment that must precede interpretation.

terms: chest x-ray — how to read it

before_you_look: Confirm PATIENT IDENTITY, date and time on the film — the wrong film is a major source of error
Projection: PA (standard, erect) or AP (portable, supine). AP magnifies the heart, so the cardiothoracic ratio is not assessable on an AP film.
Compare with any previous films — change over time is often more informative than a single image

quality_RIPE.check: The medial ends of the clavicles should be equidistant from the spinous processes
Count 5–7 anterior or 8–10 posterior ribs above the diaphragm. Poor inspiration crowds the lung bases and mimics consolidation.
PA or AP; erect or supine; is the whole chest included?
Vertebral bodies should be just visible behind the heart; the left hemidiaphragm should be traceable to the spine

systematic_ABCDE.look: Trachea central or deviated? Carina, main bronchi. Tracheal deviation AWAY suggests tension pneumothorax or large effusion; TOWARDS suggests collapse or fibrosis.

Compare left and right zone by zone (upper, mid, lower). Look for consolidation, collapse, masses, nodules, cavities, interstitial change. Trace the pleural edge for pneumothorax. Check the costophrenic angles for blunting (effusion).

Cardiothoracic ratio (normal <0.5 on a PA film). Heart borders — loss of a border is the SILHOUETTE SIGN and localises pathology. Aortic knuckle, mediastinal width, hila (size, density, position — the left hilum is normally slightly higher than the right).

Both hemidiaphragms visible and their contours smooth; right is normally slightly higher than left. FREE AIR UNDER THE DIAPHRAGM on an ERECT film means perforation. Look below the diaphragm for gastric bubble and bowel gas pattern.

Bones — ribs, clavicles, scapulae, vertebrae, humeri: fractures, lytic or sclerotic lesions. Soft tissues — surgical emphysema, breast shadows or their absence, foreign bodies. DEVICES — endotracheal tube, central line, nasogastric tube, chest drain, pacemaker, ECG leads. Review AREAS: apices, behind the heart, below the diaphragm, the periphery.

named_signs.meaning: Loss of a normal border indicates pathology in the adjacent structure — loss of the right heart border suggests right middle lobe disease; loss of the left heart border suggests lingula
Air-filled bronchi outlined by surrounding alveolar opacification — indicates airspace disease
Upward-curving edge of a pleural effusion
Abnormally deep costophrenic angle on a SUPINE film — pneumothorax in a patient who cannot sit up
Short horizontal peripheral septal lines — interstitial oedema
S-shaped fissure suggesting a central obstructing mass with distal collapse
Both sides of the bowel wall visible on an abdominal film — free intraperitoneal air

body.cannot_be_diagnosed_here: A radiograph does not diagnose a tension pneumothorax — that is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate decompression.

warnings: A TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX IS A CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS. Decompress first; do not wait for a film.
Cardiothoracic ratio cannot be assessed on an AP or portable film — the heart is magnified.
Absence of free air under the diaphragm does not exclude perforation.
Always check the review areas: apices, behind the heart, below the diaphragm, and the periphery. These are where findings hide.
A radiograph reported as normal by an inexperienced reader has not been excluded — seek senior or radiologist review when the clinical picture demands it.

flashcards.a: Rotation, Inspiration, Picture/Projection, Exposure
Loss of a normal border indicating pathology in the adjacent structure

flashcards.a: The heart is magnified by the projection

normal_values_reference_ranges.title: Normal Values — Reference Ranges
normal_values_reference_ranges.summary: Commonly used adult reference intervals, presented ONLY as educational orientation values. A laboratory-issued interval always supersedes these.

terms: reference intervals — master index and provenance rules

body.provenance_rule: A reference interval is a property of a LABORATORY, an ASSAY and a POPULATION — not of a disease and not of the internet. Scout must display the local laboratory's interval where one is configured, and must visibly mark generic values as educational.
varies_by: Specimen type (serum, plasma, whole blood, capillary)
Whether it is a population reference interval or a clinical DECISION LIMIT

haematology.orientation: Highly age- and sex-dependent; use the local formula

biochemistry.orientation: Sex-dependent; roughly 60–110 µmol/L male, 45–90 µmol/L female
3.9–5.5 mmol/L (decision limits for diabetes differ from this reference interval)
Age-dependent; markedly higher in growing children and in pregnancy
Sex-dependent; roughly <60 IU/L male, <40 IU/L female

lft_pattern_logic.hepatocellular: ALT and AST disproportionately raised relative to ALP
lft_pattern_logic.cholestatic: ALP and GGT disproportionately raised relative to ALT
lft_pattern_logic.isolated_raised_ALP: Confirm hepatic origin with GGT — if GGT is normal, consider bone (growth, Paget disease, metastases, osteomalacia) or placental (pregnancy) origin
lft_pattern_logic.AST_ALT_ratio: A ratio above 2 suggests alcohol-related liver disease; ALT usually exceeds AST in most other hepatitides
lft_pattern_logic.synthetic_function: Albumin, INR and bilirubin reflect FUNCTION; transaminases reflect INJURY. A normal transaminase does not mean a working liver.

warnings: THESE ARE ORIENTATION VALUES FOR EDUCATION ONLY. Always use the reference interval issued by the laboratory that performed the test.
Reference intervals differ in pregnancy, childhood, older age and renal disease. Applying an adult range to a child or a pregnant woman causes misdiagnosis.
A DECISION LIMIT (such as the diagnostic threshold for diabetes) is not the same as a population reference interval and the two must not be conflated.
Units matter absolutely. Mixing SI and conventional units has caused serious errors — particularly with glucose, creatinine, bilirubin and cholesterol.
limitations: No universal reference interval exists. This artifact exists to orient, not to authorise.

flashcards.q: What is a reference interval a property of?
flashcards.a: A laboratory, an assay and a population — not a disease

flashcards.q: Difference between a reference interval and a decision limit?
flashcards.a: A reference interval describes a healthy population; a decision limit is a threshold for action or diagnosis

flashcards.q: Isolated raised ALP with a normal GGT suggests?
flashcards.a: A non-hepatic source — bone or placenta
Alcohol-related liver disease

governance.nigeria_overlay: Locally derived reference intervals for Nigerian populations differ from Western-derived values for several analytes, including haemoglobin, white cell and neutrophil counts. Configure facility-specific intervals before clinical use.

triads_and_tetrads.summary: Named symptom clusters. A triad indicates a PATTERN worth considering — it does not confirm a diagnosis, and most patients with the condition do not have the full triad.

body.safety_statement: Scout reports 'pattern present' or 'pattern incomplete'. It never reports 'diagnosis confirmed'. Classic triads are frequently incomplete in real patients, and their absence never excludes the condition.

triads.note: Add hypotension and confusion for REYNOLDS' PENTAD, indicating suppurative cholangitis needing urgent decompression

triads.note: Present in a minority of cases; absence does not exclude tamponade

triads.name: Cushing's triad (raised intracranial pressure)
triads.note: A LATE and pre-terminal sign of impending herniation

triads.name: Virchow's triad (thrombosis)
triads.note: A mechanistic framework, not a clinical presentation

triads.name: Whipple's triad (hypoglycaemia)
components: Relief of symptoms on correcting the glucose

triads.note: Hyperlipidaemia is often added as a fourth feature

triads.name: Meigs' syndrome triad
triads.note: Resolves after removal of the tumour

Horner's syndrome triad
triads.note: Enophthalmos is often described as a fourth, apparent feature

triads.name: Triad of intussusception
components: Colicky abdominal pain with drawing up of the legs
triads.note: The full triad is present in a minority; redcurrant jelly stool is LATE

triads.name: Reiter's (reactive arthritis) triad
triads.note: 'Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree'

triads.name: Triad of pre-eclampsia (classical)
triads.note: OUTDATED — oedema was removed, and proteinuria is no longer mandatory if there is organ dysfunction

triads.name: Triad of aortic stenosis symptoms
triads.note: Symptom onset marks a sharp fall in survival without intervention

triads.name: Triad of Wernicke encephalopathy
triads.note: Complete in a minority; treat empirically with thiamine on suspicion

triads.name: Triad of shaken baby / abusive head trauma
triads.note: Requires expert multi-agency safeguarding assessment; the finding alone is not a determination of cause

warnings: A TRIAD IS A PATTERN, NOT A DIAGNOSIS. Most patients do not have the complete cluster, and the absence of a triad never excludes the condition.
Cushing's triad is a late, pre-terminal sign of raised intracranial pressure — do not wait for it.
The classic pre-eclampsia triad is outdated and must not be used as a diagnostic standard.

clubbing_grades_and_causes.title: Clubbing — Grades and Causes
clubbing_grades_and_causes.summary: A painless bulbous enlargement of the terminal phalanx with loss of the nail-bed angle. Graded in four stages and always a prompt to look for underlying disease.

grades.finding: Fluctuation and softening of the nail bed (increased sponginess)
Loss of the normal Lovibond angle (<160°) — the nail-fold angle is obliterated
Increased convexity of the nail — 'parrot beak' or 'drumstick' appearance
Thickening of the whole distal phalanx, giving a bulbous drumstick finger
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy — clubbing with periostitis, wrist and ankle pain and swelling

body.schamroth_window: Ask the patient to place the dorsal surfaces of corresponding fingers together, nail to nail. A normal pair leaves a diamond-shaped window between the nail beds. In clubbing, the window is OBLITERATED.

other: Unilateral: axillary or subclavian artery aneurysm, arteriovenous fistula (including dialysis fistula), Pancoast tumour

body.note_on_absence: Clubbing is NOT a feature of uncomplicated COPD or asthma. If a patient with a COPD label has clubbing, look for an alternative or additional diagnosis — commonly bronchial carcinoma or bronchiectasis.

warnings: Clubbing is not a feature of uncomplicated COPD or asthma — its presence demands a search for another cause, particularly bronchial carcinoma or bronchiectasis.
Unilateral clubbing suggests a local vascular cause and should not be dismissed.

flashcards.a: The normal diamond-shaped window between opposed nail beds is obliterated
About 160° — reduced or obliterated in clubbing

flashcards.q: Is clubbing a feature of COPD?
flashcards.a: No — look for bronchial carcinoma or bronchiectasis if it is present

diabetic_foot_examine_and_grade.title: Diabetic Foot — Examine and Grade
diabetic_foot_examine_and_grade.summary: Structured assessment of neuropathy, ischaemia and deformity, with a risk category that determines screening interval and footwear.

terms: diabetic foot — risk stratification and examination

examination_sequence: Ask the patient to remove BOTH shoes and socks — the examination is worthless otherwise.

INSPECT: skin colour, dryness, fissures, callus, corns, ulcers (including between the toes and on the heel), nail condition, fungal infection, hair loss, deformity (claw toes, hammer toes, hallux valgus, Charcot deformity, prominent metatarsal heads), amputation sites
INSPECT THE SHOES: wear pattern, foreign objects inside, fit
PALPATE: temperature (compare sides), dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, capillary refill
NEUROPATHY: 10 g monofilament at defined plantar sites, 128 Hz tuning fork vibration at the hallux, ankle reflexes, pinprick and light touch, proprioception
ISCHAEMIA: pulses, ankle-brachial pressure index where available, skin changes, rest pain, claudication history
Assess footwear, self-care ability, vision (can they see their own feet?), and ability to reach their feet

risk_categories.features: No neuropathy, no peripheral arterial disease, no other risk factor
Neuropathy OR peripheral arterial disease OR deformity
risk_categories.action: Screening every 3–6 months by a foot protection service

risk_categories.features: Neuropathy or PAD PLUS deformity or callus, OR previous ulcer, OR previous amputation, OR on renal replacement therapy
risk_categories.action: Screening every 1–2 months; specialist footwear; intensive education

risk_categories.features: Ulceration, spreading infection, critical ischaemia, gangrene, or suspected Charcot foot
risk_categories.action: URGENT referral to the doctors, nurses and other staff working together diabetic foot service, within 24 hours

wagner_ulcer_grading.description: No ulcer, but a foot at risk
Superficial ulcer, full thickness skin only
Deeper ulcer to tendon, bone or capsule
Deep ulcer with abscess or osteomyelitis
Extensive gangrene of the whole foot

body.charcot_foot: A red, hot, swollen foot in a person with neuropathy — often WITHOUT significant pain and often mistaken for cellulitis or gout. Suspect Charcot neuroarthropathy, offload IMMEDIATELY and refer urgently. Delay causes irreversible midfoot collapse (rocker-bottom deformity).
education_points: Inspect the feet daily, using a mirror if needed, and ask for help if vision or reach is limited
Never walk barefoot, indoors or outdoors
Check inside shoes before putting them on
Test bath water temperature with the elbow, not the foot
Do not use chemical corn removers or cut corns yourself
Moisturise dry skin but not between the toes
Report any new ulcer, colour change, swelling or smell the same day
Optimise glycaemic control, blood pressure and lipids

warnings: A RED, HOT, SWOLLEN FOOT IN A NEUROPATHIC PATIENT IS A CHARCOT FOOT UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. Offload immediately and refer urgently — misdiagnosis as cellulitis leads to permanent deformity and amputation.
Neuropathic ulcers are painless. The absence of pain is not reassurance; it is the mechanism of the injury.
Both shoes and socks must come off. A foot examination performed through a sock is not an examination.
Always inspect between the toes and on the heel — these are the sites most commonly missed.

flashcards.a: The 10 g monofilament, applied until it buckles

flashcards.q: Red hot swollen foot in a neuropathic patient?
flashcards.a: Charcot neuroarthropathy until proven otherwise — offload and refer urgently
Deep ulcer with abscess or osteomyelitis

flashcards.q: Where is the posterior tibial pulse felt?
flashcards.a: Behind the medial malleolus

widal_test_what_it_does_and_doesn_t_tell.title: Widal Test — What It Does and Doesn't Tell You
widal_test_what_it_does_and_doesn_t_tell.summary: A serological agglutination test for enteric fever with substantial limitations. It must never be the sole basis for diagnosis or for prolonged antibiotic courses.

terms: widal test — what it does and doesn't tell you

body.what_it_measures: Agglutinating antibodies against Salmonella Typhi somatic O and flagellar H antigens (and Paratyphi AH and BH in many kits).
principle_of_interpretation: A SINGLE titre is of very limited value.
The diagnostically meaningful finding is a FOUR-FOLD OR GREATER RISE in titre between acute and convalescent samples taken 7–14 days apart.
O antibody rises earlier and falls sooner, so it correlates better with acute infection. H antibody persists for months to years after infection or vaccination.
Any locally meaningful cut-off titre must be derived from LOCAL baseline seroprevalence — a titre that is significant in a low-endemicity country may be background in a high-endemicity one.
false_positives: High background seroprevalence in endemic areas
Cross-reaction with other Salmonella species and other Enterobacteriaceae
better_alternatives: BLOOD CULTURE is the diagnostic standard, with the highest yield in the first week of illness. Take an adequate volume before antibiotics.
Bone marrow culture has the highest sensitivity and remains positive despite prior antibiotics.
Stool and urine culture in the later weeks.
body.clinical_consequence: Over-reliance on Widal drives unnecessary antibiotic courses, contributes to antimicrobial resistance, and diverts attention from the actual diagnosis — most often malaria, urinary infection, pneumonia or another cause of fever.

warnings: A SINGLE POSITIVE WIDAL TITRE DOES NOT DIAGNOSE TYPHOID. Paired sera showing a four-fold rise, or better still a blood culture, are required.
Treating every raised Widal as typhoid is a documented driver of antimicrobial resistance and of missed alternative diagnoses.
Always consider and exclude malaria in a febrile patient in an endemic area — co-existence is common.
In a patient with prolonged fever who then develops sudden severe abdominal pain, think typhoid ileal perforation.
limitations: Sensitivity and specificity are both poor and vary widely between kits, laboratories and populations.
No universally valid cut-off titre exists.

flashcards.q: What makes a Widal result meaningful?
flashcards.a: A four-fold or greater rise in titre between acute and convalescent sera

flashcards.q: Which Widal antibody correlates better with acute infection?
flashcards.a: O antibody — it rises earlier and falls sooner than H
Blood culture, with the highest yield in the first week

flashcards.q: Which sample has the highest sensitivity even after antibiotics?
flashcards.a: Bone marrow culture

checkboxes: Blood culture taken BEFORE antibiotics where possible
Paired sera planned if Widal is used at all
Result interpreted alongside the clinical picture
Perforation risk explained to the patient

governance.nigeria_overlay: Background Widal seropositivity is high in Nigerian populations, making single-titre interpretation particularly unreliable. Prioritise blood culture where available and follow national enteric fever guidance.

tension_pneumothorax_decompress_now.title: Tension Pneumothorax — Decompress Now
tension_pneumothorax_decompress_now.summary: Air trapped under pressure in the pleural space compressing the mediastinum. A clinical diagnosis requiring immediate decompression before any imaging.

recognition: Hypotension and tachycardia progressing to arrest
Reduced or ABSENT breath sounds on the affected side
Hyper-resonance to percussion on the affected side
Distended neck veins (may be absent if the patient is hypovolaemic)
TRACHEAL DEVIATION AWAY from the affected side — a LATE sign
In a ventilated patient: sudden rise in airway pressures with falling saturations and blood pressure
immediate_action: DECOMPRESS IMMEDIATELY. Do not wait for a chest radiograph.

Needle or finger decompression: current guidance favours the 4th or 5th intercostal space in the anterior axillary line (safe triangle) over the traditional 2nd space mid-clavicular line, because chest wall thickness at the 2nd space frequently exceeds standard cannula length.
Pass over the SUPERIOR border of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.
Needle decompression is a TEMPORISING measure only. It must be followed by a formal chest drain.
Reassess immediately — improvement in oxygenation, blood pressure and breath sounds confirms the diagnosis.
aftercare: Insert a formal intercostal chest drain
Chest radiograph AFTER decompression to confirm drain position and lung re-expansion
Identify the cause: trauma, ventilation, procedure (central line, pleural tap), spontaneous, underlying lung disease
Document the indication, findings and response clearly
distinguish_from: Massive haemothorax — reduced breath sounds but DULL to percussion, and the patient is hypovolaemic
Cardiac tamponade — raised JVP and hypotension but breath sounds are equal and the chest is resonant
Main bronchus intubation — unilateral reduced breath sounds after intubation; withdraw the tube
Simple pneumothorax — no failing circulation — low BP, fast pulse, cold peripheries

warnings: DO NOT WAIT FOR A CHEST RADIOGRAPH. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and imaging delay has killed patients.
Tracheal deviation and distended neck veins are LATE signs. Their absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
Needle decompression is temporary. A chest drain must follow.
In a hypovolaemic patient the neck veins may be flat despite tension pneumothorax.
The 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line often fails because the chest wall is thicker than the cannula is long — use the safe triangle.

flashcards.q: Is tension pneumothorax a radiological or clinical diagnosis?
flashcards.a: Clinical — decompress before imaging

flashcards.q: Preferred decompression site in current guidance?
flashcards.a: 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line (safe triangle)

flashcards.q: Why avoid the 2nd space mid-clavicular line?
flashcards.a: Chest wall thickness there frequently exceeds standard cannula length

flashcards.q: Percussion note: tension pneumothorax vs massive haemothorax?
flashcards.a: Hyper-resonant vs dull

feast_2011_fluid_bolus_in_african_childr.title: FEAST (2011) — Fluid bolus in African children
feast_2011_fluid_bolus_in_african_childr.summary: Do fluid boluses improve survival in African children with severe febrile illness and impaired perfusion? Routine fluid bolus therapy INCREASED death rate in this population.

terms: feast (2011) — fluid bolus in african children

body.question: Do fluid boluses improve survival in African children with severe febrile illness and impaired perfusion?
body.design: Multicentre randomised controlled trial. Three arms: albumin bolus, saline bolus, no bolus.
body.population: 3,141 children in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania with severe febrile illness and impaired perfusion. Malaria and sepsis dominant.
body.result: 48-hour death rate was HIGHER in both bolus arms than in the no-bolus arm. Excess deaths were cardiovascular collapse, not fluid overload.
body.conclusion: Routine fluid bolus therapy INCREASED death rate in this population.
body.what_changed_in_practice: Fluid bolus is no longer given reflexively to African children with impaired perfusion but without hypotension. Resuscitate cautiously and reassess. This is the single most important African trial for paediatric emergency care.
caveats_before_you_apply_it: Excluded children with severe hypotension or gastroenteritis — those still need fluid.
Conducted where ventilation and intensive care were largely unavailable; the result may not transfer to a resourced ICU.
Does NOT mean withhold fluid from a shocked, hypotensive child.
