e_motive_2023_postpartum_bleeding_bundle.title: E-MOTIVE (2023) — Postpartum bleeding bundle
e_motive_2023_postpartum_bleeding_bundle.summary: Does early objective detection of postpartum bleeding plus an immediate treatment bundle reduce severe outcomes? Measuring blood loss with a calibrated drape and then delivering a fixed bundle immediately is dramatically better than eyeballing loss and treating stepwise.

body.question: Does early objective detection of postpartum bleeding plus an immediate treatment bundle reduce severe outcomes?
body.design: International parallel cluster-randomised trial with a baseline control phase.
body.population: 80 secondary-level hospitals in Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa and Tanzania. Women having vaginal births.
body.result: 60% reduction in the composite of severe PPH, laparotomy for bleeding, or death from bleeding. Detection rose from 51.1% to 93.1%. Bundle use rose from 19.4% to 91.2%.
body.conclusion: Measuring blood loss with a calibrated drape and then delivering a fixed bundle immediately is dramatically better than eyeballing loss and treating stepwise.
body.what_changed_in_practice: WHO revised its PPH guidance to recommend the MOTIVE bundle — Massage, Oxytocics, Tranexamic acid, IV fluids, Examination, Escalate — ideally all started within 15 minutes of detection. Nigeria was a lead site.
caveats_before_you_apply_it: The trial included training, champions, restocked trolleys and audit feedback; the drape alone is not the intervention.
Vaginal births only — caesarean bleeding was not studied.
Bundle components must all be available and in date; oxytocin cold chain and TXA stock are the usual failure points.

aquamat_2010_artesunate_vs_quinine_in_af.title: AQUAMAT (2010) — Artesunate vs quinine in African children
also_known_as: artesunate vs quinine in african children
aquamat_2010_artesunate_vs_quinine_in_af.summary: Is intravenous artesunate better than quinine for severe malaria in African children? Artesunate is superior to quinine for severe malaria in African children.

terms: aquamat (2010) — artesunate vs quinine in african children
artesunate vs quinine in african children

body.question: Is intravenous artesunate better than quinine for severe malaria in African children?
body.population: 5,425 children under 15 with severe falciparum malaria across nine African countries.
body.result: death rate 8.5% with artesunate versus 10.9% with quinine — a relative reduction of about 22.5%.
body.conclusion: Artesunate is superior to quinine for severe malaria in African children.
body.what_changed_in_practice: by injection or drip, not by mouth artesunate replaced quinine as first-line treatment for severe malaria worldwide. Quinine is now a fallback when artesunate is unavailable.
caveats_before_you_apply_it: Post-artesunate delayed haemolysis appears 1–3 weeks later — check haemoglobin at follow-up.
Supportive care quality still drives much of the outcome.
Applies to severe malaria; uncomplicated malaria is treated with oral ACT.

ambition_cm_2022_cryptococcal_meningitis.title: AMBITION-cm (2022) — Cryptococcal meningitis in Africa
ambition_cm_2022_cryptococcal_meningitis.summary: Can a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin replace a week of daily amphotericin B deoxycholate? A single 10 mg/kg dose of liposomal amphotericin B with 14 days of flucytosine and fluconazole is as good as a week of daily amphotericin and much safer.

body.question: Can a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin replace a week of daily amphotericin B deoxycholate?
body.design: Phase 3 randomised as good as — not worseity trial.
body.population: 844 adults with HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis at 8 hospitals in Botswana, Malawi, South Africa, Uganda and Zimbabwe.
body.result: 10-week death rate 24.8% with single-dose liposomal amphotericin versus 28.7% with standard care — as good as — not worse, with significantly fewer adverse events.
body.conclusion: A single 10 mg/kg dose of liposomal amphotericin B with 14 days of flucytosine and fluconazole is as good as a week of daily amphotericin and much safer.
body.what_changed_in_practice: WHO changed its cryptococcal meningitis guidance in 2022 to recommend this regimen. It shortens admission, reduces monitoring burden and cuts toxicity — all of which matter enormously in a district hospital.
caveats_before_you_apply_it: Requires flucytosine, which remains poorly available and expensive in much of Africa.
Therapeutic lumbar punctures for raised intracranial pressure remain essential — the drug does not replace pressure control.
Liposomal amphotericin cost and access are the limiting factors, not the evidence.

tb_practecal_2022_6_month_all_oral_mdr_t.title: TB-PRACTECAL (2022) — 6-month all-oral MDR-TB regimen
tb_practecal_2022_6_month_all_oral_mdr_t.summary: Can a 6-month all-oral regimen replace 9–20 months of treatment for drug-resistant TB? BPaLM (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin) for 6 months is markedly better than long injectable-containing regimens.

body.question: Can a 6-month all-oral regimen replace 9–20 months of treatment for drug-resistant TB?
body.design: Multicountry open-label randomised controlled trial (stage 2 was effectively phase 3).
body.population: Adults with MDR/RR-TB in Belarus, South Africa and Uzbekistan.
body.result: Treatment success about 89% with BPaLM versus about 52% with the standard of care regimens of the time, with less failure, death and loss to follow-up.
body.conclusion: BPaLM (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin) for 6 months is markedly better than long injectable-containing regimens.
body.what_changed_in_practice: WHO recommends BPaLM as the preferred regimen for MDR/RR-TB and pre-XDR-TB. Injectable-based long regimens are now the exception.
caveats_before_you_apply_it: Not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding — limited pretomanid safety data.
All four drugs prolong QT; ECG and electrolyte monitoring are mandatory.
Linezolid causes myelosuppression, peripheral neuropathy and optic neuritis — monitor weekly.
Pretomanid availability is the practical bottleneck in many national programmes.

reality_2017_advanced_hiv_in_africa.title: REALITY (2017) — Advanced HIV in Africa
reality_2017_advanced_hiv_in_africa.summary: Does an enhanced prevention package reduce death in people starting ART with advanced HIV? People presenting with advanced HIV need a prevention package, not just ART.

body.question: Does an enhanced prevention package reduce death in people starting ART with advanced HIV?
body.design: Open-label randomised trial with a factorial design.
body.population: 1,805 adults and children over 5 with CD4 below 100 starting ART in Kenya, Malawi, Uganda and Zimbabwe.
body.result: Enhanced prevention (co-trimoxazole plus isoniazid/pyridoxine, fluconazole, azithromycin, albendazole) reduced 24-week death rate from 12.2% to 8.9%.
body.conclusion: People presenting with advanced HIV need a prevention package, not just ART.
body.what_changed_in_practice: WHO advanced HIV disease packages now include enhanced prevention. Starting ART alone in a profoundly immunosuppressed patient is not enough.
caveats_before_you_apply_it: Applies to advanced disease (CD4 <100), not to routine ART initiation.
Requires CD4 or clinical staging capacity to identify the group.
Drug availability of the full package is variable.

tract_2019_transfusion_in_african_childr.title: TRACT (2019) — Transfusion in African children with severe anaemia
also_known_as: transfusion in african children with severe anaemia
tract_2019_transfusion_in_african_childr.summary: What transfusion volume and threshold is best for African children with severe anaemia? Higher transfusion volumes are not automatically better, and not every child with severe anaemia needs immediate blood.

terms: tract (2019) — transfusion in african children with severe anaemia
transfusion in african children with severe anaemia

body.question: What transfusion volume and threshold is best for African children with severe anaemia?
body.population: Over 3,000 children with severe anaemia in Uganda and Malawi.
body.result: Immediate transfusion of 20 mL/kg versus 30 mL/kg showed no overall death rate difference at 28 days; effects varied with fever. In uncomplicated severe anaemia, immediate transfusion did not reduce 28-day death rate compared with a conservative approach.
body.conclusion: Higher transfusion volumes are not automatically better, and not every child with severe anaemia needs immediate blood.
body.what_changed_in_practice: Supports more conservative, protocol-driven transfusion in stable children with severe anaemia — important where blood supply is scarce.
caveats_before_you_apply_it: Complex results with subgroup variation; read the protocol before generalising.
Does not apply to children with decompensation, shock or ongoing bleeding.
Local blood availability and haemoglobinopathy prevalence change the calculus.

body.question: Does biannual mass azithromycin distribution reduce childhood death rate in high-death rate settings?
body.population: Communities in Niger, Malawi and Tanzania; children 1–59 months.
body.result: Overall childhood death rate was about 13.5% lower in azithromycin communities; the effect was concentrated in Niger and in the youngest infants.
body.conclusion: Mass azithromycin reduces child death rate where baseline death rate is very high.
body.what_changed_in_practice: WHO issued conditional guidance for mass azithromycin administration in selected very-high-death rate settings, with antimicrobial resistance surveillance attached.

body.question: Is hydroxyurea safe and effective for children with sickle cell anaemia in sub-Saharan Africa?
body.population: Children with sickle cell anaemia in Angola, DRC, Kenya and Uganda.

palm_2019_ebola_monoclonal_antibodies.summary: Which therapeutic agent is most effective for Ebola virus disease? Monoclonal antibody therapy markedly improves Ebola survival, especially when given early with low viral load.

body.question: Which therapeutic agent is most effective for Ebola virus disease?
body.design: Randomised controlled trial run during an active outbreak.
body.population: 681 patients in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
body.result: REGN-EB3 and mAb114 produced substantially lower death rate than ZMapp or remdesivir.
body.conclusion: Monoclonal antibody therapy markedly improves Ebola survival, especially when given early with low viral load.
body.what_changed_in_practice: Established mAb114 (ansuvimab) and REGN-EB3 as standard therapy for Ebola. Also proved that rigorous randomised trials can be run inside an active outbreak in a conflict zone.

body.question: Is routine laboratory monitoring necessary for ART in hospital where staff, drugs or equipment are shorts?
body.design: Randomised trial comparing clinically driven monitoring with routine laboratory monitoring.
body.population: 3,316 adults starting ART in Uganda and Zimbabwe.
body.result: Survival was good in both arms; routine laboratory monitoring gave a modest additional benefit that appeared mainly after the second year.
body.conclusion: ART can be delivered safely with clinically driven monitoring where laboratory capacity is limited.
body.what_changed_in_practice: Supported large-scale ART rollout across Africa without waiting for universal laboratory infrastructure — a decision that saved very large numbers of lives.

body.conclusion: One dose of HPV vaccine may be enough for protection against the oncogenic types that matter most.

body.question: Should kangaroo mother care start immediately after birth rather than after stabilisation?
body.population: 3,211 infants weighing 1.0–1.799 kg in Ghana, India, Malawi, Nigeria and Tanzania.
body.result: Neonatal death rate by 28 days was significantly lower with immediate kangaroo mother care (12.0% vs 15.7%). The trial was stopped early for benefit.
body.conclusion: Starting skin-to-skin care immediately, before stabilisation, saves the lives of low-birth-weight infants.
body.what_changed_in_practice: WHO changed its recommendation: kangaroo mother care should begin immediately after birth, not after a stabilisation period. Nigeria was a study site.
caveats_before_you_apply_it: Requires a mother-newborn intensive care unit model where mother and baby are kept together.
Facility layout and staffing often need reorganisation to deliver this.

body.population: Nearly 30,000 women across 23 sites in 10 countries, including several in Africa.
body.result: Heat-stable carbetocin was as good as — not worse to oxytocin for preventing blood loss of 500 mL or more.
body.conclusion: A uterotonic that does not need refrigeration works as well as oxytocin.
body.what_changed_in_practice: WHO added heat-stable carbetocin as a recommended option for PPH prevention where oxytocin cold chain cannot be guaranteed — a direct answer to a real African supply problem.

body.conclusion: A second malaria vaccine with strong efficacy and a manufacturing profile suited to mass supply.
body.what_changed_in_practice: WHO recommended R21/Matrix-M in 2023 alongside RTS,S/AS01. Rollout has begun in several African countries including Nigeria.

body.design: Randomised controlled trial with factorial design.
body.population: 2,056 adults with HIV in Côte d'Ivoire.
body.result: Early ART reduced severe illness and death; six months of isoniazid preventive therapy gave additional benefit that persisted for years.
body.conclusion: Start ART early irrespective of CD4, and give TB preventive therapy.
body.what_changed_in_practice: Together with START, this drove the global 'treat all' policy. Also established TB preventive therapy as standard for people living with HIV.

body.question: Does co-trimoxazole prevention reduce death rate in HIV-infected African children?
body.design: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, stopped early for benefit.
body.population: 541 HIV-infected children in Zambia.
body.result: death rate reduced by 43% and hospital admissions by 23%.
body.conclusion: Daily co-trimoxazole substantially reduces death in HIV-infected children.
body.what_changed_in_practice: Co-trimoxazole prevention became standard of care for HIV-exposed and HIV-infected children across Africa — one of the highest-impact, lowest-cost interventions in the region.

crash_2_2010_tranexamic_acid_in_trauma.summary: Does tranexamic acid reduce death in bleeding trauma patients? Early tranexamic acid saves lives in bleeding trauma.

body.question: Does tranexamic acid reduce death in bleeding trauma patients?
body.design: Randomised placebo-controlled trial in 274 hospitals across 40 countries, including many in Africa.
body.population: 20,211 adult trauma patients with or at risk of significant bleeding.
body.result: All-cause death rate reduced from 16.0% to 14.5%; death due to bleeding reduced. Benefit was confined to treatment given within 3 hours; treatment after 3 hours was associated with harm.
body.conclusion: Early tranexamic acid saves lives in bleeding trauma.
body.what_changed_in_practice: TXA within 3 hours became standard in trauma protocols worldwide. It is cheap, stable and does not need refrigeration — ideal for African trauma systems.
caveats_before_you_apply_it: Give within 3 hours. After 3 hours it may increase death from bleeding.
Not a substitute for surgical haemorrhage control.
Isolated head injury has separate evidence — see CRASH-3.

body.conclusion: Early TXA reduces death in mild-to-moderate TBI.
body.what_changed_in_practice: TXA is now given early in TBI in many protocols, with the benefit concentrated in less severe injury treated quickly.

body.conclusion: Early tight control produces benefits that persist for decades.
body.what_changed_in_practice: Established metformin as first-line in overweight type 2 diabetes and cemented blood pressure control as at least as important as glucose control.

rales_1999_spironolactone_in_heart_failu.summary: Does spironolactone reduce death rate in severe heart failure? Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism reduces death in heart failure.

body.question: Does spironolactone reduce death rate in severe heart failure?
body.design: Randomised placebo-controlled trial, stopped early for benefit.
body.population: 1,663 patients with severe HFrEF.
body.result: All-cause death rate reduced by 30%.

how_to_read_a_trial_in_60_seconds: What was the QUESTION? If you cannot state it in one sentence, be suspicious.
Who was IN it? Age, country, severity. Is your patient in that group?
What was the COMPARATOR? 'Better than nothing' is a weaker claim than 'better than current best care'.
Was the outcome one that MATTERS (death, disability) or a surrogate (a lab number)?
Absolute or relative? A 50% relative reduction of a 2% risk is a 1% absolute gain.
Was it STOPPED EARLY? Early stopping for benefit tends to overestimate effect size.
Has it been REPLICATED? PROWESS is the standing reminder of why this matters.
Does the setting match yours? FEAST is the standing reminder of why this matters.

body.paper_speed: Standard 25 mm/s and 10 mm/mV. One small square = 0.04 s and 0.1 mV. One large square = 0.2 s. Five large squares = 1 second. CHECK THE CALIBRATION MARK before measuring anything.

components.too_tall: P pulmonale — right atrial enlargement (cor pulmonale, tricuspid disease)
components.too_wide_or_bifid: P mitrale — left atrial enlargement (mitral stenosis)

components.represents: Start of atrial depolarisation to start of ventricular depolarisation
components.long: First-degree heart block; progressive lengthening = Mobitz I (Wenckebach)
components.short: Pre-excitation — Wolff-Parkinson-White with a delta wave

components.wide: Bundle branch block, ventricular origin, hyperkalaemia, sodium-channel blocker toxicity, paced rhythm
components.tall: Ventricular hypertrophy — Sokolow-Lyon: S in V1 + R in V5 or V6 > 35 mm suggests LVH
components.pathological_Q: Deep (>25% of R height) and wide (>0.04 s) — prior full-thickness infarct

components.depressed: Ischaemia, NSTEMI, digoxin effect (down-sloping 'reverse tick'), hypokalaemia, reciprocal change

components.inverted: Ischaemia, ventricular strain, PE (T inversion V1–V4), raised intracranial pressure, normal in V1 and in children

components.normal: Corrected QT (QTc) roughly <440 ms in men and <460 ms in women

territories.leads: Tall R and ST depression in V1–V2

jvp_waveform_a_c_v_and_what_each_abnorma.summary: The jugular venous pulse has three peaks and two troughs. Each one belongs to a specific event in the cardiac cycle, and each abnormality points to a specific lesion.

terms: jvp waveform — a, c, v and what each abnormality means

body.how_to_measure: Patient at 45°, head turned slightly left, good tangential lighting. Look between the two heads of sternocleidomastoid. Measure the VERTICAL height above the sternal angle and add 5 cm for right atrial pressure. Normal is up to about 3–4 cm above the sternal angle.
jvp_vs_carotid: JVP has two peaks per cycle; carotid has one
JVP is non-palpable; carotid is palpable
JVP falls on inspiration (normally); carotid does not
JVP is obliterated by light pressure at the base of the neck
JVP varies with position; carotid does not

waves.large_in: Tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary stenosis, pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular hypertrophy
waves.cannon: CANNON a waves — atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve: complete heart block, ventricular tachycardia, junctional rhythm

waves.event: Tricuspid valve bulging into the atrium at the start of ventricular systole
Atrial relaxation and downward pull of the tricuspid ring
Atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve
waves.giant_in: TRICUSPID REGURGITATION — giant fused cv wave

waves.event: Tricuspid opening and rapid ventricular filling

body.key_discriminator: CONSTRICTION versus TAMPONADE — constrictive pericarditis has a PROMINENT y descent; tamponade has an ABSENT or blunted y descent. Both may have a raised JVP.
body.kussmaul_sign: JVP RISES on inspiration instead of falling. Seen in constrictive pericarditis, right ventricular infarction, restrictive cardiomyopathy and severe right heart failure. Classically ABSENT in tamponade.

warnings: A raised JVP with hypotension is tamponade, obstructive shock or right heart failure — not hypovolaemia.
In a hypovolaemic patient the JVP may be flat even with tension pneumothorax or tamponade.
Do not measure the JVP along the neck — measure the vertical height above the sternal angle.

flashcards.a: Atrium contracting against a closed tricuspid valve — complete heart block, VT, junctional rhythm
Tricuspid regurgitation

flashcards.q: y descent in tamponade vs constriction?
flashcards.a: Absent/blunted in tamponade; prominent and sharp in constriction
JVP rises on inspiration — constriction, RV infarct, restrictive cardiomyopathy

eeg_basics_rhythms_seizure_patterns_and_.title: EEG Basics — Rhythms, Seizure Patterns and Artefacts
eeg_basics_rhythms_seizure_patterns_and_.summary: The four background rhythms, what each seizure type looks like, and the artefacts that fool people into calling normal traces abnormal.

terms: eeg basics — rhythms, seizure patterns and artefacts

background_rhythms.state: Alert, concentrating; increased by benzodiazepines and barbiturates
Awake, relaxed, EYES CLOSED. Attenuates on eye opening.
Drowsiness, light sleep; normal in children; abnormal if focal and persistent in an adult
Deep sleep; in an awake adult suggests encephalopathy or a structural lesion

seizure_patterns.note: Provoked by hyperventilation — a bedside test
Centrotemporal spikes in benign rolandic epilepsy
Chaotic high-amplitude disorganised background — a paediatric emergency
Classically herpes simplex encephalitis, stroke, abscess

seizure_patterns.condition: Deep anaesthesia or severe brain injury
seizure_patterns.note: A target in not responding to treatment status epilepticus; a poor sign after arrest
Consider in any patient who does not wake after clinical seizures stop

body.practical_note: EEG is a supporting test. A normal interictal EEG does NOT exclude epilepsy, and a non-specific abnormality does NOT diagnose it. The diagnosis of epilepsy is clinical, built on a good eyewitness account.

warnings: A normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy, and an abnormal one does not diagnose it.
Hypsarrhythmia in an infant with spasms is an emergency — treatment delay costs development.
If a patient does not regain consciousness after convulsions stop, consider non-convulsive status.

flashcards.a: 8–13 Hz, occipital, eyes closed
Childhood absence epilepsy
Infantile spasms / West syndrome
Metabolic encephalopathy

circle_of_willis_arteries_and_stroke_ter.title: Circle of Willis — Arteries and Stroke Territories
circle_of_willis_arteries_and_stroke_ter.summary: The arterial ring at the base of the brain, which artery supplies what, and the deficit you see when each one blocks.

terms: circle of willis — arteries and stroke territories

body.why_it_exists: Collateral supply. A complete circle allows perfusion to be maintained when one feeding vessel occludes. The circle is anatomically complete in only a minority of people, which is part of why identical occlusions produce different deficits in different patients.

territories.supplies: Medial frontal and parietal lobes, including the leg area of the motor strip
territories.occlusion: CONTRALATERAL LEG weakness and sensory loss more than arm; urinary incontinence; abulia; grasp reflex

territories.supplies: Lateral hemisphere, including face and arm motor and sensory areas, Broca and Wernicke areas
territories.occlusion: Contralateral FACE AND ARM weakness more than leg; hemisensory loss; homonymous hemianopia; APHASIA if dominant hemisphere; NEGLECT if non-dominant. The commonest large-vessel stroke.

territories.supplies: Occipital lobe, inferomedial temporal lobe, thalamus
territories.occlusion: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia WITH MACULAR SPARING; visual agnosia; thalamic pain syndrome
Reduced consciousness, cranial nerve palsies with crossed signs, quadriparesis, locked-in syndrome. High death rate.
LACUNAR syndromes — pure motor hemiparesis, pure sensory stroke, ataxic hemiparesis, dysarthria-clumsy hand
WALLENBERG (lateral medullary) syndrome — ipsilateral facial sensory loss, Horner syndrome, dysphagia, hoarseness, ataxia, with CONTRALATERAL body pain and temperature loss

body.aneurysm_note: Berry (saccular) aneurysms form at branch points, most commonly the anterior communicating artery, posterior communicating artery and MCA bifurcation. A posterior communicating aneurysm classically compresses the third cranial nerve, producing a PAINFUL PUPIL-INVOLVING third nerve palsy.
body.cortical_vs_lacunar: Cortical signs (aphasia, neglect, hemianopia) mean a large vessel. Their absence with a pure motor or pure sensory deficit suggests a lacunar (small vessel) stroke.

warnings: Face and arm weakness with aphasia is an MCA stroke until proven otherwise — a large-vessel occlusion that may be thrombectomy-eligible.
A painful, pupil-involving third nerve palsy is a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until excluded.
Posterior circulation strokes present with vertigo, ataxia and diplopia and are frequently missed.

flashcards.a: MCA: face and arm more than leg. ACA: leg more than arm.
PCA occlusion — homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
PICA — lateral medullary syndrome
Anterior communicating, posterior communicating, MCA bifurcation

dermatomes_and_myotomes_levels_that_matt.title: Dermatomes and Myotomes — Levels That Matter
dermatomes_and_myotomes_levels_that_matt.summary: The sensory levels and movement levels you actually use: where to test, what a level means, and the landmarks worth memorising.

terms: dermatomes and myotomes — levels that matter

landmark_dermatomes.landmark: Dorsum of foot / first web space

clinical_uses: A SENSORY LEVEL means spinal cord pathology — find it and act; cord compression is time-critical.
SADDLE ANAESTHESIA with bladder or bowel change is CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME — an emergency needing urgent MRI.
Nipple line T4 and umbilicus T10 are the two levels worth memorising cold.
'S2, 3, 4 keep the pelvic floor off the floor' — the sacral roots for continence and erection.
Sciatica maps to a root: L5 gives dorsum of foot and great toe extension weakness; S1 gives lateral foot, plantarflexion weakness and a lost ankle jerk.

warnings: Saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg symptoms, or new bladder or bowel dysfunction is cauda equina syndrome — urgent MRI and surgical referral.
A sensory level is a spinal cord finding and demands imaging, not reassurance.
Dermatome maps differ slightly between textbooks; the landmarks are reliable, the exact borders are not.

flashcards.a: T4

flashcards.q: Which root for great toe extension?
flashcards.a: L5
S1 (with S2)
Cauda equina syndrome until proven otherwise

ion_channels_and_pumps_by_organ_and_drug.title: Ion Channels and Pumps — By Organ and Drug Target
ion_channels_and_pumps_by_organ_and_drug.summary: The transporters that actually get targeted by drugs: where each one sits, what it moves, and which drug blocks it.

terms: ion channels and pumps — by organ and drug target

by_organ.moves: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, using ATP
by_organ.why_it_matters: Creates the electrochemical gradient every other transport process depends on
by_organ.drug: DIGOXIN inhibits it → intracellular Na⁺ rises → less Ca²⁺ extrusion via Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange → makes the heart squeeze harder

by_organ.why_it_matters: Excitation-contraction coupling and AV nodal conduction
by_organ.drug: Verapamil and diltiazem (rate-limiting); amlodipine and nifedipine act mainly on vascular smooth muscle
Class I antiarrhythmics; also blocked in tricyclic antidepressant overdose — hence wide QRS, treated with sodium bicarbonate
IVABRADINE slows the rate without affecting contractility or blood pressure

by_organ.moves: Na, K and 2 Cl into the cell
by_organ.drug: LOOP DIURETICS (furosemide) — powerful natriuresis, hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia, ototoxicity
THIAZIDES — hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, HYPERcalcaemia, hyperuricaemia, hyperglycaemia

by_organ.why_it_matters: Final sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion
by_organ.drug: AMILORIDE and triamterene block it directly; SPIRONOLACTONE blocks the aldosterone receptor upstream. Both cause hyperkalaemia.

by_organ.why_it_matters: Potassium excretion — explains why loop and thiazide diuretics waste potassium
by_organ.drug: Indirectly affected by all the above
DAPAGLIFLOZIN, EMPAGLIFLOZIN — glycosuria, osmotic diuresis, cardiorenal protection, euglycaemic DKA risk
Absent/resistant in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; LITHIUM is a classic cause
OMEPRAZOLE and other PPIs — irreversible inhibition; long-term risks include hypomagnesaemia, B12 deficiency, C. difficile, fracture

by_organ.why_it_matters: Hydration of airway surface liquid and secretions
by_organ.drug: Defective in CYSTIC FIBROSIS; modulators (ivacaftor, lumacaftor, elexacaftor) target specific mutation classes
BENZODIAZEPINES increase frequency of opening; BARBITURATES increase duration; also alcohol and propofol
Blocked by non-depolarising relaxants (vecuronium); persistently opened by suxamethonium; attacked by antibodies in MYASTHENIA GRAVIS
Basis of radioiodine uptake scanning and treatment; blocked by perchlorate and thiocyanate

body.exam_shortcut: Diuretic site is easiest learned by following the nephron: acetazolamide (proximal, carbonic anhydrase) → mannitol (osmotic, loop) → furosemide (NKCC2, thick ascending limb) → thiazide (NCC, distal convoluted) → spironolactone/amiloride (collecting duct).

warnings: Combining an ACE inhibitor, an MRA and a potassium-sparing diuretic stacks three hyperkalaemia mechanisms.
Thiazides RAISE calcium; loop diuretics LOWER it. This reversal is a common exam and clinical trap.
Digoxin toxicity is potentiated by hypokalaemia because potassium competes at the same Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase site.

flashcards.a: NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
NCC in the distal convoluted tubule
They RAISE serum calcium (loop diuretics lower it)
Inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → raised intracellular Na⁺ → less Ca²⁺ extrusion → positive inotropy

flashcards.q: Which drug targets the funny current?
flashcards.a: Ivabradine

reversal_agents_and_antidotes.title: Reversal Agents and Antidotes
reversal_agents_and_antidotes.summary: What reverses what, how fast, and the traps. Reversal is rarely just 'give the antidote' — timing, dose logic and what happens afterwards all matter.

agents.notes: Titrate to RESPIRATORY RATE, not to consciousness. Half-life is shorter than most opioids, so re-sedation is expected — observe or infuse. In dependent patients, over-rapid reversal precipitates severe withdrawal and agitation.
RARELY INDICATED. Precipitates seizures in chronic users and in mixed overdose with tricyclics. Supportive airway care is usually safer.

Most effective within 8 hours. Use the treatment nomogram against the timed level. In staggered or unknown-time ingestion, treat empirically. Anaphylactoid reactions are rate-related — slow the infusion, do not abandon treatment.

agents.antidote: Vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate (or FFP if PCC unavailable)
agents.notes: PCC works in minutes; vitamin K takes 6–24 hours but is needed to prevent rebound. Give BOTH in major bleeding. Dose of vitamin K depends on whether you intend to keep the patient anticoagulated afterwards.
Full reversal. Give slowly — rapid administration causes hypotension, bradycardia and anaphylactoid reaction. Only PARTIALLY reverses low molecular weight heparin.
Specific monoclonal antibody fragment; rapid and near-complete.
Availability and cost are the limiting factors in most settings.
For life-threatening arrhythmia or significant hyperkalaemia in acute overdose. AVOID intravenous calcium in digoxin toxicity with hyperkalaemia. Digoxin is not dialysable.
Glucagon bypasses the beta-receptor via a separate cyclic AMP route. Atropine and pacing are often insufficient.

agents.antidote: Calcium salts, high-dose insulin-euglycaemia, blood-pressure-raising drug (adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine)s
agents.notes: High-dose insulin with glucose is the mainstay in significant toxicity and is consistently under-used.

agents.antidote: ATROPINE (large repeated doses) plus pralidoxime for organophosphates
agents.notes: Titrate atropine to DRYING OF SECRETIONS, not to heart rate. Doses required are far larger than clinicians expect. Decontaminate and protect staff. Common in agricultural poisoning.
Urine turns 'vin rosé'. Watch for hypotension with rapid infusion.
Raised osmolar gap early, raised anion gap later. Dialysis removes both the parent alcohol and the toxic metabolites.
CONTRAINDICATED in G6PD deficiency — causes haemolysis. Saturation reads around 85% and does not improve with oxygen.
For QRS widening and arrhythmia. Sodium loading overcomes fast sodium channel blockade. AVOID class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics.
Every location performing regional blocks must stock lipid emulsion and have the protocol displayed.
Must be physically at the bedside before magnesium infusion starts in eclampsia.
Protects the myocardium; does NOT lower potassium. Insulin-dextrose, salbutamol and definitive removal must follow.

agents.antidote: Polyvalent antivenom appropriate to the region
agents.notes: Give for systemic envenoming or significant local progression, not for every bite. Anticipate anaphylaxis — adrenaline drawn up and ready. Do NOT apply a tourniquet, cut, or suck the wound. Immobilise the limb and transfer.
Pulse oximetry is FALSELY NORMAL — it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin.

body.general_rule: Supportive care saves more poisoned patients than antidotes do. Airway, breathing, circulation, glucose, temperature and decontamination come first. Then ask what specific antidote exists.

warnings: Naloxone is titrated to respiratory rate, not consciousness, and its short half-life means re-sedation must be anticipated.
Flumazenil can precipitate seizures — it is rarely the right answer.
Methylene blue causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, which is common in West Africa.
Pulse oximetry is falsely reassuring in carbon monoxide poisoning and methaemoglobinaemia.
Atropine in organophosphate poisoning is titrated to secretion drying and requires far higher doses than expected.
Never delay supportive care while hunting for an antidote.

flashcards.q: What do you titrate naloxone to?
flashcards.a: Respiratory rate, not consciousness
Calcium gluconate — kept at the bedside

flashcards.q: Which antidote is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency?
flashcards.a: Methylene blue
Glucagon, then high-dose insulin-euglycaemia therapy

flashcards.q: Why is pulse oximetry misleading in CO poisoning?
flashcards.a: It cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin

checkboxes: Antidote dose checked against local protocol
Anaphylaxis kit ready if antivenom or NAC
Re-sedation/rebound anticipated and observation period set
Mental health assessment planned if intentional

governance.nigeria_overlay: Antivenom must match the snakes of the region — confirm the polyvalent product stocked and its species coverage. Organophosphate poisoning is common in agricultural areas; ensure atropine stock is adequate for the very large doses required.

chronic_liver_disease_peripheral_stigmat.title: Chronic Liver Disease — Peripheral Stigmata
chronic_liver_disease_peripheral_stigmat.summary: The signs outside the abdomen that tell you the liver is chronically damaged, grouped by where you find them.

chest_and_trunk: SPIDER NAEVI — fill from the centre outward on blanching; more than five in the SVC distribution is abnormal
Loss of body and axillary hair
abdomen: Ascites with shifting dullness and fluid thrill
CAPUT MEDUSAE — distended periumbilical veins, filling AWAY from the umbilicus (in IVC obstruction they fill towards it)
Hepatomegaly early, small shrunken liver late

why_they_happen.spider_naevi_palmar_erythema_gynaecomast: Impaired hepatic oestrogen metabolism → relative hyperoestrogenaemia
why_they_happen.asterixis_fetor: Failure to clear nitrogenous waste → encephalopathy
why_they_happen.bruising: Reduced synthesis of clotting factors and thrombocytopenia

warnings: Asterixis with jaundice is hepatic encephalopathy — assess the airway and look hard for the precipitant.
A few spider naevi can be normal in pregnancy and in young women; more than five in the SVC distribution is not.
Kayser-Fleischer rings in a young person with liver disease means Wilson disease until excluded — a treatable cause.

flashcards.q: How does a spider naevus blanch?
flashcards.a: From the centre outwards — it fills from a central arteriole

flashcards.q: Which liver stigmata come from excess oestrogen?
flashcards.a: Spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, loss of body hair
Away from the umbilicus in portal hypertension; towards it in IVC obstruction

fever_patterns_and_what_they_suggest.title: Fever Patterns and What They Suggest
fever_patterns_and_what_they_suggest.summary: The shape of a temperature chart carries information. Six named patterns and the diagnoses they point towards.

terms: fever patterns and what they suggest

patterns.description: Stays raised, varying less than about 1 °C, never touching normal
patterns.suggests: Typhoid (in the second week), lobar pneumonia, urinary tract infection, brucellosis, some drug fevers

patterns.description: Rises a little higher each day over the first week, then plateaus
patterns.suggests: CLASSIC TYPHOID (enteric fever). Often accompanied by relative bradycardia (Faget sign).

patterns.description: Fluctuates by more than 1 °C but never returns to normal
patterns.suggests: Many bacterial infections, infective endocarditis, viral infections

patterns.description: Spikes then returns to normal within each 24 hours
patterns.suggests: Pyogenic abscess, pyelonephritis, malaria, tuberculosis, lymphoma

patterns.description: Tertian spikes every 48 hours; quartan every 72 hours
patterns.suggests: MALARIA — tertian with P. vivax and P. ovale, quartan with P. malariae. P. falciparum is usually irregular and does NOT show a neat periodicity — do not wait for a pattern to treat.

patterns.description: Febrile days alternating with several afebrile days
patterns.suggests: Borrelia (louse- and tick-borne relapsing fever), rat-bite fever, malaria

patterns.description: Days to weeks of fever alternating with similar afebrile periods
Wide daily swings with rigors and sweats

associated_clues.suggests: Typhoid, brucellosis, legionella, yellow fever, drug fever
Measles, dengue, typhoid rose spots, meningococcaemia, drug reaction, rickettsial disease
ALWAYS take a travel history with dates and prevention — malaria until excluded

body.honest_caveat: Fever patterns are far less reliable in practice than in textbooks. fever medicine like paracetamols, antibiotics given before presentation, HIV, immunosuppression and mixed infection all flatten the pattern. Use the pattern as a hint that generates hypotheses, never as a diagnosis.

warnings: Never wait for a fever pattern to develop before treating suspected malaria or sepsis.
Paracetamol given before presentation destroys the pattern.
Falciparum malaria usually has NO regular periodicity — the absence of a tertian pattern does not exclude it.

flashcards.a: Classic typhoid, often with relative bradycardia
Hodgkin lymphoma

flashcards.q: Which malaria species give tertian fever?
flashcards.a: P. vivax and P. ovale (quartan is P. malariae)
Relative bradycardia with fever — typhoid, brucellosis, legionella, yellow fever

visuals.why_it_matters: The patterns are only recognisable when seen against each other

urine_colour_what_each_one_means.title: Urine Colour — What Each One Means
urine_colour_what_each_one_means.summary: Urine colour is a free bedside test. Ten colours, the causes behind each, and the ones that need action today.

terms: urine colour — what each one means

colours.causes: High fluid intake, diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, diuretics, CKD with loss of concentrating ability
Concentrated urine from dehydration; B vitamins
RIFAMPICIN (also stains tears and contact lenses), phenazopyridine, dehydration, bilirubin
BILIRUBINURIA (conjugated) — obstructive or hepatocellular jaundice. Froths yellow on shaking. Pale stools accompany it.

HAEMOGLOBINURIA or MYOGLOBINURIA. Think: blackwater fever in falciparum malaria, G6PD haemolysis, mismatched transfusion, RHABDOMYOLYSIS after crush injury or prolonged immobility, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (smoky brown). Dipstick positive for blood with NO red cells on microscopy = haemoglobin or myoglobin, not haematuria.
colours.action: Urgent — check renal function, potassium, creatine kinase; start fluids

colours.causes: HAEMATURIA — stones, infection, tumour, trauma, schistosomiasis, glomerulonephritis, anticoagulation. Also beetroot, rifampicin, senna, porphyria.
colours.action: Painless visible haematuria in an adult is urological cancer until excluded

colours.causes: Glomerular bleeding — red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells on microscopy
Chyluria — lymphatic obstruction, classically lymphatic filariasis
Methylene blue, propofol, amitriptyline, Pseudomonas infection, biliverdin
Not urine — the classic description of amoebic liver abscess pus

body.the_key_test: Dipstick positive for blood + microscopy shows NO red cells → haemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria. This single distinction separates a urological problem from a haemolytic or muscle-breakdown emergency.
always_ask: Any recent crush injury, prolonged lying, seizure or extreme exertion?
Any fever or recent malaria treatment?

warnings: Cola-coloured urine after crush injury, prolonged immobility or seizure is rhabdomyolysis — check creatine kinase and potassium and start fluids urgently.
Painless visible haematuria in an adult is a urological cancer until proven otherwise.
Blackwater fever (haemoglobinuria in falciparum malaria) signals severe disease.
Reassuring a patient because 'it is just rifampicin' without checking the drug chart is a recognised error.

flashcards.q: Dipstick blood positive but no red cells on microscopy?
flashcards.a: Haemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria — not haematuria

flashcards.q: Cola-coloured urine after a crush injury?
flashcards.a: Rhabdomyolysis — check CK and potassium, give fluids

flashcards.q: Which TB drug turns urine orange?
flashcards.a: Rifampicin — it also stains tears and contact lenses
Chyluria — classically lymphatic filariasis

visuals.why_it_matters: Colour is a bedside test that costs nothing and is routinely under-used

prescription_shorthand_bd_tds_stat_prn_a.title: Prescription Shorthand — BD, TDS, STAT, PRN and the Rest
prescription_shorthand_bd_tds_stat_prn_a.summary: Every abbreviation you will see on a drug chart, what it means, and the ones that are banned because they kill people.

terms: prescription shorthand — bd, tds, stat, prn and the rest

frequency.caution: ALSO means right eye (oculus dexter) and overdose — context matters
Also read as 'heart sounds' in notes

frequency.meaning: As required — MUST have an indication, a maximum dose and a minimum interval

route.caution: HIGH RISK — intrathecal chemotherapy errors have been fatal; separate checking procedures apply

orders.meaning: If needed (used interchangeably with PRN in some systems — clarify locally)

BANNED_ABBREVIATIONS.why: Misread as 0 or 4 — has caused ten-fold insulin overdoses and deaths
Misread as mg — a thousand-fold error
Confused with each other and with QID

BANNED_ABBREVIATIONS.do_not_write: Drug name abbreviations like AZT, MTX, HCT

body.prescription_minimum: Every prescription needs: patient identifiers, allergy status, drug GENERIC name, dose, units in full, route, frequency, start date, duration or review date, indication for PRN and antibiotics, and a legible signature with a printed name.

warnings: WRITE 'UNITS' IN FULL. The abbreviation 'U' misread as a zero has caused fatal ten-fold insulin overdoses.
Never use a trailing zero (1.0 mg) or a naked decimal (.5 mg).
MS is ambiguous between morphine sulfate and magnesium sulfate — write the name out.
Intrathecal prescriptions require separate, enhanced checking; errors here have been fatal.
Local abbreviation conventions differ — confirm against your facility's approved list.

flashcards.a: Three times daily
An indication, a maximum dose and a minimum interval

flashcards.q: Why must 'units' be written in full?
flashcards.a: 'U' misread as a zero has caused fatal ten-fold insulin overdoses
It is ambiguous between morphine sulfate and magnesium sulfate

checkboxes: Dose written clearly with no trailing zero or naked decimal
Start date and review or stop date
Indication recorded for PRN and antibiotics
Maximum dose and minimum interval stated for PRN

breathlessness_words_dyspnoea_orthopnoea.title: Breathlessness Words — Dyspnoea, Orthopnoea, PND and Others
breathlessness_words_dyspnoea_orthopnoea.summary: The words used to describe difficult breathing, each defined precisely, because each one points somewhere different.

terms: breathlessness words — dyspnoea, orthopnoea, pnd and others

terms.definition: The subjective sensation of uncomfortable or difficult breathing. It is what the PATIENT feels, not what you observe.
terms.note: Distinguish from tachypnoea (fast rate) and hyperpnoea (deep breathing) — those are observed.

terms.definition: Breathlessness brought on by physical effort
terms.note: QUANTIFY it: how many metres on the flat, how many stairs, compared with six months ago

terms.definition: Breathlessness on LYING FLAT, relieved by sitting up
terms.note: Quantify by pillows. Mechanism: increased venous return and redistribution of pulmonary blood volume plus the diaphragm being pushed up. Causes: left heart failure, large pleural effusion, massive ascites, obesity, diaphragmatic paralysis.

terms.definition: Waking from sleep, usually 1–3 hours in, gasping and needing to sit up or go to a window
terms.note: More specific for left heart failure than orthopnoea. Ask directly — patients rarely volunteer it.

terms.definition: Breathlessness in one lateral position but not the other
terms.note: Unilateral lung disease, large unilateral effusion, or a mediastinal mass

terms.definition: Breathlessness on SITTING UP, relieved by lying flat — the opposite of orthopnoea
terms.note: Rare and specific. Hepatopulmonary syndrome, intracardiac shunt, arteriovenous malformation. Often paired with orthodeoxia (desaturation on sitting up).

terms.definition: Respiratory rate above normal for age
terms.note: An OBSERVED sign. Adult >20/min. Age-specific in children — it is the single most useful sign in childhood pneumonia.
Kussmaul breathing in metabolic acidosis is deep and sighing

terms.definition: Cyclical crescendo-decrescendo breathing with apnoeic pauses
terms.note: Heart failure, stroke, raised intracranial pressure, high altitude, end of life
Severe metabolic acidosis — DKA, uraemia, salicylate poisoning

terms.definition: Harsh noise from UPPER airway narrowing, usually inspiratory
terms.note: An airway emergency until proven otherwise

terms.definition: Musical noise from LOWER airway narrowing, usually expiratory
terms.note: A silent chest in known asthma is worse than a wheezy one

nyha_functional_class.description: Slight limitation — comfortable at rest, ordinary activity causes symptoms
Marked limitation — less than ordinary activity causes symptoms
Symptoms at rest, unable to carry out any physical activity without discomfort

warnings: Stridor is an upper airway emergency — do not sit and observe.
A silent chest in asthma means the patient is not moving enough air to wheeze; it is a pre-terminal sign.
PND must be asked about directly; patients rarely offer it spontaneously.
Always quantify exertional dyspnoea in metres or stairs and compare with a previous baseline.

flashcards.a: Breathlessness lying flat, relieved by sitting up — quantify by pillows
Waking 1–3 hours into sleep gasping, needing to sit up — more specific for left heart failure
Breathlessness on sitting up, relieved by lying flat — hepatopulmonary syndrome, intracardiac shunt
Severe metabolic acidosis — deep sighing respiration
Marked limitation — less than ordinary activity causes symptoms

counselling_the_gather_approach.title: Counselling — The GATHER Approach
counselling_the_gather_approach.summary: A structure for any counselling conversation, with a worked example. Counselling is a clinical skill with steps, not a personality trait.

terms: greet ask tell help explain return

do: Greet warmly and by name
Introduce yourself and your role
Ensure privacy and seating at the same level
State how long you have
Confirm confidentiality
gather.say: 'Good morning. I'm Dr ___. We have about fifteen minutes. Whatever we discuss stays between us.'

do: Ask open questions first
Find out what they already know
Find out what they are worried about
Ask about their circumstances — who is at home, what they can afford, what they can get to
LISTEN more than you talk
gather.say: 'What have you already been told about this? What worries you most?'

do: Give information in small chunks
Use plain words, no jargon
Prioritise what they need to know NOW
Be honest about uncertainty
Use pictures or written material where possible
gather.say: Chunk and check: give one piece, then pause.

do: Lay out the real options including doing nothing
Give balanced pros and cons
Ask what matters most to them
Support their decision even if it is not what you would choose
Do not decide for them, and do not pretend there is no choice when there is
gather.say: 'Which of these feels most possible for you?'

do: Explain exactly what to do: dose, timing, how long
Explain what side effects to expect and which need urgent review
Explain what to do if a dose is missed
TEACH-BACK: ask them to say it back in their own words
Write it down or give a card
gather.say: 'Just so I know I explained it well — tell me how you'll take this.'

do: Give a specific return date
Say clearly what should bring them back sooner
Give a contact route
Confirm they can get there and afford it
Document what was discussed and agreed
gather.say: 'Come back in two weeks. But come immediately if any of these happen.'

worked_example_contraception.greet: Private room, seated, confidentiality stated, partner asked to wait unless the woman wants him present.
worked_example_contraception.ask: What she knows, what she has used, what she has heard from others, whether she wants more children and when, breastfeeding status, whether her partner knows, whether she can attend for repeat visits.
worked_example_contraception.tell: Realistic options for her situation: implant, injectable, IUCD, pills, condoms, LAM, permanent methods. Effectiveness in plain terms, duration, and how quickly fertility returns.
worked_example_contraception.help: Weigh what she said mattered — discretion, duration, return to fertility, bleeding pattern, cost, travel distance.
worked_example_contraception.explain: How to use it, what bleeding change to expect, which side effects are normal and which need review, and that no method except condoms protects against sexually transmitted infection. Teach-back.
worked_example_contraception.return: Follow-up date; red flags; where to come if she wants it removed or changed.

breaking_bad_news_spikes: S — SETTING: privacy, seated, no interruptions, someone with them if they wish
P — PERCEPTION: find out what they already understand
I — INVITATION: ask how much they want to know
K — KNOWLEDGE: warning shot, then the news in plain words, then silence
E — EMPATHY: name the emotion, allow silence, do not rush to fix it
S — STRATEGY and SUMMARY: what happens next, who to contact, written information, follow-up
cross_cutting: Use the language the patient is most comfortable in; use a trained interpreter, not a family member, where possible.
Check literacy before handing over written material.
Never counsel about an intimate matter with a family member present unless the patient asks for it.
Document that counselling took place, what was covered, and that understanding was checked.

flashcards.a: Greet, Ask, Tell, Help them choose, Explain, Return
Asking the patient to explain the plan back in their own words to check your explanation worked
Breaking bad news — Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Empathy, Strategy

checkboxes: Information given in chunks, in plain language
Options laid out including doing nothing
Side effects and red flags explained
Return date and red flags given

visuals.must_show: GATHER as a six-step circular flow with the key question for each step
visuals.why_it_matters: Counselling is a sequence; showing it as a loop makes the return step visible

surgical_and_bedside_landmarks_that_chan.title: Surgical and Bedside Landmarks That Change Decisions
surgical_and_bedside_landmarks_that_chan.summary: The anatomical landmarks you actually use to decide where to cut, where to put a needle, and what a finding means.

terms: surgical and bedside landmarks that change decisions

landmarks.why_it_matters: Reference point for JVP measurement; level of the carina, aortic arch and start/end of the aortic arch; second costal cartilage attaches here — count ribs from it
THE discriminator between inguinal (above and medial) and femoral (below and lateral) hernia

landmarks.where: One third along a line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus
landmarks.why_it_matters: Point of maximal tenderness in appendicitis; classic incision site
THE anatomical divider between UPPER and LOWER gastrointestinal bleeding. Bleeding above it presents as haematemesis and melaena; below it as haematochezia.

landmarks.where: Bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi, a horizontal line at about the 5th intercostal space, with the apex below the axilla
landmarks.why_it_matters: Insertion outside it risks the liver, spleen, heart and long thoracic nerve
Always pass a needle or drain OVER the top of the rib — the intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in the groove beneath each rib
The only complete tracheal ring; level of cricoid pressure, of the start of the oesophagus, and of the first oesophageal constriction

Divides the anal canal. ABOVE: visceral innervation, painless, internal haemorrhoids, portal venous drainage, columnar epithelium. BELOW: somatic innervation, PAINFUL, external haemorrhoids and fissures, systemic drainage, squamous epithelium. This is why internal piles are painless and fissures are agonising.

landmarks.where: Bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the inferior border of the liver
landmarks.why_it_matters: Contains the cystic artery; the critical view of safety in cholecystectomy is achieved here. Misidentification causes bile duct injury.

landmarks.where: Bounded by the inferior epigastric vessels, the lateral border of rectus, and the inguinal ligament
landmarks.why_it_matters: DIRECT inguinal hernias pass through it; indirect hernias pass lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels
Pylorus, fundus of gallbladder, neck of pancreas, hila of kidneys, origin of superior mesenteric artery
Intraosseous access site; reference for McBurney's point and for the inguinal ligament
Posterior tibial pulse; the pulse most often recorded as absent because it was sought in the wrong place
Normal apex beat position; displacement means cardiomegaly or mediastinal shift

warnings: Always pass chest drains and needles over the SUPERIOR border of the rib.
Bleeding above the ligament of Treitz is upper GI; below it is lower GI — this determines the whole workup.
Misidentifying structures in Calot's triangle is the mechanism of bile duct injury in cholecystectomy.

flashcards.q: Which landmark separates upper from lower GI bleeding?
flashcards.a: The ligament of Treitz
The pubic tubercle — inguinal above and medial, femoral below and lateral
They arise above the dentate line, which has visceral (not somatic) innervation
The cystic artery

visuals.why_it_matters: Five landmarks that between them cover most bedside procedural decisions

glucose_pathways_where_sugar_comes_from_.title: Glucose Pathways — Where Sugar Comes From and Goes
glucose_pathways_where_sugar_comes_from_.summary: Glycolysis, glycogen, gluconeogenesis and ketones, explained as a single connected story, then mapped onto the drugs and diseases that break each step.

terms: glucose pathways — where sugar comes from and goes

body.the_story: Between meals, the body must keep blood glucose steady for the brain and red cells. It does this in three stages, each with a longer time horizon: first it breaks down stored glycogen (hours), then it makes new glucose from other molecules (a day or more), then it switches most tissues to burning fat and makes ketones so that the little remaining glucose is reserved for the brain.

stages.what_happens: Glucose is taken into muscle and fat via GLUT4, stored as glycogen and converted to fat. Lipolysis is suppressed.
stages.fails_when: Type 1 diabetes (no insulin), severe insulin resistance

stages.what_happens: GLYCOGENOLYSIS — liver glycogen is broken down to glucose. Liver glycogen lasts roughly 12–24 hours.
stages.fails_when: Alcohol-related starvation, liver failure, glycogen storage diseases. THIS is why glucagon does not work in a starved alcoholic — the store is empty.

stages.what_happens: GLUCONEOGENESIS — new glucose made from lactate (Cori cycle), glycerol (from fat breakdown) and amino acids (mainly alanine from muscle). Note that fatty acids CANNOT be converted to glucose.
stages.fails_when: Liver failure, adrenal insufficiency, some inborn errors

stages.what_happens: Massive lipolysis → free fatty acids → beta-oxidation → acetyl-CoA in excess of what the Krebs cycle can accept → KETOGENESIS producing beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate. Ketones fuel the brain and spare protein.
stages.fails_when: When insulin deficiency is total, ketogenesis runs unchecked → DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS

body.why_dka_happens: Insulin deficiency does two things at once: glucose cannot enter cells (hyperglycaemia, osmotic diuresis, dehydration) AND lipolysis is unrestrained (ketogenesis, acidosis). That is why treatment must address fluid, insulin and potassium together, and why insulin must continue until the ketones clear even after the glucose has fallen.

drug_and_disease_map.targeted_by: Sulfonylureas (close K-ATP channel), GLP-1 agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors

drug_and_disease_map.stimulated_by: GLUCAGON — only works if glycogen stores exist

clinical_hooks: Alcohol inhibits gluconeogenesis — hence hypoglycaemia in a starved drinker, where glucagon will fail and glucose is needed.
Fatty acids cannot make glucose — which is why fat stores do not prevent hypoglycaemia in prolonged starvation.
Lactate rises when tissues run anaerobically; the Cori cycle recycles it in the liver, so liver failure worsens lactic acidosis.
Euglycaemic DKA on SGLT2 inhibitors happens because glucose is being excreted while insulin is still too low to stop ketogenesis.

flashcards.q: Why does glucagon fail in a starved alcoholic?
flashcards.a: Hepatic glycogen stores are depleted and alcohol also inhibits gluconeogenesis

flashcards.q: Can fatty acids be converted to glucose?
flashcards.a: No — this is why fat stores do not prevent hypoglycaemia in starvation
Reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis

flashcards.q: Why must insulin continue in DKA after glucose normalises?
flashcards.a: Glucose falls before ketogenesis stops — add dextrose and keep the insulin running

visuals.must_show: Single connected diagram: fed state to starvation across four panels, showing which pathway dominates and which hormone drives it
visuals.why_it_matters: Learning these as four separate pathways is why students find it hard; it is one continuous story
visuals.alt_text: Single connected diagram: fed state to starvation across four panels, showing which pathway dominates and which hormone drives it

samples_container_transport_and_why_they.title: Samples — Container, Transport and Why They Get Rejected
samples_container_transport_and_why_they.summary: For each common sample: what container, how much, how fast it must reach the laboratory, and the reasons samples come back rejected.

terms: samples — container, transport and why they get rejected

specimens.volume: Adult 8–10 mL PER BOTTLE — volume is the single biggest determinant of yield. Paediatric volumes are weight-based.
specimens.timing: BEFORE antibiotics, if this does not delay treatment in sepsis
specimens.technique: Skin antisepsis and allow to dry fully; disinfect bottle tops; ideally two sets from separate sites
specimens.rejected_if: Under-filled, contaminated, wrong bottles, delayed to incubator

specimens.container: Sterile universal (boric acid container if delay expected)
specimens.timing: To the laboratory within 2 hours, or refrigerate
specimens.technique: Clean, mid-stream, discard first and last portion
specimens.rejected_if: Delayed at room temperature (overgrowth), obvious contamination, leaking container

specimens.volume: At least 2–5 mL of purulent material
specimens.timing: Early morning is best; keep cool and transport promptly
specimens.technique: Deep cough from the chest, NOT saliva. Rinse mouth first. Collect in a ventilated area or outdoors with infection control.
specimens.rejected_if: Saliva rather than sputum, insufficient volume, leaking

specimens.container: Sterile universals, numbered in order of collection
specimens.volume: About 1 mL per tube; more if TB or cytology suspected
specimens.timing: IMMEDIATELY — cells lyse and glucose falls with delay. Never refrigerate samples for meningococcal culture.
specimens.technique: Send paired blood glucose at the same time. Note opening pressure.
specimens.rejected_if: Delay, wrong tube order, insufficient volume, clotted

specimens.container: Charcoal transport swab; ideally ASPIRATED PUS in a sterile container
specimens.technique: Pus in a syringe beats a swab every time. Sample the base of a debrided wound, not the surface slough.

specimens.container: Sterile container; specific media for cholera or parasites
specimens.timing: Prompt; three separate samples for parasites
specimens.technique: Avoid urine and toilet water contamination
specimens.rejected_if: Contaminated with urine or water, delayed

specimens.volume: Formalin at least 10 times the tissue volume
specimens.technique: ORIENT the specimen with a suture or diagram and say so on the form. Never put tissue for culture into formalin. Never send fresh tissue without discussing with the laboratory.
specimens.rejected_if: Inadequate fixative, no orientation, unlabelled, dried out

specimens.technique: HAND-LABEL AT THE BEDSIDE at the moment of draw, against the patient's identity band. This is not bureaucracy — it is the control that prevents fatal ABO-incompatible transfusion.
specimens.rejected_if: ANY labelling discrepancy — and it should be. Do not argue with the blood bank about this.

top_rejection_reasons: Request form and sample do not match
Haemolysed (drawn through too fine a needle, shaken, or prolonged tourniquet)
No clinical details on the form
body.clinical_details_matter: A microbiology form with no clinical details gets a generic panel. A form saying 'immunosuppressed, 3 weeks fever, recent travel, on antibiotics' gets the right tests. The form is part of the test.

warnings: Blood culture volume is the single biggest determinant of yield — under-filling wastes the test.
Never put tissue intended for culture into formalin; it kills the organisms.
Label transfusion samples by hand, at the bedside, at the time of draw. No exceptions.
Haemolysed samples give falsely raised potassium — a common cause of a spurious 'critical' result and inappropriate treatment.

flashcards.q: Adult blood culture volume per bottle?
flashcards.a: 8–10 mL — volume is the main determinant of yield
Cells lyse and glucose falls with delay
Aspirated pus in a sterile container is always better

flashcards.q: Commonest cause of a spuriously high potassium?
flashcards.a: Haemolysis of the sample

checkboxes: Patient identity confirmed at the bedside
Request form matches the sample exactly
Clinical details and antibiotic history written on the form
Transport arranged within the required window
Cold chain or ambient requirement respected

unit_converter_lab_results_and_measureme.title: Unit Converter — Lab Results and Measurements
unit_converter_lab_results_and_measureme.summary: Change any common lab result or measurement from one unit to another. Includes glucose, creatinine, urea, bilirubin, haemoglobin, HbA1c, weight, height and temperature.

terms: unit converter — lab results and measurements

body.the_one_rule: There is NO single mg/dL to mmol/L conversion. The number you divide by depends on the SUBSTANCE, because it comes from its molecular weight. Glucose divides by 18. Creatinine multiplies by 88.4. Bilirubin multiplies by 17.1. Using the wrong one gives a confidently wrong answer, so Scout gives you a table, not a single box.
body.note_on_glucose_units: Glucose is reported in mg/dL or mmol/L, not g/dL. g/dL is used for haemoglobin and albumin. If a glucose result comes back in g/dL, query it with the laboratory before acting on it.

lab_conversions.note: Glucose is reported in mg/dL or mmol/L — NOT g/dL. If you see g/dL on a glucose result, query it.
Mixing these two up is a common cause of a wrong drug dose, because Cockcroft-Gault uses different constants for each unit.
BUN measures the NITROGEN only; urea measures the whole molecule. They are not the same quantity, which is why the factor is 2.8 and not 6.
Newborn phototherapy charts differ by country in which unit they use — check the chart before plotting.
Some labs report mEq/L: mmol/L × 2 = mEq/L for calcium, because it is divalent.
Different factor from cholesterol — do not reuse the 38.67.
THIS is the one measured in g/dL. Some labs use mmol/L for haemoglobin (× 0.6206 from g/dL) — rare, but check the unit on the report.

anchors: 4.0 g/dL = 40 g/L (reference point for corrected calcium)
lab_conversions.note: Corrected-calcium formulas differ depending on which albumin unit you use.
Also reported in mEq/L: mmol/L × 2 = mEq/L (divalent).
For these SINGLY charged ions mEq/L and mmol/L are numerically identical. For calcium and magnesium (double charge) they are NOT — divide mEq by 2.
Two entirely different scales, not a simple multiplication. Nigeria mostly reports %, the UK reports mmol/mol.

other_conversions.note: Weigh in kg. Drug doses in Nigeria are prescribed per kg.
Needed for BMI, BSA and lung-protective tidal volume.
Blood gases are reported in kPa in some labs and mmHg in others. PaO2 of 60 mmHg = 8 kPa.
Ventilator pressures are cmH2O; CVP may be either — check.
See the IV fluid drip rate card.
Write 'microgram' in full. 'mcg' misread as 'mg' is a 1000-fold overdose.
1% lidocaine = 10 mg/mL. 0.9% saline = 9 mg/mL sodium chloride. 50% dextrose = 500 mg/mL. This is the one that catches people out.
Adrenaline. 1:1000 is the IM ampoule; 1:10,000 is the pre-filled cardiac arrest syringe. Giving 1:1000 intravenously by mistake has killed patients.

warnings: Check which unit YOUR laboratory reports before converting. Mixing units mid-calculation is one of the commonest ways a dose goes wrong.
Percent solutions catch people out. 1% means 1 gram in 100 mL, which is 10 mg/mL. So 50% dextrose is 500 mg/mL, and 2% lidocaine is 20 mg/mL.
Adrenaline 1:1000 is 1 mg/mL and is the INTRAMUSCULAR ampoule. Adrenaline 1:10,000 is 0.1 mg/mL and is the cardiac arrest syringe. Giving 1:1000 into a vein by mistake has killed patients.
Write microgram in full. 'mcg' misread as 'mg' is a thousand-fold overdose.
HbA1c percent and mmol/mol are two different scales, not a simple multiplication.

flashcards.a: Divide by 18
Multiply by 88.4
10 mg/mL — so 50% dextrose is 500 mg/mL
1 mg/mL — the IM ampoule
No — mg/dL or mmol/L. g/dL is for haemoglobin and albumin.

governance.nigeria_overlay: Most Nigerian laboratories report glucose in mg/dL and creatinine in mg/dL. Confirm your own laboratory's units and set them as the default in Scout settings.
